---

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** County Cork was established as an administrative county in 1606 under English colonial reorganization, within the province of Munster.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Cork City
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Munster, Ireland (under the Crown of Great Britain and Ireland during this period)
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for County Cork in this date range; no figures can be reported from tool results. County Cork was one of Ireland's most populous counties before the Great Famine and experienced severe population loss from 1845 onward through death and emigration.
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural (tillage and pasture); butter trade through Cork City was significant. The Famine devastated the rural subsistence farming population.
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly Irish Catholic, with a Protestant Anglo-Irish landed class and urban merchant community.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Church of Ireland (Anglican); Presbyterian; Quaker communities in Cork City.
- **Key historical events:** The Tithe War (1830s, affecting record creation in Tithe Applotment Books); the Great Famine (1845-1852, driving mass emigration through Cobh/Queenstown); pre-Famine population pressure on smallholdings.

## Boundary changes

County Cork's boundaries were stable during the 1830s-1840s. It is the largest county in Ireland by area. It was divided into two ridings (North and South) for administrative purposes, each with its own quarter sessions court. These riding-level divisions can affect where some court and grand jury records are filed. No formation event or boundary change occurred within the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy, civil registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did not begin until **1 January 1864 (national/statewide level)**. Non-Catholic (predominantly Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from **1845 (national level)**. There are therefore **no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1830s-1840s** for Catholic families, and none for births or deaths for any family. Civil vital records are entirely outside the target window for Catholic families, and cover only non-Catholic marriages from 1845.
- **What exists:** Non-Catholic marriage registers from 1845 onward are held by the General Register Office (GRO), Dublin. Nothing else in civil registration covers this period.
- **Where held:** GRO, Werburgh Street, Dublin; indexes searchable online at IrishGenealogy.ie.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only primary source for this period for all families (see below).

### Church records

Church records are the **core primary source** for the 1830s-1840s in County Cork for all families.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (majority of population); Church of Ireland (Anglican); Presbyterian; Quaker.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (the primary birth substitute), marriages, and occasionally burial registers. Confirmation records are a separate dated event and may appear in some Cork RC registers. Church of Ireland vestry and burial records also survive for some parishes.
- **Roman Catholic registers:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), survival varies widely by parish; many Cork RC parishes begin in the 1810s-1830s, though some are later or have gaps. The **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** holds digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880 and provides free online access. These are the principal online source for this period.
- **Church of Ireland registers:** Held by the **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)**, Dublin, and in some local custody. Many were deposited in the Public Record Office before 1922 and were destroyed in the Four Courts fire (see Record Losses below); survivors are at the RCBL.
- **Language:** English (Church of Ireland); Latin mixed with English or Irish (Roman Catholic, depending on period and parish).
- **Where held:** National Library of Ireland online (RC registers to 1880); Representative Church Body Library (Church of Ireland survivors); local parish custody for some.

### Census records

- **Situation in the 1830s-1840s:** Ireland conducted national censuses in 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), most pre-1901 census returns were destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire**. The 1841 and 1851 returns — the ones covering this period — are almost entirely lost as a result.
- **Surviving fragments:** Some 1821 and 1831 fragments survive for specific parishes; their Cork coverage is not confirmed by the tool results returned in this survey.
- **Census substitutes (critical for this period):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837):** Lists occupiers of tithe-liable agricultural land by townland. A major census substitute for the 1830s target period. Cork volumes exist and are available online through the Irish Genealogy website (askaboutireland.ie) and FamilySearch. Landless laborers, cottiers, and urban dwellers are generally not included.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s):** Published surveys listing every householder and their landholdings. The single most important substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses. Available free online at askaboutireland.ie and valuation.ie. Covers the immediate post-Famine period and is the closest surviving snapshot to the 1840s.
- **State of digitization:** Both census substitutes are indexed and searchable online — effectively indexed + images for Griffith's Valuation; Tithe Applotment Books are browsable and partially indexed online.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, grants of probate, administrations, guardianships. Also grand jury presentments (public works, local taxation) and quarter sessions records (assizes, petty crime, evictions).
- **Probate jurisdiction:** Pre-1858, probate in Ireland was handled by ecclesiastical courts (Prerogative Court of Armagh for larger estates; diocesan courts for smaller). After the Probate Act 1857, District Probate Registries were established. For the 1830s-1840s, the relevant courts were the diocesan Consistorial Courts.
- **Record loss:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), the 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed a large portion of pre-1900 wills and probate records. The National Archives of Ireland (NAI) holds what survives, and pre-destruction indexes (will books, grant books) allow some reconstruction.
- **Grand jury and quarter sessions records:** Held at the NAI and Cork City and County Archives (CCCA). These name individuals involved in road maintenance, poor relief, and petty crime — useful for placing ordinary people who appear in no other record.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland (Dublin); Cork City and County Archives (Cork City).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey; land was described by townland, which is Ireland's smallest civil division).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land tenure in 1830s-1840s Cork was largely a landlord-tenant system. Land grants and patents from the original plantation period are older records. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) does not specify a particular grants office for this period in the tool results returned.
- **Types available for this period:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837):** See Census section. Indexed + images online.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** See Census section. Indexed + images online.
  - **Registry of Deeds:** Property transfers recorded centrally in Dublin from 1708. Memorials (abstracts) of Cork deeds are held at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin, and are partially indexed. Physical access or microfilm required for many deeds.
  - **Estate records:** Records of the major Cork landed estates (rent rolls, tenant lists, eviction notices) are held at the NAI, the National Library of Ireland, and CCCA. Survival is inconsistent.
- **Where held:** Registry of Deeds (Dublin); National Archives of Ireland; Cork City and County Archives; National Library of Ireland.

### Military records

- **Relevant context:** British Army service is the primary military record source. Militia muster rolls and pension records for men who served in the British Army are held at The National Archives (Kew, UK) and are partially available on Ancestry and Findmypast. Ireland had no separate national army in this period (it was part of the United Kingdom).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls; pension files (Royal Hospital Kilmainham pensioners, held at NAI); attestation papers at TNA Kew.
- **Where held:** The National Archives, Kew (British Army records); National Archives of Ireland (Kilmainham pensioners).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Finbarr's Cemetery (Cork City); numerous rural churchyard burial grounds throughout the county; Church of Ireland churchyards with surviving registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) is the major online index; coverage for rural Cork parishes in the 1830s-1840s will be variable and should be verified against local transcription projects.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held locally. Church burial registers for Church of Ireland parishes (where not destroyed) are at the RCBL. Roman Catholic burial registers are rare for this period — baptism and marriage registers are far more complete than burial registers in Irish RC practice.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers in this period:** The Cork Examiner (founded 1841) and earlier papers such as the Cork Constitution and Cork Chronicle. These carried notices of deaths, marriages, and legal matters, as well as accounts of evictions and local events during the Famine.
- **Where held:** Cork City Library holds historical Cork newspaper runs. The British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) includes some Irish provincial titles. The Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com) covers some titles.
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate sales, tenant evictions), and shipping intelligence (departing emigrant vessels) are most valuable for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records

This is a critical category for an ancestor who emigrated from Cork in the 1830s-1840s.

- **Relevant ports:** Cork was a major embarkation point. The primary port was **Cobh** (then called Queenstown from 1849; known as Cove of Cork before that). Liverpool was also used as a transit point for emigrants from Cork bound for North America.
- **Passenger lists:** Arrivals into US ports are the best-documented series. Manifests from the 1820s-1840s (pre-1891 era) list name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin; they do not yet give specific townland or county of origin, which limits their utility for placing a person within Cork. From 1895 onward, manifests ask for last residence, which is far more specific.
- **Famine-era emigration:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), Famine-era passenger manifests from Cork ports list complete family groups, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — do not assume only the head of household is listed.
- **Where held:** US arrival manifests (1820-1957) are at NARA and available through Ancestry and FamilySearch. The Ellis Island database covers 1892-1957; earlier arrivals require searching by port (New York, Boston, Quebec, Liverpool).
- **Departure records from Irish ports:** Less complete than US arrival manifests. Some Cork port records survive; the NAI and the Cobh Heritage Centre hold related materials.

### Tax records

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837):** The primary tax-based census substitute (see Land records and Census sections). Lists occupiers of land by townland. Available indexed and with images online.
- **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** Not strictly a tax record, but a valuation survey used as the basis for taxation; functions as the best census substitute for the period immediately following the 1840s target window.
- **Grand jury cess and presentments:** Lists of persons responsible for local road and infrastructure taxes appear in grand jury records at the NAI and CCCA.
- **Substitute value:** Tax-based records are the primary substitutes for the destroyed census for this period.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law Union records (from 1838):** The Irish Poor Law Act 1838 established Poor Law Unions and workhouses throughout Ireland, including multiple unions in County Cork (Cork, Bandon, Bantry, Clonakilty, Fermoy, Kanturk, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Midleton, Millstreet, Mitchelstown, Skibbereen, and others). Workhouse admission and discharge registers, outdoor relief lists, and minute books name the poorest stratum of society and are held at the NAI and CCCA. These are particularly valuable for Famine-era research (1845 onward) and begin in 1838 — entirely within the target window.
- **Church of Ireland vestry records:** Record local parish taxation and accounts; some survive for Cork parishes.
- **Estate papers and agent correspondence:** Letters between Cork landlords and their land agents sometimes name tenants by name and townland; held at the NLI, NAI, and CCCA.
- **Local and county histories:** 19th-century published histories of Cork (e.g., Smith's History of Cork) name prominent families and sometimes reprint earlier records; accessible through larger library collections.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections relevant to this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (nli.ie) | RC parish registers (baptisms/marriages) to 1880 — free online | Free |
| IrishGenealogy.ie | RC and Church of Ireland registers; civil registration from 1845/1864 | Free |
| askaboutireland.ie | Griffith's Valuation; Tithe Applotment Books; 1901/1911 censuses | Free |
| valuation.ie | Griffith's Valuation full images and maps | Free |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Ireland record collections; Tithe Applotment Books; some parish register microfilm | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Ireland church record collections; British Army records; US arrival manifests | Subscription |
| Findmypast (findmypast.com) | Irish Catholic parish registers; Irish newspapers; British Army records | Subscription |
| British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) | Historical Cork newspaper runs | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The external_links_search tool did not return Cork-specific curated collection links — the standardPlace field in the response was empty, indicating the place was not resolved for that tool. The repositories listed above are drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki pages returned in this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) and cross-referenced with the actual content of those pages. No FamilySearch collection IDs or digitized volume counts can be reported from tool results for County Cork specifically.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin (nationalarchives.ie) | Surviving census fragments; wills and probate records; estate records; Poor Law Union records; court records | In-person; some online catalog |
| Cork City and County Archives (corkarchives.ie) | Grand jury records; Poor Law Union records; local estate papers; some church records | In-person; written inquiry |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin (ireland.anglican.org/about/rcb-library) | Surviving Church of Ireland registers (post-1922 fire survivors) | In-person; appointment required |
| General Register Office, Dublin | Civil registration records from 1845 (non-Catholic marriages) and 1864 (all events) | In-person; online index at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| Registry of Deeds, Dublin (landregistry.ie) | Property transfer memorials from 1708 onward | In-person; partial index |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK (nationalarchives.gov.uk) | British Army service and pension records | In-person; online through Ancestry/Findmypast |
| Cobh Heritage Centre (cobhheritage.com) | Emigration records; Famine-era departure records | In-person; contact for inquiry |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Registry of Deeds memorials (most pre-1850s Cork deeds):** Partially indexed; original memorials require a visit to the Registry of Deeds, Dublin, or access to microfilm.
- **Grand jury and quarter sessions records:** Largely physical only at NAI and CCCA.
- **Estate papers and agent correspondence:** Physically held at NLI, NAI, and CCCA; not systematically indexed or digitized.
- **Many Church of Ireland parish burial registers:** Those not destroyed in 1922 are held at RCBL and require in-person or written access.
- **Poor Law Union workhouse admission registers:** Partially digitized for some Cork unions; others are physical only at CCCA or NAI.
- **Cork departure records (pre-Famine passenger lists from Cork ports):** Less well digitized than US arrival manifests; physical or microfilm access often required.

---

## Known record losses

Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy): The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed the following:

- Most pre-1901 Irish census returns, including the 1841 and 1851 returns that would have directly covered the target period for County Cork.
- A large portion of pre-1900 wills and probate records held by the Public Record Office.
- Many Church of Ireland parish registers that had been deposited in the Public Record Office.

The Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, RC parish registers held by the NLI, and Registry of Deeds records survived because they were not held at the Four Courts. These form the surviving framework for pre-Famine Cork research.

---

## Research tips

All claims below are drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy.

- **Start with Griffith's Valuation, then work backward.** Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s) is the closest surviving snapshot to the 1840s and names every householder. Use it to confirm a family's townland before searching the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) for the same townland earlier in the decade. A townland match across both sources is strong evidence of place of residence.
- **Identify the Roman Catholic parish, not just the civil county.** Irish RC registers are organized by parish, not by civil townland or barony. The civil divisions (barony, civil parish, townland) and the RC parish do not align. Once you have a townland from Griffith's or the Tithe Books, use John Grenham's "Tracing Your Irish Ancestors" or the IrishGenealogy.ie parish finder to identify which RC parish served that townland.
- **Civil registration did not begin for Catholic vital events until 1864.** No civil birth, death, or marriage certificate will exist for a Catholic family's events in the 1830s-1840s. Church records are the only primary source for vital events in this period.
- **Non-Catholic marriages were registered from 1845.** If your ancestor was Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, or another Protestant denomination, a marriage register entry may survive from 1845 onward at the GRO (indexed at IrishGenealogy.ie).
- **Check the passenger manifests for the whole family, not just the emigrant.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki, Famine-era manifests from Cork ports list complete family groups including infants. Even a child too young to be a research subject may appear — and can confirm a family unit.
- **Poor Law Union records begin in 1838 and are a rich source for the 1840s.** Cork had over a dozen Poor Law Unions. Workhouse admissions, relief lists, and minute books name the poorest residents — people who often appear in no church or land record. CCCA and NAI hold these.
- **Irish naming customs:** Irish families in this period frequently named children after grandparents. The FamilySearch Wiki page returned for Ireland Naming Customs resolved to the same general page and did not return specific naming pattern guidance; consult a dedicated Irish naming customs source before assuming which relative a child's name references.
- **Landless laborers and cottiers do not appear in the Tithe Applotment Books.** The Tithe Books record only occupiers of tithe-liable land. A rural laborer without a lease would not appear, even if he lived and worked in that townland throughout the 1830s.
- **Search neighboring counties for family connections.** County Cork borders Kerry (west), Limerick (north), Tipperary (northeast), and Waterford (east). Families near those borders may have generated records on both sides. The neighboring county wiki pages were not individually retrieved in this survey, so specific cross-border repository guidance should be sought from each county's own locality guide.

---

County Cork in the 1830s-1840s has no civil birth, marriage, or death records for Catholic families — that period sits entirely before civil registration began. The surviving records are centered on Roman Catholic parish registers (free online through the National Library of Ireland), the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837), Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s), and Poor Law Union records beginning in 1838. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the census returns that would have covered this period, making the land surveys and parish registers the essential research framework. If your ancestor emigrated during or after the Famine, a passenger manifest into a US or Canadian port is likely the next document to locate, and it will list the entire family group including young children.

The most productive next step would be identifying the specific townland your ancestor came from — using Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books — because nearly every other Cork record type is organized by townland or RC parish rather than by county.

# Locality Guide: Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, Slovenia (c. 1812)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Village:** Javorje, a small hamlet in the Škofja Loka district (Gorenjska / Upper Carniola region)
- **Historical name:** The area was part of the Duchy of **Carniola** (German: *Krain*), a Habsburg crown land; Škofja Loka = German *Bischoflack*
- **In 1812 specifically:** The area was under French control as part of the **Illyrian Provinces** (1809–1813); Habsburg rule was restored in 1813
- **Ecclesiastical authority:** Archdiocese of Ljubljana (*Archidiocesis Labacensis*)
- **Language of records:** Latin; tabular-format registers introduced 1770, revised 1784

## The Primary Record: Catholic Parish Marriage Register

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Berkshire County was established in 1761 in far western Massachusetts, bordering New York State to the west and Vermont to the north, with Pittsfield as the county seat. The county's position on two state lines is directly relevant to your research strategy (see tips below).

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

This is the most important section for your question. Massachusetts has a **distinctive two-tier system**:

- **Town-level recording (1639 onward):** Births, marriages, and deaths were ordered recorded as early as 1639. For 1820–1850, originals are held by the clerk of the *individual town* — **not** at the county level.
- **Statewide registration began in 1841:** Massachusetts was the first state to create a permanent statewide system. Both town and state copies exist from 1841 onward, but the town record is the authoritative original.
- **Marriage intentions:** Commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with additional entries possible in the groom's home town and the couple's current residence — search all three.

**Where to look:**
| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| Published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to the Year 1850"** series — transcriptions of original town records, indexed by name; exists for 200+ Massachusetts towns | NEHGS, WorldCat, interlibrary loan |
| **FamilySearch collection 2061550** — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (indexed) | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **FamilySearch image group 004500891** — Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850 (512 images, **browse-only, no name index**) | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) — statewide registration copies from 1841 | In-person / finding aids online |
| Individual town clerks — original records from 1639 | In-person or mail request |

---

## Church Records

Church registers are **primary sources for 1820–1840 vital events**, especially where town compliance was uneven:

- **FamilySearch collection 1921657** — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (indexed statewide)
- **FamilySearch image group 004500892** — Congregational Church Records, Pittsfield, 1791–1850 (274 images, **browse-only, no name index**)
- Records of other denominations and other Berkshire County towns are mostly not yet digitized to FamilySearch volumes.

---

## Census Records

- **1820, 1830, 1840 censuses:** Named the head of household only; other members appear as tick-mark tallies.
- **1850 census:** First to name *every* household member with age, sex, occupation, and birthplace — a major leap in genealogical value.
- **1850 mortality schedule:** Lists deaths in the year preceding the census (June 1849–May 1850) — a useful substitute for missing death records at the end of your period.
- Available on FamilySearch, Ancestry.com, and other platforms.

---

## Probate Records

- Filed at the **county level** — Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield.
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901** — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" covers the full target period.
- Estate inventories, administration bonds, and guardian appointments name children, spouses, and kin — often with ages — making these invaluable when vital records are sparse.

---

## Land Records

- **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** holds deed books from 1761 in a virtually complete run.
- Grantor/grantee indexes can trace a family's presence in a specific town across the full 1820–1850 window even when vital records are thin.

---

## Military Records

- **War of 1812** (ended 1815) veterans may have pension files containing extensive family data — dates and places of birth and marriage.
- **Mexican-American War** (1846–1848) falls within your period.
- Available at **NARA** (archives.gov) and **Fold3** (fold3.com).

---

## Other Useful Sources

| Record Type | Repository |

Where a specific wiki page did not return, that fact is noted below rather than being filled from memory.

## Boundary changes

Berkshire County was established in 1761 and is situated in far western Massachusetts, bordering New York State to the west and Vermont to the north. No boundary changes during the 1820–1850 target period were returned by any tool. `place_search_all` returned no results, so no pre-formation predecessor records were surfaced.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

**This is the most important section for your question, and Massachusetts has a distinctive two-tier system.**

For the full 1820–1850 period, the originals remain with the clerk of the town or city where the event occurred — not at the county level.

- **Statewide registration (1841):** Massachusetts was the first state to create a permanent statewide recording system, which began in 1841. The originals remain with the town clerk; the state system is a parallel filing. Boston did not report to the state system until 1850 (when a stricter regulation was implemented), but that does not affect Berkshire County towns.

- **What this means for 1820–1850:** For 1820–1840, you must search each individual town's vital records — there is no county-level vital register. From 1841 onward, both town and state copies exist, but the town record remains the authoritative original.

- **Marriage intentions:** Per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page, marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with additional recordings possible in the groom's home town and their current place of residence. Search all three locations.

- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume covering Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850 (imageGroupNumber 004500891, 512 images). It is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only**. You must go page by page with no name search.

- **Published "Vital Records to 1850" series:** The Massachusetts Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) states that published compilations titled "Vital Records of [Town Name] to the Year 1850" exist for over 200 Massachusetts towns. These are transcriptions of the original town records and are an important finding aid. Check whether the specific Berkshire County town you are researching has a volume in this series.

Church records are especially important for 1820–1840 (before statewide registration) as the primary source for vital events.
- **Language:** The confirmed volumes are in English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The years 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 all fall within the target period. County probate records for the 1820–1850 period would be at the Berkshire County Probate Court or its successor repository; the Massachusetts_Probate_Records wiki page returned only generic content in this run.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Massachusetts is a state-land state with a metes-and-bounds survey system.

- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and grantor/grantee indexes at the Registry of Deeds.

Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) carries digitized military records. Massachusetts adjutant general records for militia service may be at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **War of 1812 pensions:** If your family had a veteran from the War of 1812 who was still alive 1820–1850, pension files at NARA could contain extensive family information including dates and places of birth and marriage.

Legal notices of estate proceedings were required to be published, making newspapers especially useful when probate records are thin.

- **Relevant ports:** The Massachusetts Passenger Lists collection covers 1820–1891. Boston was the primary Massachusetts port of entry.
- **Indexed collection:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) covers the full target period.
- **Naturalization:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) covers the period. Berkshire County court records should be searched for declarations of intention and naturalization petitions.

> **A note on tool coverage:** The FamilySearch place-resolution tools returned no results for any Irish place name queried (including Billy civil parish, County Antrim, and Ireland itself). As a result, tools depending on a resolved place (collections_search, volume_search, external_links_search, place_population, wiki_place_page) could not run. Every Ireland-specific wiki page URL attempted returned only generic U.S.-centric boilerplate. The one substantive Ireland-specific result was the Ireland **Naming Customs** wiki page. Gaps caused by tool limitations are flagged throughout.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Billy civil parish** is a civil parish in the historic county of Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland. Its nearest town is **Bushmills**, within the **Barony of Cary**. Throughout the target period (1780–1870), it fell under the Acts of Union 1800 as part of Great Britain and Ireland.

- **Ecclesiastical jurisdictions:** The civil parish overlaps both **Church of Ireland (Anglican)** and **Presbyterian** ecclesiastical boundaries and does not align with any single congregation's catchment area. Consult PRONI and the Representative Church Body (RCB) Library to identify which congregation served a given townland.
- **Economy:** A mixed agricultural and linen-weaving economy; Bushmills hosted a licensed whiskey distillery. Substantial emigration occurred throughout the period, especially after the Great Famine (late 1840s).
- **Religious composition:** Predominantly Ulster-Scots (Presbyterian) and Church of Ireland (Protestant), with a Catholic minority — a crucial factor shaping which records exist and where they are held.

---

## Boundary Changes

The civil-parish system did not change materially within 1780–1870. The **Poor Law Union of Ballymoney** (established 1839) overlapped parts of this area and generated its own administrative records. From **1864**, civil vital registration was organised into Superintendent Registrar's Districts; Billy civil parish likely fell in the **Ballymoney or Ballycastle** district — confirm at the General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI) or PRONI.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

| Event | Start date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Catholic marriages | 1845 | National civil registration |
| All births, marriages, deaths | 1864 | All denominations |

Post-1864 originals: **General Register Office (GRO)**, Dublin, and **GRONI**, Belfast (County Antrim records post-partition held at GRONI). Before 1864, church records are the primary source.

---

### Church Records *(most important class for 1780–1864)*

| Denomination | Notes | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Church of Ireland** | Established church; registers sometimes include non-conformists and Catholics; earliest registers | RCB Library, Dublin; PRONI |
| **Presbyterian** | Very large population in north Antrim; registers begin at varying dates | PRONI; individual congregation archives |
| **Roman Catholic** | Many registers begin early 19th century; generally later start dates | PRONI; local parish offices |
| **Methodist / other** | Non-conformist registers may exist | PRONI |

**Key access point:** PRONI's **eCatalogue** (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) and the **Irish Genealogy portal** (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) are recommended starting points. Always verify which congregation served the specific townland using PRONI's parish-map tool or a contemporary estate map.

---

### Census Records

| Year | Status |
|---|---|
| 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851 | Destroyed in the **1922 fire** at the Public Record Office of Ireland |
| 1861, 1871 | Deliberately destroyed by government |
| 1901, 1911 | Survive in full; online at https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie (outside the target period, useful for working back) |

**Census substitutes for 1780–1870:**

- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Lists of landholders paying tithes to the Church of Ireland, organised by townland. County Antrim coverage exists. Available at the National Archives of Ireland; also digitised online.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864):** Survey of all landholders and occupiers, townland by townland — the most important census substitute for the mid-19th century. Verify the exact survey date for County Antrim at the National Archives of Ireland or PRONI.

---

### Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books** — See Census Substitutes above.
- **Griffith's Valuation** — Lists occupiers and their landlords. See Census Substitutes above.
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (est. 1708):** Memorials of deeds, mortgages, and wills. Main repository for pre-1858 property transactions; indexes available online.
- **Estate records:** Leases, rent rolls, and correspondence for local estates (including the Antrim estate / Viscount Dunluce / Earl of Antrim) held at **PRONI** and the **National Library of Ireland (NLI)**.
- **Landed Estates Court records (from 1849):** Post-Famine encumbered estate sales; at the National Archives of Ireland.

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Before 1858:** Ecclesiastical probate — **Prerogative Court** (multi-diocese estates) and **Consistorial Courts** (diocesan level; County Antrim fell under the Diocese of Connor / Prerogative Court of Armagh). Many of these records were **destroyed in the 1922 fire**.
- **After 1858:** Civil probate district registries; the relevant registry for County Antrim was at Belfast.
- **What survives:** Will calendars (indexes) survive even where original wills were destroyed. **Betham's genealogical abstracts** from Prerogative Court wills (pre-fire) are at the National Archives of Ireland.
- **Access:** PRONI holds surviving records and indexes.

---

### Military Records

The 1780–1870 period covers the 1798 United Irish Rebellion, the Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815), and other engagements.

- **British Army:** Service records (muster rolls, description books, pension records) at **TNA, Kew** (WO series) and PRONI.
- **Out-pension records:** At the National Archives of Ireland and TNA.
- **County Antrim Militia:** At PRONI.

---

### Cemetery Records

- Church of Ireland churchyards in the area have burial registers (where surviving) at **PRONI** or the **RCB Library**.
- **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com) and the **Irish Genealogy portal** (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) may have memorial transcriptions for some graveyards.

---

### Newspaper Records

| Paper | Founded | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *Belfast News-Letter* | 1737 | Oldest surviving daily; covers all of Ireland |
| *Coleraine Chronicle* | 1844 | Local north Antrim paper |
| *Ballymena Observer* | 1855 | Local paper |

**Where held:** The **British Newspaper Archive** (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) has digitised many Northern Ireland papers. The **Linen Hall Library, Belfast**, holds physical runs. Content value: obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale advertisements, local legal notices.

---

### Immigration and Emigration Records

County Antrim had one of the highest emigration rates in Ireland. Primary destinations: United States, Canada, and Scotland (via Larne and Belfast ports).

- **U.S. arrival passenger lists:** More reliable than departure manifests; available at NARA, Ancestry, and other databases.
- **U.S. naturalizations:** Filed in any court of record; county of origin named (granularity improves from 1906 onward).
- **Scotland:** Kirk session records (Register House, Edinburgh) may document County Antrim migrants.

---

### Tax and Poor Law Records

- **Poor Law rate books (from 1839):** Ballymoney Union rate books list householders and valuations — an important census substitute for the 1840s–1860s. Held at PRONI.
- **Freeholders' records:** Lists those qualified to vote as 40-shilling freeholders; can substitute for missing land records.

---

### Other Notable Records

- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs of Ireland (1830s):** Compiled parish-by-parish; name families, customs, and livelihoods townland by townland for north Antrim. Held at the Royal Irish Academy; a published transcription series issued by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast. *An extraordinary starting resource.*
- **National school registers (from 1831):** List pupils and parents; County Antrim school registers held at PRONI (ED series).
- **Presbyterian session records:** Disciplinary minutes naming ordinary parishioners; held at PRONI and some congregations.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Holdings for this area | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI**, Titanic Boulevard, Belfast | Church registers, estate records, Poor Law records, school records, militia records, wills, newspapers | Free in-person; growing online catalogue at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **GRONI**, Belfast | Civil registration (births/marriages/deaths from 1864; County Antrim records post-partition) | In-person and online at https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk |
| **Irish Genealogy portal** | Church of Ireland, some Catholic and Presbyterian registers | Free at https://www.irishgenealogy.ie |
| **National Archives of Ireland**, Dublin | Betham abstracts, pre-1858 probate indexes, Tithe Applotment Books, estate records, 1901/1911 census | In-person and online at https://www.nationalarchives.ie |
| **Registry of Deeds**, Dublin | Deeds, mortgages, will memorials from 1708 | In-person; some indexes online at Ancestry |
| **RCB Library**, Dublin | Church of Ireland original registers | In-person by appointment |
| **TNA, Kew, London** | British Army records, pension files, Admiralty | In-person and online at https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk |
| **National Library of Ireland**, Dublin | Estate papers, newspapers, photographs | In-person; growing digital collections |
| **Linen Hall Library**, Belfast | Local newspapers, local history | In-person |

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1922 fire (Public Record Office of Ireland):** Destroyed original census returns for 1821–1851, Prerogative Court wills and associated probate records, and some church register originals that had been deposited there. Verify the fate of specific records at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland.
- **1861 and 1871 censuses:** Deliberately destroyed by the government before they could be preserved.
- **Compensating sources:** Betham will abstracts; surviving will-calendar indexes published by the National Archives of Ireland; private transcriptions made before 1922.

---

## Naming Conventions *(from the FamilySearch Wiki)*

The [FamilySearch Ireland Naming Customs page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs) describes a traditional naming pattern followed by Irish parents until the later 19th century:

| Child | Typically named for |
|---|---|
| 1st son | Father's father |
| 2nd son | Mother's father |
| 3rd son | Father |
| 4th son | Father's eldest brother |
| 1st daughter | Mother's mother |
| 2nd daughter | Father's mother |
| 3rd daughter | Mother |

**This is a clue, not a rule.** The wiki notes it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

**Surname variation (from the same page):** Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were anglicised under English rule. Prefixes such as *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson/descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored. A family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn in different documents; spelling was not standardised.

**Given-name variation (from the same page):** Gaelic given names were anglicised, producing multiple variants. Some given names served both males and females (Florence, Sydney, Evelyn). Some nicknames bear no obvious resemblance to the formal name (Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah are all variants of the same name).

---

## Research Tips

1. **Civil parish ≠ church parish.** Always establish which specific congregation served the townland of interest before pulling records.
2. **Search all denominations.** The mixed nature of the Billy civil parish area means baptisms, marriages, and burials sometimes appear in the "wrong" denomination's register.
3. **Use the Ordnance Survey Memoirs first.** For 1830s baseline context — family names, occupations, townland layout — these are unparalleled.
4. **Cross-check Dublin and Belfast.** County Antrim records are primarily at PRONI and GRONI (Belfast), but some pre-partition material is in Dublin repositories. Check both.
5. **Identify adjoining parishes.** Families near parish boundaries will have records in more than one civil and church parish. Use an Ordnance Survey six-inch map to identify neighbours and search their registers too.
6. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly.** The FamilySearch place-resolution tool returned no results for Ireland in this survey. Search https://www.familysearch.org/catalog by place ("Antrim" → county → civil parish) to identify microfilmed and digitised holdings — this step is still outstanding.
7. **Confirm the registration district.** For post-1864 civil records, confirm whether Billy civil parish falls in the Ballymoney or Ballycastle Superintendent Registrar's District before searching GRONI.

---

FamilySearch place-resolution returned no standardPlace for any Irish location; collections_search, volume_search, external_links_search, and wiki_place_page therefore could not be run. The FamilySearch Catalog search and PRONI contact are the recommended immediate next steps.*

- **Sexton records:** Where sexton records survive, they are held at the relevant church or at PRONI.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The north Antrim area was served by papers including the *Ballymena Observer* (founded 1855) and *Coleraine Chronicle* (founded 1844), both within the target period's later years. Earlier coverage may appear in the *Belfast News-Letter* (founded 1737), the oldest surviving daily newspaper in Ireland.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) digitized many Northern Ireland newspapers. The Linen Hall Library, Belfast, holds physical runs of local papers. No FamilySearch tool confirmed specific digitization coverage for these papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale advertisements, and local legal notices. For the 1780–1820 period, newspaper coverage is sparse; it improves from the 1840s onward.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** County Antrim had one of the highest emigration rates in Ireland throughout this period. The primary destinations were North America (especially the United States and Canada) and Scotland. Emigration from north Antrim ports (Larne, Belfast) to Scottish ports was also common for seasonal and permanent migration.
- **Passenger lists:** Departure manifests for Ireland are incomplete. Arrival passenger lists at U.S. ports (NARA, digitized at Ancestry and other databases) are the more reliable record. For the early period (1780–1820), records are sparse. From the 1840s, U.S. arrival manifests become more complete.
- **Naturalizations:** For emigrants who settled in the United States, naturalization declarations and petitions were filed in any court of record and may name the Irish county of origin (from 1906 onward they name the town, but within the target period, granularity varies).
- **Passenger list content note:** Arrival manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Inland emigration records:** For emigrants to Scotland, the Registers of Scots (Register House, Edinburgh) and kirk session records may document County Antrim migrants. No FamilySearch tool result in this survey confirmed specific collections.

### Tax records

- **Tithe Applotment Books:** See Census section above. A primary substitute for missing census records.
- **Hearth Money Rolls (17th century):** Pre-date the target period but useful for establishing family presence.
- **Poor Law rate books:** After 1838, each Poor Law Union (Ballymoney Union for this area) maintained rate books listing householders and their valuations. These are held at PRONI and are an important census substitute for the 1840s–1860s.
- **No FamilySearch tool result** confirmed specific digitization or indexing status for the Ballymoney Union rate books.

### Other record types

- **School records:** National schools were established in Ireland from 1831. School registers naming pupils and parents were kept from this date. Registers for County Antrim schools are held at PRONI (ED series). The Public Record Office wiki page returned only generic content.
- **Freeholders' records:** Lists of those qualified to vote as 40-shilling freeholders (before the 1829 Catholic Emancipation Act and subsequent franchise changes) name property-holders and can substitute for missing land records.
- **Town and county histories:** The *Ordnance Survey Memoirs of Ireland* (1830s), compiled parish-by-parish, are an extraordinary source for the Antrim area, naming families, customs, and livelihoods townland by townland. The originals are held at the RIA; a published transcription series was issued by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast.
- **Presbyterian session records:** Many Presbyterian congregations in County Antrim kept session (disciplinary) minutes that name ordinary parishioners. These are held at PRONI and some individual congregations.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

No FamilySearch-curated collection IDs, external link URLs, or FamilySearch catalog hits for Billy civil parish or County Antrim were returned by any tool in this survey. The external_links_search, collections_search, and volume_search tools could not be run because place_search returned no standardPlace for any Irish location. The following repositories are named only because they are the known custodians of the record types described above; their URLs are not taken from a tool result in this survey and should be verified directly:

| Repository | Relevance to this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) | Church registers, estate records, Poor Law records, school records, militia records, wills | Free online catalogue; some records online at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI) | Civil registration births/marriages/deaths from 1864 (County Antrim records post-partition held here) | In-person and online at https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk |
| Irish Genealogy portal | Church registers (Church of Ireland, some Catholic and Presbyterian) for many counties including Antrim | Free at https://www.irishgenealogy.ie |
| National Archives of Ireland | Betham will abstracts, pre-1858 probate indexes, Tithe Applotment Books, some estate records | In-person and online at https://www.nationalarchives.ie |
| Registry of Deeds, Dublin | Deeds, mortgages, and will memorials from 1708 | In-person; some indexes online at Ancestry |
| The National Archives (UK), Kew | British Army service records, pension files | In-person and online at https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk |
| Linen Hall Library, Belfast | Local newspapers, local history collections | In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch digitized-volume and collection surveys could not be run. No FamilySearch collection IDs or volume details are stated because none were returned by any tool.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| PRONI, Titanic Boulevard, Belfast | Church registers on microfilm/digital, estate papers, Poor Law records, school records | In-person (free) and growing online catalogue |
| RCB Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers (some originals) | In-person by appointment |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Tithe Applotment Books, pre-1858 will indexes, Betham abstracts, 1901/1911 census | In-person and online (https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie) |
| National Library of Ireland, Dublin | Estate papers, newspapers, photographs | In-person; growing digital collections |
| TNA, Kew, London | British Army records, Royal Irish Constabulary records, Admiralty | In-person and online (Discovery catalogue) |

## Records NOT online (as far as tool results confirm)

No FamilySearch tool returned the digitization status of any specific record set for Billy civil parish or County Antrim. Therefore this section can only report that the following classes of records are known to exist in physical form and may or may not be digitized or indexed online:

- Church register originals at PRONI and the RCB Library (some may be digitized via irishgenealogy.ie)
- Poor Law rate books at PRONI (not confirmed as online by any tool result)
- School registers at PRONI (not confirmed as online by any tool result)
- Estate papers at PRONI and NLI (not confirmed as online by any tool result)
- Pre-1858 will originals (largely destroyed 1922; Betham abstracts are at the National Archives of Ireland)
- Freeholders' records at PRONI

## Known record losses

No FamilySearch wiki tool result in this survey confirmed any specific record losses for Billy civil parish or County Antrim. A well-documented historical fact — the 1922 destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland — affected probate records (Prerogative and Consistorial Court wills and associated records) and some church register originals that had been deposited there. However, because no tool result in this survey confirmed this specifically, it is stated here as background context to investigate and verify, not as a confirmed finding of this guide. The researcher should verify the fate of specific record sets at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland.

**Known substitute sources** (for whatever was lost): The Betham will abstracts, surviving indexes to destroyed wills (published as the National Archives of Ireland's will calendars), and private transcriptions made before 1922 by researchers such as Sir William Betham and others partially compensate for probate losses.

## Research tips

- **Naming conventions (from the FamilySearch Wiki):** The Ireland Naming Customs page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs describes a traditional naming pattern used by Irish parents until the later 19th century. In this pattern, the first son was usually named for the father's father; the second son for the mother's father; the third son for the father; the fourth son for the father's eldest brother; the first daughter for the mother's mother; the second daughter for the father's mother; and the third daughter for the mother. The page notes this is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.
- **Surname variation:** The same wiki page notes that Irish surnames of Gaelic origin underwent anglicization under English rule, producing multiple forms. Prefixes such as Mac (son of) and O (grandson/descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored across records, so a family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn in different documents. Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways within one parish register.
- **Given-name variation:** The same wiki page notes that Gaelic given names were anglicized, producing variants. Some given names used for both males and females (Florence, Sydney, Evelyn). Some given names have nicknames that do not resemble the formal name (Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah are all variations of the same name).
- **Civil parish vs. Church parish:** The civil parish of Billy does not necessarily correspond to any single Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, or Catholic congregation's territory. Always establish which congregation actually served the specific townland and family before pulling records.
- **Multi-denominational research:** Because the Billy civil parish area was served by Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and Catholic congregations, and because the population was mixed, always search records of all three traditions regardless of the family's assumed religion. Baptisms, marriages, and burials sometimes appear in the "wrong" denomination's register.
- **The Ordnance Survey Memoirs:** For the 1830s, the Ordnance Survey Memoirs provide an unparalleled baseline description of each townland's population, housing, occupations, and social customs. Use them to understand the parish community before searching other records.
- **Searching across the border:** After partition in 1921, County Antrim records are held at GRONI and PRONI (Belfast), not at Dublin repositories. For the target period (1780–1870), records were created under a unified Irish administrative system, but physical custody has since been divided. Cross-check both Dublin and Belfast repositories.
- **Adjoining parishes:** Billy civil parish borders other north Antrim civil parishes. Families near parish boundaries will have records in both parishes. The tool results in this survey did not return the specific neighboring parishes from a FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy civil parish (the county genealogy page returned only generic content). Consult an Ordnance Survey six-inch map to identify the adjoining parishes and search their registers as well.
- **The Ballymoney district registers:** For civil registration post-1864, search the Superintendent Registrar's district covering Billy civil parish. Confirm the district name at GRONI before searching.
- **FamilySearch Catalog:** The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey because the place_search tool returned no standardPlace for any Irish location. Searching the catalog directly at https://www.familysearch.org/catalog by place name ("Antrim" → county → civil parish) is a recommended next step to identify microfilmed and digitized holdings.

---

No project file (research.json) was found in the working directory, so Step 6 (persisting a `localities` entry) does not apply. The guide above is the full output of this survey.

Billy civil parish in County Antrim occupied a corner of the northern Antrim coast, in what is now Northern Ireland, during a period when the population was mixed Church of Ireland and Presbyterian with a Catholic minority, and when nearly the entire community relied on church registers rather than civil records for the documentation of births, marriages, and deaths. The most important records for 1780–1870 are therefore denomination-specific church registers held at PRONI and the RCB Library in Dublin; the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation serve as census substitutes for much of this period because the original Irish census returns for these years were largely destroyed. The most critical warnings for any researcher are that civil registration of all births and deaths did not begin until 1864, that the 1922 fire in Dublin destroyed much of the pre-1858 probate record and some church material, and that the civil parish does not map onto any single congregation — every denomination's registers must be checked for each townland. The FamilySearch place-resolution and wiki tools returned no usable Ireland-specific content in this survey beyond the naming customs page, so the guide's next step is for the researcher to search the FamilySearch Catalog directly by place name and to contact PRONI for a holdings list specific to Billy civil parish.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide (1840–1880)

**County background:** Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 in the Pennsylvania anthracite coal region, which drove significant immigration (especially Irish and German) throughout the 1840–1880 period.

### FamilySearch Digitized Record Sets

| Record Set | Images | Indexing |
|---|---|---|
| Deed records | 543 | 22% name-indexed |
| Probate records | 412 | Browse-only |
| Naturalization records | 298 | Browse-only |
| Church records | 187 | Browse-only (includes German-language entries) |
| Marriage records | 94 | Browse-only |
| Pennsylvania Probate Records (statewide) | 3.2 million | Browse-only |

Additionally, **two compiled marriage collections** on FamilySearch are name-indexed and cover this period.

### Key Finding — Vital Records Gap
Pennsylvania did **not** have statewide civil birth or death registration during 1840–1880. **Church records are the essential substitute** for vital events (births, christenings, deaths, burials). The county marriage register only begins at 1870, so pre-1870 marriages must be sought in church registers.

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Church records** — prioritize for births, deaths, and pre-1870 marriages; note that German-language entries may require translation.
2. **Naturalization records** — important for immigrant ancestors arriving in the anthracite coal era.
3. **Deed and probate records** — browse-only, so page-by-page image browsing will be required.
4. **FamilySearch Wiki** — visit [Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) for additional jurisdiction-specific tips.

A research plan can now be built from this locality survey to guide searches for specific individuals across these record types.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (per FamilySearch place record, date range +1811/)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by tool results; no jurisdiction-specific wiki page was returned during this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for Schuylkill County; no census-year population figures are available from tool results.
- **Economy, ethnic composition, religious denominations, key historical events:** Not confirmed by tool results. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Schuylkill County and Pennsylvania returned only generic fallback content. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly.

## Boundary changes
The FamilySearch place_search returned Schuylkill County as a single continuous jurisdiction from 1811 forward, with no additional split entries. No boundary change information within 1840–1880 was returned by any tool. Researchers should verify against historical county atlases.

## Available record types

Jurisdictional holding levels below are based on what the survey tools returned. The Pennsylvania Vital Records and related topical wiki pages were not returned with jurisdiction-specific content — level and start date claims that could not be grounded in a tool result are flagged explicitly.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) did not return Pennsylvania-specific content during this survey. Based on collection date ranges returned: statewide death certificates begin at 1906 (collection 2255317); county marriage registration appears around 1885 (collection 1921317). Civil birth registration start dates at any level were not confirmed by any tool result.
- **What exists for 1840–1880:** Civil statewide vital registration was not in effect during this window based on returned collection start dates. Church records and compiled marriage collections are the primary alternatives for births, marriages, and burials.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim (Bushmills area), 1780–1870

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, Barony of Cary, County Antrim, Ulster
- **Main settlement:** Bushmills, on the north Antrim coast
- **Post-1922 jurisdiction:** Northern Ireland (United Kingdom)
- **Primary archive:** Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast
- **Religious makeup:** Church of Ireland (Anglican) and Presbyterian were the dominant traditions (together ~60% of Northern Ireland's 1861 population), with a Catholic minority. County Antrim was heavily settled by Scottish Presbyterian planters from 1605, so Presbyterian records are especially important here.

---

## Civil Registration

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths **did not begin until 1 January 1864** (Protestant marriages from 1 April 1845). For most of the 1780–1870 window, **church records are the primary — often the only — vital-record source**. Post-1864 registrations for County Antrim are held by **GRONI** (General Register Office Northern Ireland). The online portal IrishGenealogy.ie covers some areas, but County Antrim coverage should be verified before searching.

---

## Church Records (the core record type for this period)

### Church of Ireland (Anglican) — your specific question

- **Survival for Northern Ireland:** Church of Ireland registers nationwide were two-thirds destroyed in the **1922 Dublin PRO fire** — but County Antrim registers were **not** held in Dublin. Because the parish is in Northern Ireland, registers deposited locally or in Belfast before 1922 were unaffected. Survival rates for Co. Antrim Church of Ireland registers are therefore generally **better** than for parishes in the Republic.
- **Definitive survival check:** Consult **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** (PDF: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf), which lists every Northern Ireland parish, which registers exist, and whether they are held at PRONI in original or microfilm form.
- **Online access at PRONI:** Check the PRONI Digitized Church Records portal: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni (free).
- **RCB Library** (Representative Church Body Library, Dublin): Maintains a list of all surviving Church of Ireland registers — for Northern Ireland parishes the registers are generally at PRONI, not Dublin. Genealogy searches: https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy; register list PDF: https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf
- **Ffolliott Collection on FindMyPast** (paid subscription): Indexed baptisms/confirmations, marriages, and burials from Church of Ireland registers — may cover Billy parish.
- **Marriage license bonds:** FamilySearch collection 3460239 — *Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866* (free, index & images) covers pre-civil-registration Church of Ireland marriages.

### Presbyterian

- Average start date for registers: **c. 1830**, though some Co. Antrim congregations date from the 1600s.
- Given the heavy Scottish plantation settlement in the Bushmills area, Presbyterian registers may rival or exceed Church of Ireland registers in importance.
- Held at **PRONI**; partially indexed on **FindMyPast** (Ireland Non-Conformist Births, Burials, Marriages — paid).
- Note: Presbyterian registers frequently **do not include burial registers** — use Church of Ireland burials instead.

### Roman Catholic

- Rural parishes typically began keeping registers around **1828** (Catholic Emancipation). Coverage before that date is sparse for rural Antrim.
- Registers are freely available via the **National Library of Ireland** portal: https://registers.nli.ie/
- Also on **Ancestry** (paid): *Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915* (collection 61039).
- Catholic registers also frequently **do not include burials**.

### Other denominations

- Methodist, Reformed Presbyterian (Covenanter), and other non-conformist congregations existed in Co. Antrim. FindMyPast's Non-Conformist collections (paid) and PRONI hold these records.
- Quaker records: Free index on FindMyPast; FamilySearch catalog 322759.

---

## Census Records

Pre-1870 Irish census returns are largely lost:

| Census year | Fate |
|---|---|
| 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851 | Destroyed in the 1922 Dublin PRO fire |
| 1861, 1871 | Officially destroyed by government order |
| 1901, 1911 | Survive nearly complete — freely searchable at https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/ (useful for backtracking) |

**Census substitutes for 1780–1870:**
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists landholders paying tithes to the Church of Ireland
- **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864):** Comprehensive survey of all landholders — the best census substitute for this period
Both are held at PRONI; check IrishGenealogy.ie and Ancestry for online access.

---

## Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books** and **Griffith's Valuation** (see above) are the primary land/census-substitute sources.
- **Estate papers:** County Antrim landlord estate papers may survive at PRONI for families on those estates.
- Consult PRONI's online catalog for specific Co. Antrim land record holdings.

---

## Probate Records

- Pre-1858: Administered by Church of Ireland diocesan courts (Consistorial Courts). Most records held in Dublin were destroyed in 1922; indexes survive.
- Post-1858: Civil probate (Principal Probate Registry and District Registries).
- **Online indexes:** FamilySearch / Ancestry: *Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591–1866* (Ancestry collection 62077, paid).
- **Substitutes for lost wills:** Betham, Crossle, and Thrift Genealogical Abstracts (FindMyPast, paid) — specifically compiled as substitutes for records destroyed in 1922.
- Original surviving documents: **PRONI**.

---

## Military Records

- British Army service records, pension files, and discharge papers for Co. Antrim men: **The National Archives, Kew** (England).
- Local militia and yeomanry records: **PRONI**.
- Periods covered by this window: American Revolutionary War era, Napoleonic Wars, and Crimean War.

---

## Newspapers

- **Belfast News-Letter** (founded 1737): The main regional paper. Contains marriage, death, and legal notices.
- **Coleraine Chronicle** (founded 1844): Nearest local paper to Bushmills.
- Access: **British Newspaper Archive** (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/, paid) and **Irish Newspaper Archive** (https://www.irishnewsarchive.com/, paid).

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI**, 2 Titanic Blvd, Belfast BT3 9HQ | Church registers (CoI, Presbyterian, others); civil registration; estate papers; wills; land records | In person / email proni@communities-ni.gov.uk. Free enquiry service. |
| **PRONI Digitized Church Records portal** | Digitized church registers for Northern Ireland parishes | Free — https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni |
| **RCB Library**, Dublin | Church of Ireland register list; registers not held at PRONI | In person or paid search — https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy |
| **GRONI** | Civil births, marriages, deaths from 1864 (Co. Antrim) | Via PRONI or directly |
| **NLI Registers portal** | Catholic parish registers | Free — https://registers.nli.ie/ |
| **FamilySearch** | Marriage License Bonds 1623–1866 (free); Catholic Qualification Rolls (free); Catalog | Free — https://www.familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry** | Catholic Parish Registers; Probate indexes; Irish Records Index | Paid |
| **FindMyPast** | Ffolliott Collection (CoI); Non-Conformist; Betham/Crossle/Thrift Abstracts | Paid |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | Ulster emigration databases; Co. Antrim specialized indexes | Paid — http://www.ancestryireland.com/ |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Civil registration; some church records | Free — https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/ (verify Co. Antrim coverage) |
| **The National Archives, Kew** | British Army service/pension records | In person or online (some collections on FindMyPast/Ancestry) |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with PRONI's Guide to Church Records** before anything else. It will confirm precisely which Billy/Bushmills registers survive and where they are held.
2. **Search Church of Ireland registers even if your ancestor was not Church of Ireland.** Mixed or uncertain-denomination families often appear in CoI records.
3. **Presbyterian records are critical in Co. Antrim** due to the plantation heritage — do not overlook them in favour of CoI records alone.
4. **Civil registration only from 1864.** For 1780–1863, church records and census substitutes (Tithe Applotment, Griffith's) are the primary sources.
5. **The 1922 Dublin fire affects Northern Ireland less.** Co. Antrim registers were not in the Dublin PRO; check PRONI before concluding a register is lost.
6. **Identify civil parish, CoI parish, and Catholic parish boundaries separately** — they differ from each other and from townland boundaries.
7. **Use genealogical abstracts** (Betham/Crossle/Thrift on FindMyPast) as substitutes for any pre-1922 records that may have been lost.

---

*Primary source for grounded claims: FamilySearch Research Wiki, Ireland Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records). The FamilySearch place-search and collection-search tools do not cover Ireland; sections marked with repository recommendations are based on that wiki page and standard Northern Ireland genealogy practice. Confirm specific record availability and years of coverage directly with PRONI before planning searches.*
