# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1811
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Target period:** 1840–1869

---

## Available Record Types

### Census Records
The most accessible records for this period:
- **FamilySearch** — U.S. Federal Census 1850–1860, image group **007621224** (412 images, **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable**)
- **Ancestry** — [1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/)
- The 1840 census was not returned by tool results; search FamilySearch and Ancestry directly for that year

### Church Records
Church registers are the **primary source for vital events** in this period (births, baptisms, marriages, burials), as civil registration was not yet established:
- **FamilySearch** — Church Records (Lutheran) 1840–1875, image group **004288771** (198 images, **browse-only — no name index**)
  - Must be browsed image by image with no search assistance
  - Portions are in **English and German** — reading German is required for some entries
- No digitized records for non-Lutheran denominations were found; records may exist on FamilySearch microfilm or at denominational archives

### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch** — Probate Records 1845–1880, image group **004812990** (286 images, **4% name-indexed, full-text searchable**)
  - Only 4% indexed — use full-text search first; be prepared to browse images directly
- **FamilySearch** — Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196); 3.2M images, **browse-only**)

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No digitized civil birth, marriage, or death records for Schuylkill County in 1840–1869 were found
- **Church records are the substitute** for this period

### Land Records & Tax Records
- No digitized land or tax records for 1840–1869 were found online
- Must be consulted at the Schuylkill County courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives (in-person or by mail)

### Military Records
- Relevant conflicts: Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and Civil War (1861–1865)
- Federal records held at **NARA**; Pennsylvania state records at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**
- No Schuylkill County–specific military volumes were returned by the tools

### Court Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any Pennsylvania court of record**, including Schuylkill County's own courts — search county court records, not only federal courts
- No court record volumes for the target period were found online

### Cemetery Records
- No online cemetery collections were found for Schuylkill County
- Sexton records and burial registers may be held by local churches and the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collection | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | U.S. Federal Census 1850–1860 (96% indexed) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records 1845–1880 (4% indexed, FTS) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Lutheran Church Records 1840–1875 (browse-only) | Free |
| FamilySearch | PA Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 U.S. Federal Census – Schuylkill County | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse | Deeds, court records, probate files, naturalizations |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level, county, and military records |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local histories, newspapers, photographs, manuscripts |
| Denominational archives | Church registers not yet microfilmed |

---

## Records Not Yet Online
- Civil vital records (births, marriages, deaths)
- Land records and deeds, 1840–1869
- Tax records, 1840–1869
- Court records beyond probate (naturalizations, civil suits, minute books)
- Cemetery and sexton records
- Non-Lutheran church records
- Newspapers

---

## Key Research Tips

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch collections_search, volume_search, and catalog_search tools all returned zero results when queried at both county and state levels — the tool response showed empty standardPlace values, indicating a place-resolution failure rather than confirmed absence of FamilySearch collections. The online resources in the table above come directly from the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched in this survey. Search FamilySearch.org's catalog directly at https://www.familysearch.org/catalog-search using "Pulaski, Kentucky" to verify current digitization status.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main Street #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds (1799–); deeds (1799–); court orders (1799–); wills (1801–) | In-person or mail |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 vital records; state records | In-person or online request |
| Pulaski County Historical Society | Surname vertical files; church records; local newspaper obituaries | Contact for hours and access |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, newspapers, genealogical collections, land records | In-person; some digitized |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents (1793–) | In-person or contact for records |
| National Archives (NARA) | Federal census; military service and pension records; passenger lists; pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person (Washington DC / regional facilities); indexes on Ancestry and Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- County deed books from 1799 beyond what FamilySearch has digitized — physical at Pulaski County Courthouse; microfilmed copies at KDLA.
- Court order books and civil/criminal case files — physical at Pulaski County Courthouse; microfilmed at KDLA.
- Individual congregation church registers — physical at local churches, Pulaski County Historical Society, or denominational archives.
- Naturalization petitions filed in Pulaski County Circuit Court (pre-1906) — physical at courthouse.
- Tax lists for years not covered by Ancestry — physical at courthouse or KDLA.

## Known record losses
The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page states that a disaster destroyed some records in 1838 and again in 1871 ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)). The 1871 loss falls within the 1840–1880 research window. The specific record types affected by each disaster are not stated in the wiki page. An empty search result for county-level records predating 1871 may reflect record loss rather than nonexistence of a record. Substitute sources for the affected years include church records, tax lists, KDLA-held microfilm, and newspaper notices. Verify survival of specific series with the Pulaski County Courthouse or KDLA before treating a negative result as definitive.

## Research tips
- **No statewide vital registration during the target period:** During 1840–1880, births and deaths were registered at county level only for 1853–1862 and 1874–1878, with poor compliance. Church records and cemetery records are primary alternatives. Source: [Kentucky Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **1871 courthouse disaster:** When a document appears missing, consult the Pulaski County Historical Society's surname files, KDLA's microfilm holdings, and church records before concluding the record never existed.
- **Kentucky is a state-land state:** Grants and patents were issued by the Kentucky Land Office (Frankfort), not the Bureau of Land Management. For land acquired during the Virginia era (before 1792), search Virginia records. Source: [Kentucky Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **No Kentucky state census:** Federal decennial censuses (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) are the primary enumeration source. County tax lists are the best substitute for intercensal years. Source: [Kentucky, United States Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy).
- **Pulaski County Historical Society is a first-stop repository:** Surname vertical files and local church record holdings make it a high-priority resource for any Pulaski County family. Source: [Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy).
- **Civil War border-state research:** Search both Union and Confederate service and pension records at NARA; men from the same Pulaski County family sometimes served on opposite sides. KDLA also holds Kentucky state adjutant general records.
- **Neighboring counties — neighbors not listed:** The Pulaski County wiki page did not return a neighboring counties table. Before concluding research, identify bordering counties and search their records for families who lived near county lines.
- **Direct FamilySearch catalog search recommended:** The FamilySearch collections and volume tools did not resolve the place during this survey. Go to https://www.familysearch.org/catalog-search and search place 'Pulaski, Kentucky' to find all filmed and digitized holdings.
- **Greenup County and Boyd County not surveyed:** This guide covers Pulaski County only. Separate locality surveys are needed for Greenup County and Boyd County, Kentucky, 1840–1880.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality-guide subagent found:

---

Researching an ancestor who lived in the Alabama region around 1800 takes you into a layered set of jurisdictions: the territory was under the **Mississippi Territory** from 1798 to 1817, then the **Alabama Territory** until statehood in 1819, and the Mobile area specifically was under **Spanish colonial administration** until 1813. That means the records created for a person living there around 1800 were not "Alabama" records at all — they were Mississippi territorial records, or in Mobile's case, Spanish colonial records.

**Key archives and repositories:**

- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)** — holds the Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, as well as early county records.
- **National Archives** — federal land patents, War of 1812/Creek War military records.
- **BLM General Land Office website** — original land patents.
- **Archivo General de Indias (Seville), with Library of Congress copies** — for the Mobile area under Spanish rule before 1813.
- **FamilySearch** — four indexed collections covering Alabama from 1803/1809 onward, plus two browse-only digitized volumes (image groups 004512889 and 004512890) for the 1808–1820 period (not name-indexed; must be read image by image).
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (France)** — French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763.

**Critical warnings:**
- Do **not** search for "Alabama" records before 1817 — search **Mississippi Territory** instead.
- If your ancestor was near Mobile before 1813, begin with **Spanish colonial archives**, not American ones.

The next step is to narrow down which part of Alabama and which exact records apply to your ancestor, so a focused research plan can be built around the specific county that existed at the time of the events you are trying to document.

quirks: Around 1800, most of present-day Alabama was under the Mississippi Territory (1798-1817); records from that period are filed under Mississippi Territory or its counties, not under Alabama — search both Alabama and Mississippi territorial record sets.
The Mobile area remained under Spanish control as part of West Florida until 1813; records for Mobile-area residents before 1813 are colonial Spanish records, not American territorial records.

Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covered settlers in present-day Alabama and are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.

No civil vital registration existed during the territorial period; the earliest county-level marriage records on FamilySearch begin in 1809; births and deaths were not systematically recorded — church records and family Bibles are the primary substitutes.

Alabama is a federal land state; original land patents from the territorial and early statehood period are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website (glorecords.blm.gov), not at a state land office.

French colonial records for the Mobile area are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for Alabama 1808-1820 (image groups 004512889 and 004512890) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image.

The Mississippi Territory was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass all of present-day Alabama; records from before 1804 may have been created under the original narrow-strip territory and are sparse for the northern and eastern parts of present-day Alabama.
The Creek War of 1813-1814 displaced many Native American and settler communities; records of property and individuals may be disrupted or absent for that period in affected areas.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1785–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed as a state:** 14 December 1819, from the Alabama Territory
- **Alabama Territory:** organized 3 March 1817, from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory
- **Mississippi Territory:** organized 7 April 1798; expanded 1804 and 1812 to cover present-day Alabama in full
- **Mobile area colonial control:** French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), Spanish (1780–1813)
- **Administrative center during territorial period:** St. Stephens (Washington County) served as the capital of the Alabama Territory
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, then the United States federal government
- **Population during period:** Place population data was not returned by the tool for this period. Wikipedia notes significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia occurred after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The 1810 federal census (conducted under the Mississippi Territory) is the earliest enumeration of present-day Alabama settlers.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and commercial agriculture (cotton beginning to expand), fur trade, and small-scale settlement along river corridors (Tombigbee, Alabama, Cahaba rivers)
- **Ethnic composition:** American settlers (primarily Scots-Irish and English descent, migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia); Creek and Cherokee nations holding most of the interior; French Creole and Spanish colonial settlers in Mobile; African Americans (enslaved)
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist and Methodist circuit riders served the interior; Roman Catholic parishes served Mobile and the Gulf Coast (the only established churches in the colonial Mobile area)
- **Key historical events:** Organization of the Mississippi Territory (1798); territorial expansion (1804, 1812); Creek War / Fort Mims massacre (1813–1814); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Alabama Territory organized (1817); Alabama statehood (1819)

## Boundary changes
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory created from a narrow strip along the 31st–32nd parallels; only the southern fringe of present-day Alabama was included.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to include most of present-day Alabama as far as the Tennessee border.
- **1812:** Final expansion of the Mississippi Territory to its full extent, covering all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- **1813:** The United States seized the Mobile District from Spain; Mobile-area residents came under American authority for the first time. Spanish colonial records up to this date are the governing record set for Mobile-area families.
- **1817:** The eastern half of the Mississippi Territory was organized as the Alabama Territory when Mississippi achieved statehood. Records from the territorial period (1798–1817) for the Alabama portion were created and filed under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction.
- **1819:** Alabama achieved statehood. County-level record-keeping was already underway in several counties formed during the territorial period.

Records follow the creating jurisdiction: events before 1817 for present-day Alabama were recorded under Mississippi Territory authority. Events in the Mobile area before 1813 were recorded under Spanish colonial authority.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the territorial period. The FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408) shows that some county-level marriage bonds and licenses begin as early as 1809, at the county level, during the territorial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey, so no statewide registration date can be cited from tool results.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1809 (for counties formed during the territorial period). No systematically created birth or death records for the pre-statehood period.
- **Where held:** County probate court (marriage records); FamilySearch collection 1598408 (indexed + images, county marriages 1809–1950)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths are not in any systematically created civil record for this period. Early county records may be sparse or missing for counties formed late in the territorial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism registers, family Bibles, estate inventories (which often name heirs and ages), and tombstone inscriptions

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area, established throughout the colonial period); Baptist and Methodist circuit churches (interior, from approximately 1808 onward)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (Catholic parishes); meeting minutes and membership lists (Baptist, Methodist)
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic records for Mobile: Diocese of Mobile archives; Spanish colonial-era Catholic registers are also held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and in copies at the Library of Congress ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
  - FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396): 156,789 records, indexed + images, beginning 1803
  - Protestant church records: denominational archives (Southern Baptist Historical Library and Archives, Nashville; Methodist archives)
- **Language:** Catholic colonial records are in French (French colonial period) or Spanish (Spanish colonial period); early American-period Catholic records may be in English or French

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory, including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census is the first taken after Alabama statehood.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756): 287,634 records, name-indexed, no images (index only). This is the primary online starting point for pre-statehood census substitutes.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Tax lists and militia rolls from the territorial period can substitute for missing census coverage.
- **Access:** The index-only collection on FamilySearch (collection 2016756) is searchable by name but has no linked images. Original records require consulting the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins from county formation dates during the territorial period; Washington County, formed 1800, is among the earliest.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764): 438,210 records, indexed + images, beginning 1809
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch image group 004512890 covers Washington County deed and probate records 1803–1820 (96 images, browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image by image.
- **Territorial court records:** FamilySearch image group 004512889 covers Alabama territorial court and land records 1808–1819 (214 images, browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image by image.
- **Notes on testate vs. intestate:** Wills (testate) are filed in probate; intestate administrations are filed separately. Both series begin from county formation in the territorial period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal land state — land was distributed by the federal government, not a state land office)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government through the General Land Office; original land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov). The FamilySearch Wiki for Alabama Land and Property did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (original entries), Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area), territorial-era deed books, tax records, militia land bounties
- **Colonial land grants (Mobile area):** Spanish and British colonial land grants precede American authority. Spanish grants are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)). French colonial grants may be at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence) and Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Territorial-era deeds:** Filed at county level from county formation; Washington County records from 1803 onward are in FamilySearch image group 004512890 (browse-only).
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents; county deed books at county courthouses and the Alabama Department of Archives and History; colonial grants in foreign archives as noted above

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia service (1798–1819)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for Creek War and War of 1812 veterans), militia muster rolls (territorial period)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and regional facilities; FamilySearch and Fold3 (fold3.com) carry many NARA military collections online
- **Territorial militia:** Militia rolls for the Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory may be at the Alabama Department of Archives and History

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Formal cemeteries were sparse in this period; burials were often on private land or in church yards
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) indexes headstone photos contributed by volunteers; coverage for pre-1820 graves in Alabama is limited but worth checking
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this early period are generally not available; church burial registers (especially Catholic, Mobile) are the best physical source

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Mobile Centinel* began publication in 1811, making it among the earliest newspapers in present-day Alabama. The *Halcyon and Tombeckbe Public Advertiser* (St. Stephens) began ca. 1818.
- **Content value:** Notices of land sales, estate settlements, legal notices, and occasionally obituaries appear in early territorial newspapers
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for digitized issues; physical holdings at the Alabama Department of Archives and History

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf of Mexico), New Orleans (Mississippi River route)
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); naturalization records (territorial and early state courts, pre-1906 — any court of record); Spanish colonial census returns that enumerate settlers by origin
- **Notes:** Most settlers arriving around 1800 came overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee — not by ship. I'm researching an ancestor who lived in the Alabama region around 1800, before statehood. What archives or record repositories will hold for that locality and period?

Locality guide written as loc_001.

---

Researching an ancestor who lived in the Alabama region around 1800 takes you into a layered set of jurisdictions: the territory was under the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819, and the Mobile area specifically was under Spanish colonial administration until 1813. That means the records created for a person living there around 1800 were not "Alabama" records at all — they were Mississippi territorial records, or in Mobile's case, Spanish colonial records. The most important repositories are the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery (which holds the Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 as well as early county records), the National Archives (for federal land patents, War of 1812/Creek War military records), the BLM General Land Office website for original land patents, and for the Mobile area, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville with Library of Congress copies. FamilySearch has four indexed collections covering Alabama from 1803/1809 onward, and two additional browse-only digitized volumes (image groups 004512889 and 004512890) for the 1808-1820 period — neither is name-indexed, so they must be read image by image. French colonial records for Mobile (1702-1763) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in France. The biggest warnings: do not search for "Alabama" records before 1817 — search Mississippi Territory; and if the ancestor was near Mobile before 1813, begin with Spanish colonial archives rather than American ones.

The next step is to narrow down which part of Alabama and which exact records apply to your ancestor so a focused research plan can be built around the specific county that existed at the time of the events you are trying to document.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1785–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed as a state:** 14 December 1819, from the Alabama Territory
- **Alabama Territory:** organized 3 March 1817, from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory
- **Mississippi Territory:** organized 7 April 1798; expanded 1804 and 1812 to cover present-day Alabama in full
- **Mobile area colonial control:** French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), Spanish (1780–1813)
- **Administrative center during territorial period:** St. Stephens (Washington County) served as the capital of the Alabama Territory
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, then the United States federal government
- **Population during period:** Place population data was not returned by the tool for this period. Wikipedia notes significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia occurred after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The 1810 federal census (conducted under the Mississippi Territory) is the earliest enumeration of present-day Alabama settlers.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and commercial agriculture (cotton beginning to expand), fur trade, and small-scale settlement along river corridors (Tombigbee, Alabama, Cahaba rivers)
- **Ethnic composition:** American settlers (primarily Scots-Irish and English descent, migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia); Creek and Cherokee nations holding most of the interior; French Creole and Spanish colonial settlers in Mobile; African Americans (enslaved)
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist and Methodist circuit riders served the interior; Roman Catholic parishes served Mobile and the Gulf Coast (the only established churches in the colonial Mobile area)
- **Key historical events:** Organization of the Mississippi Territory (1798); territorial expansion (1804, 1812); Creek War / Fort Mims massacre (1813–1814); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Alabama Territory organized (1817); Alabama statehood (1819)

## Boundary changes
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory created from a narrow strip along the 31st–32nd parallels; only the southern fringe of present-day Alabama was included.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to include most of present-day Alabama as far as the Tennessee border.
- **1812:** Final expansion of the Mississippi Territory to its full extent, covering all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- **1813:** The United States seized the Mobile District from Spain; Mobile-area residents came under American authority for the first time. Spanish colonial records up to this date are the governing record set for Mobile-area families.
- **1817:** The eastern half of the Mississippi Territory was organized as the Alabama Territory when Mississippi achieved statehood. Records from the territorial period (1798–1817) for the Alabama portion were created and filed under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction.
- **1819:** Alabama achieved statehood. County-level record-keeping was already underway in several counties formed during the territorial period.

Records follow the creating jurisdiction: events before 1817 for present-day Alabama were recorded under Mississippi Territory authority. Events in the Mobile area before 1813 were recorded under Spanish colonial authority.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the territorial period. The FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408) shows that some county-level marriage bonds and licenses begin as early as 1809, at the county level, during the territorial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey, so no statewide registration date can be cited from tool results.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1809 (for counties formed during the territorial period). No systematically created birth or death records for the pre-statehood period.
- **Where held:** County probate court (marriage records); FamilySearch collection 1598408 (indexed + images, county marriages 1809–1950)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths are not in any systematically created civil record for this period. Early county records may be sparse or missing for counties formed late in the territorial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism registers, family Bibles, estate inventories (which often name heirs and ages), and tombstone inscriptions

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area, established throughout the colonial period); Baptist and Methodist circuit churches (interior, from approximately 1808 onward)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (Catholic parishes); meeting minutes and membership lists (Baptist, Methodist)
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic records for Mobile: Diocese of Mobile archives; Spanish colonial-era Catholic registers are also held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and in copies at the Library of Congress ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
  - FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396): 156,789 records, indexed + images, beginning 1803
  - Protestant church records: denominational archives (Southern Baptist Historical Library and Archives, Nashville; Methodist archives)
- **Language:** Catholic colonial records are in French (French colonial period) or Spanish (Spanish colonial period); early American-period Catholic records may be in English or French

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory, including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census is the first taken after Alabama statehood.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756): 287,634 records, name-indexed, no images (index only). This is the primary online starting point for pre-statehood census substitutes.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Tax lists and militia rolls from the territorial period can substitute for missing census coverage.
- **Access:** The index-only collection on FamilySearch (collection 2016756) is searchable by name but has no linked images. Original records require consulting the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins from county formation dates during the territorial period; Washington County, formed 1800, is among the earliest.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764): 438,210 records, indexed + images, beginning 1809
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch image group 004512890 covers Washington County deed and probate records 1803–1820 (96 images, browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image by image.

- **Notes on testate vs. intestate:** Wills (testate) are filed in probate; intestate administrations are filed separately. Both series begin from county formation in the territorial period.

Here is the locality guide for Arkansas before 1800 (Spanish colonial period):

---

**Arkansas Region, Pre-1800 (Spanish Colonial Era)**

The Arkansas region before 1800 was under Spanish colonial control (preceded by French administration before 1763), and virtually all European settlement was concentrated at a single post — **Arkansas Post**. Because no American-style civil registration, county courts, or federal census existed for this period, surviving records come from two primary sources:

### Catholic Church Records
- **Sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) for Arkansas Post
- FamilySearch has digitized one volume covering **1763–1800** (64 images, browse-only, in Spanish, no name index)
- Physical originals are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock**

### Spanish Colonial Government Records
- **Padrón (census) lists** — population tallies by household
- **Land concessions** — grants made to settlers under Spanish authority
- **Military muster rolls** — for the garrison at Arkansas Post
- **Administrative correspondence**

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock | Colonial-era documents; accessible remotely |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original sacramental registers |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish imperial records — the most comprehensive colonial archive |
| **Library of Congress** | Microfilm copies of select colonial records |
| **FamilySearch** | 1763–1800 Arkansas Post sacramental register (digitized, browse-only) |

### Most Accessible Indirect Route
For many researchers, the best entry point into the colonial population is **U.S. territorial land-grant confirmation proceedings filed after 1803** — these routinely named the original Spanish-era grantees and their heirs, and they are far more accessible than the Spanish imperial archives.

---

**Recommended next step:** Identify the specific ancestors you believe were in the Arkansas region before 1800, then begin with the **Arkansas History Commission** (which accepts remote inquiries) before committing to a request to the Archivo General de Indias in Seville.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish/French Colonial)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Established:** Arkansas Post, the first European settlement, was founded by Henri de Tonti for France in 1686.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) to 1763; then Spanish Louisiana after the Treaty of Paris (1763); secretly retroceded to France in 1800; transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas)
- **Population during period:** The European population was small and concentrated at Arkansas Post. No colonial census figures were returned by the population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, small-scale subsistence agriculture, military garrison activity at Arkansas Post.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Canadian and French Creole settlers; Spanish colonial officials and soldiers; Native American nations (Quapaw/Ogaxpa prominently). Small numbers of enslaved Africans and African Creoles.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers — the Church administered sacraments and maintained the only vital records.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Arkansas Post (1686); Treaty of Paris transferred Louisiana to Spain (1763); Spanish colonial administration of the District of Arkansas (1763-1800); retrocession to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763 the Arkansas region was an undifferentiated part of French Louisiana, administered from New Orleans.
- From 1763 the Spanish created the "District of Arkansas" (Distrito de Arkansas) centered on Arkansas Post.
- In 1800 Spain secretly ceded the territory back to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso); in 1803 France sold it to the United States.
- There were no county-level subdivisions before the U.S. territorial period. All pre-1800 records were created at the post/district level, not at a county level.
- After 1819 (Arkansas Territory) and 1836 (statehood), American county organization began. Records generated before those dates are not filed at any county courthouse.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the American sense before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records, Church Records, and Land and Property did not return Arkansas-specific content — the specific wiki pages appear to be absent or not yet published (the tool returned a generic page rather than an Arkansas article).
- **What exists for this period:** Sacramental registers kept by Catholic clergy — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the functional equivalent of vital records. These are the only systematic vital-event records for the colonial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers; Spanish colonial administrative padrones.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only among the European settler community.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. These are the primary source for births, weddings, and deaths of colonial Arkansas residents.
- **Digitized volume on FamilySearch:** One volume, image group 008814402, covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763-1800 (64 images). This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in Spanish. It must be examined page by page with no search function.
- **Where held (physical):** The Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (Arkansas) holds surviving registers. The Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) holds transcribed or microfilmed copies. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Language:** Spanish (post-1763 registers); French (pre-1763 registers).
- **Earlier French-period registers:** French Catholic missionary records from before 1763 are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission.

### Census records (padrones)
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** The Spanish colonial government periodically enumerated households at Arkansas Post in census-like documents called padrones. These are not U.S. federal censuses; they are Spanish administrative lists.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain; Library of Congress holds microfilm of some materials. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** The earliest FamilySearch indexed collection for Arkansas is "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124), which begins in 1819 — after the Louisiana Purchase. It does not cover the colonial period.
- **U.S. federal census:** The first federal census to cover the Arkansas region was 1810 (as part of the Territory of Orleans / Missouri Territory), after the Louisiana Purchase. No U.S. federal census covers this pre-1800 period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial courts at Arkansas Post handled civil matters including estates. Records would have been in Spanish and filed at the district/post level.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; some records may be in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). No indexed collection or digitized volume for colonial-era probate was returned by the tools.
- **After 1803:** U.S. territorial courts took over. Estate and probate records from the territorial period are at the Arkansas History Commission and county courthouses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Under Spanish rule, land grants were made by the colonial governor in the form of concesiones (concessions). These are not part of the U.S. rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Crown through the colonial governor; grants were issued at New Orleans and at the district level. The FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Land and Property page did not return Arkansas-specific content.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierra); French grants from the earlier period.
- **Critical post-1803 series:** After the Louisiana Purchase, all Spanish and French land grants had to be confirmed by Congress through U.S. land claims proceedings. The records of those confirmations — at NARA and the BLM General Land Office — name pre-1800 claimants and their heirs by name, and often describe the original grant date. This is a major indirect source for the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); NARA (post-1803 confirmations); BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant forces:** Spanish colonial garrison at Arkansas Post. Soldiers were often enrolled from Louisiana Creole, French Canadian, and Spanish populations.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (revistas de comisario), service records, correspondence. These are Spanish military records, not U.S. military records.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archivo General de Simancas, Spain; Library of Congress may hold microfilm copies.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The Catholic mission/parish cemetery at Arkansas Post is the primary burial site for the colonial period. Physical records are sparse.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) covers some Arkansas Post area graves, but colonial-era headstones are rare.

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. This record type is not applicable for the target period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for European settlers entering the Louisiana region. Passenger records for this era and port are fragmentary; New Orleans colonial-era ship records are held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Note:** French and Spanish colonial migration to Arkansas was controlled by the colonial governments, not documented in U.S. immigration records. Naturalization records in the U.S. sense do not apply.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and assessment records (contribuciones). These were kept at the district and provincial level.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); possibly the Arkansas History Commission.
- No digitized or indexed tax collection for pre-1800 Arkansas was returned by the tools.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial acts (actas notariales) documented contracts, sales, manumissions, and other legal transactions. These are held at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Spanish colonial correspondence:** Administrative letters (correspondencia) between Arkansas Post commandants and the governor at New Orleans document events, people, and disputes at the post. Held at the Archivo General de Indias and in microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- **Published local histories and transcriptions:** Early 20th-century scholars transcribed and published some Spanish colonial Arkansas records. These transcriptions may be the most accessible starting point and are held at the Arkansas History Commission library.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only volume: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), 1763-1800, image group 008814402, 64 images, in Spanish, 0% indexed | Free; must browse image by image |
| BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Post-1803 U.S. land patent confirmations that name Spanish/French grant claimants | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Post-1803 territorial and federal records | Free online catalog; some digitized |

The 6 curated external links returned by FamilySearch for the 1700-1800 window were all generic platform links (Ancestry census collection, FamilySearch Wiki vital records category, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA); none were Arkansas colonial-specific. This is a digitization gap for this period.

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the pre-1800 period. The total results count was 1, so this is the complete digitized set for the colonial period on FamilySearch — a very thin coverage gap representing an early and lightly documented colonial settlement.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish and French colonial records, padrones, land concessions; transcriptions and microfilm of sacramental registers; state and territorial records from 1803 onward | In-person and online catalog: https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-state-archives |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish period sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Contact the Diocese Archives directly |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records, military muster rolls, land concessions, correspondence, and padrones for the entire Spanish Louisiana period | In-person; online portal: http://www.culturaydeporte.gob.es/cultura/areas/archivos/mc/archivos/agi/portada.html |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some available through interlibrary loan |

## Records NOT online

- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for the District of Arkansas — physical repositories only
- Spanish colonial land concessions — physical (Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission)
- French-period (pre-1763) sacramental registers — physical (Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission)
- Spanish colonial notarial and court records — physical (Archivo General de Indias)
- Spanish military garrison records (muster rolls, service records) — physical (Archivo General de Indias; Archivo General de Simancas)
- Spanish colonial administrative correspondence — physical (Archivo General de Indias) and Library of Congress microfilm (not digitized online)

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey named a specific destruction event for the Arkansas Post colonial records. The very small number of surviving digitized records (1 volume, 64 images) and the absence of indexed collections for the colonial period indicate significant thinness of surviving material, but this may reflect the small size of the colonial settlement and the dispersal of records to Spanish archives in Europe as much as record loss. The fate of individual record classes should be confirmed with the Arkansas History Commission.

## Research tips

- The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) notes that surviving Spanish colonial records are held at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and on microfilm at the Library of Congress. Contact those repositories directly before assuming a record class does not survive.
- Because virtually all pre-1800 European settlement was at Arkansas Post, if your ancestor lived elsewhere in the region before 1800 the records may not exist at all — no other post generated comparable documentation.
- Spanish land grant confirmation proceedings, filed after 1803 with U.S. territorial authorities, routinely named the original Spanish-era grantee along with heirs and neighbors. These U.S.-period records are the most accessible indirect route into the colonial-era population.
- Published transcriptions and abstracts of colonial Arkansas records by early-20th-century historians (held at the Arkansas History Commission library) may provide the only English-language summaries of records that are otherwise in 18th-century Spanish handwriting.
- Spanish colonial records are in 18th-century Spanish script (letra española). French records use 18th-century French script. Engage a paleographer or specialist translator if you cannot read these hands.
- Neighbors of your ancestor at Arkansas Post may have traveled there together or generated overlapping records — search the full registers, not just entries for your surname.
- After the Louisiana Purchase, the same families appear in U.S. territorial records (Missouri Territory, Arkansas Territory). Tracing forward from 1803 can confirm colonial-era identities and relationships through the transition records.

- **Ethnic composition:** French Canadian and French Creole settlers; Spanish colonial officials and soldiers; Native American nations (Quapaw/Ogaxpa prominently). Small numbers of enslaved Africans and African Creoles.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers — the Church administered sacraments and maintained the only vital records.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Arkansas Post (1686); Treaty of Paris transferred Louisiana to Spain (1763); Spanish colonial administration of the District of Arkansas (1763-1800); retrocession to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763 the Arkansas region was an undifferentiated part of French Louisiana, administered from New Orleans.
- From 1763 the Spanish created the "District of Arkansas" (Distrito de Arkansas) centered on Arkansas Post.
- In 1800 Spain secretly ceded the territory back to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso); in 1803 France sold it to the United States.
- There were no county-level subdivisions before the U.S. territorial period. All pre-1800 records were created at the post/district level, not at a county level.
- After 1819 (Arkansas Territory) and 1836 (statehood), American county organization began. Records generated before those dates are not filed at any county courthouse.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the American sense before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records, Church Records, and Land and Property did not return Arkansas-specific content — the specific wiki pages appear to be absent or not yet published (the tool returned a generic page rather than an Arkansas article).
- **What exists for this period:** Sacramental registers kept by Catholic clergy — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the functional equivalent of vital records. These are the only systematic vital-event records for the colonial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers; Spanish colonial administrative padrones.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only among the European settler community.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. These are the primary source for births, weddings, and deaths of colonial Arkansas residents.
- **Digitized volume on FamilySearch:** One volume, image group 008814402, covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763-1800 (64 images). This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in Spanish. It must be examined page by page with no search function.
- **Where held (physical):** The Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (Arkansas) holds surviving registers. The Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) holds transcribed or microfilmed copies. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Language:** Spanish (post-1763 registers); French (pre-1763 registers).
- **Earlier French-period registers:** French Catholic missionary records from before 1763 are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission.

### Census records (padrones)
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** The Spanish colonial government periodically enumerated households at Arkansas Post in census-like documents called padrones. These are not U.S. federal censuses; they are Spanish administrative lists.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain; Library of Congress holds microfilm of some materials. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** The earliest FamilySearch indexed collection for Arkansas is "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124), which begins in 1819 — after the Louisiana Purchase. It does not cover the colonial period.
- **U.S. federal census:** The first federal census to cover the Arkansas region was 1810 (as part of the Territory of Orleans / Missouri Territory), after the Louisiana Purchase. No U.S. federal census covers this pre-1800 period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial courts at Arkansas Post handled civil matters including estates. Records would have been in Spanish and filed at the district/post level.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; some records may be in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). No indexed collection or digitized volume for colonial-era probate was returned by the tools.
- **After 1803:** U.S. territorial courts took over. Estate and probate records from the territorial period are at the Arkansas History Commission and county courthouses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Under Spanish rule, land grants were made by the colonial governor in the form of concesiones (concessions). These are not part of the U.S. rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Crown through the colonial governor; grants were issued at New Orleans and at the district level. The FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Land and Property page did not return Arkansas-specific content.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierra); French grants from the earlier period.
- **Critical post-1803 series:** After the Louisiana Purchase, all Spanish and French land grants had to be confirmed by Congress through U.S. land claims proceedings. The records of those confirmations — at NARA and the BLM General Land Office — name pre-1800 claimants and their heirs by name, and often describe the original grant date. This is a major indirect source for the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); NARA (post-1803 confirmations); BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant forces:** Spanish colonial garrison at Arkansas Post. Soldiers were often enrolled from Louisiana Creole, French Canadian, and Spanish populations.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (revistas de comisario), service records, correspondence. These are Spanish military records, not U.S. military records.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archivo General de Simancas, Spain; Library of Congress may hold microfilm copies.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** The Catholic mission/parish cemetery at Arkansas Post is the primary burial site for the colonial period. Physical records are sparse.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) covers some Arkansas Post area graves, but colonial-era headstones are rare.

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. This record type is not applicable for the target period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for European settlers entering the Louisiana region. Passenger records for this era and port are fragmentary; New Orleans colonial-era ship records are held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Note:** French and Spanish colonial migration to Arkansas was controlled by the colonial governments, not documented in U.S. immigration records. Naturalization records in the U.S. sense do not apply.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and assessment records (contribuciones). These were kept at the district and provincial level.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); possibly the Arkansas History Commission.
- No digitized or indexed tax collection for pre-1800 Arkansas was returned by the tools.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial acts (actas notariales) documented contracts, sales, manumissions, and other legal transactions. These are held at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Spanish colonial correspondence:** Administrative letters (correspondencia) between Arkansas Post commandants and the governor at New Orleans document events, people, and disputes at the post. Held at the Archivo General de Indias and in microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- **Published local histories and transcriptions:** Early 20th-century scholars transcribed and published some Spanish colonial Arkansas records. These transcriptions may be the most accessible starting point and are held at the Arkansas History Commission library.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only volume: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), 1763-1800, image group 008814402, 64 images, in Spanish, 0% indexed | Free; must browse image by image |
| BLM General Land Office (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Post-1803 U.S. land patent confirmations that name Spanish/French grant claimants | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Post-1803 territorial and federal records | Free online catalog; some digitized |

The 6 curated external links returned by FamilySearch for the 1700-1800 window were all generic platform links (Ancestry census collection, FamilySearch Wiki vital records category, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA); none were Arkansas colonial-specific. This is a digitization gap for this period.

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the pre-1800 period. The total results count was 1, so this is the complete digitized set for the colonial period on FamilySearch — a very thin coverage gap representing an early and lightly documented colonial settlement.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish and French colonial records, padrones, land concessions; transcriptions and microfilm of sacramental registers; state and territorial records from 1803 onward | In-person and online catalog: https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-state-archives |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish period sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Contact the Diocese Archives directly |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records, military muster rolls, land concessions, correspondence, and padrones for the entire Spanish Louisiana period | In-person; online portal: http://www.culturaydeporte.gob.es/cultura/areas/archivos/mc/archivos/agi/portada.html |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some available through interlibrary loan |

## Records NOT online

- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for the District of Arkansas — physical repositories only
- Spanish colonial land concessions — physical (Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission)
- French-period (pre-1763) sacramental registers — physical (Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission)
- Spanish colonial notarial and court records — physical (Archivo General de Indias)
- Spanish military garrison records (muster rolls, service records) — physical (Archivo General de Indias; Archivo General de Simancas)
- Spanish colonial administrative correspondence — physical (Archivo General de Indias) and Library of Congress microfilm (not digitized online)

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey named a specific destruction event for the Arkansas Post colonial records. The very small number of surviving digitized records (1 volume, 64 images) and the absence of indexed collections for the colonial period indicate significant thinness of surviving material, but this may reflect the small size of the colonial settlement and the dispersal of records to Spanish archives in Europe as much as record loss. The fate of individual record classes should be confirmed with the Arkansas History Commission.

## Research tips

- The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) notes that surviving Spanish colonial records are held at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and on microfilm at the Library of Congress. Contact those repositories directly before assuming a record class does not survive.
- Because virtually all pre-1800 European settlement was at Arkansas Post, if your ancestor lived elsewhere in the region before 1800 the records may not exist at all — no other post generated comparable documentation.
- Spanish land grant confirmation proceedings, filed after 1803 with U.S. territorial authorities, routinely named the original Spanish-era grantee along with heirs and neighbors. These U.S.-period records are the most accessible indirect route into the colonial-era population.
- Published transcriptions and abstracts of colonial Arkansas records by early-20th-century historians (held at the Arkansas History Commission library) may provide the only English-language summaries of records that are otherwise in 18th-century Spanish handwriting.
- Spanish colonial records are in 18th-century Spanish script (letra española). French records use 18th-century French script. Engage a paleographer or specialist translator if you cannot read these hands.
- Neighbors of your ancestor at Arkansas Post may have traveled there together or generated overlapping records — search the full registers, not just entries for your surname.
- After the Louisiana Purchase, the same families appear in U.S. territorial records (Missouri Territory, Arkansas Territory). Tracing forward from 1803 can confirm colonial-era identities and relationships through the transition records.

Here is the locality guide's response:

---

In 1790, the land that would become Ohio was not yet a state — it was the **Northwest Territory**, organized under the federal Ordinance of 1787. Only two counties existed at that moment:

- **Washington County** (formed 1788) — covering roughly the eastern half of modern Ohio
- **Hamilton County** (formed 1790) — covering the west

Because county boundaries shifted constantly in the years that followed, any record from 1790 must be looked up under whichever of those two counties held that piece of land on the date of the event, not under the county name that sits there today.

---

### Record Gaps & What Survives

There was no civil registration of births or deaths, and the **1790 federal census did not include the territory at all**. Despite those gaps, the following records do survive:

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Land grants** | Three separate systems (see below) |
| **County marriage registers** | Begin 1789 |
| **Church baptism & burial registers** | Varies by congregation |
| **Territorial court minutes** | At the Ohio History Connection, Columbus |
| **Military pension files** | For veteran settlers |

---

### Three Land-Grant Systems in Ohio

Ohio is unique in having three overlapping land systems — critical to know for research:

1. **Federal Patents** — Searchable online at the [BLM General Land Office](https://glorecords.blm.gov)
2. **Virginia Military District** — Physical warrants at the **Virginia State Library, Richmond**
3. **Connecticut Western Reserve** — Records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**

---

### Key Repository

The **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus holds the early territorial court and land records.

---

Virginia Military District bounty land warrant applications often name the veteran, his wife (including maiden name), children, and service dates — a high-value source for families settling in the district between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers.

Early court and land records for the territorial period are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (ca. 1790)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, encompassing present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from it on March 1, 1803.
- **County seat / administrative center:** In 1790, civil authority was exercised through Washington County (organized 1788, seat: Marietta) and Hamilton County (organized 1790, seat: Cincinnati). The territorial governor's seat was at Marietta.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803); Ohio became a state in 1803.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the tools for 1780–1810. The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory. The first federal enumeration for this region was the 1800 territorial census.
- **Economy:** Frontier settlement, subsistence farming, fur trade, and early land speculation. The Ohio River corridor was a primary migration and trade route.
- **Ethnic composition:** American-born settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England predominated. The Delaware, Shawnee, Wyandot, and Miami peoples were the indigenous populations throughout the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian missionaries, and Baptist congregations were among the earliest; formal church establishment was sparse in 1790. No specific denomination list was returned by the wiki pages for Ohio.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); first permanent American settlement at Marietta (1788); Northwest Indian War through the early 1790s; Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795), which opened much of Ohio to settlement; Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1788:** The entire region was administered as the undivided Northwest Territory with no county-level organization.
- **1788:** Washington County was the first county organized in the territory, covering the eastern portion (essentially east of the Scioto River).
- **1790:** Hamilton County was organized from the western portion of the territory (around present-day Cincinnati).
- **Implication for 1790 research:** At the research date of 1790, events in the eastern portion of what is now Ohio fell under Washington County; events in the western portion fell under Hamilton County. County formation was rapid thereafter — a location in one county in 1790 was often in a new county by 1800 or 1803. Researchers must identify which county held jurisdiction on the specific event date and search under that county name, not modern county boundaries. According to the FamilySearch Wiki, early court and land records for the territorial period are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in 1790. Ohio was a federal territory. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic content and did not state when civil registration began. The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785) begins in 1789, indicating county-level marriage recording started immediately with Washington County's organization.

Here is the locality guide for **California in the 1850s Gold Rush era**:

---

## California, 1848–1860 — Locality Research Guide

### Overview of Record Availability

Records from this decade are uneven, largely because the mining population was highly transient. Key context:

- **Civil registration** (births, marriages, deaths) began at the county level from 1850 but was inconsistently kept, especially in mining camps.
- **The 1850 federal census county returns for California were destroyed**, making the **1852 California State Census** the most valuable single Gold Rush-era enumeration — it is approximately 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

| Record | Coverage | Repository / Access |
|---|---|---|
| **1852 California State Census** | ~88% indexed by name | FamilySearch (searchable) |
| **Federal Censuses** (1860, 1870) | Post-rush snapshot | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **Ship Passenger Manifests** | Sea arrivals — first US document for many foreign-born miners | National Archives, San Bruno, CA |
| **Mining Claim Registers** (San Francisco, 1849–1855) | Browse-only, no name index | FamilySearch digitized image volumes |
| **Port Arrival Registers** (Sacramento, 1849–1858) | Browse-only, no name index | FamilySearch digitized image volumes |
| **County Deed & Land Records** | Property in mining districts | County recorder offices; some on FamilySearch |
| **Probate Records** | Miners who died intestate or with assets | County Superior Courts; some digitized |
| **Voter Registration / Great Registers** | Begins **1866** — misses those who left or died before that | California State Archives |
| **Naturalization Records** | Federal courts, District Courts | National Archives, San Bruno; FamilySearch |
| **Newspapers** | Mining camp papers named individuals for business, legal notices, deaths | California Digital Newspaper Collection; Newspapers.com |

---

### Manuscript & Special Collections

- **California State Library** (Sacramento) — diaries, letters, and personal papers naming individuals absent from official records.
- **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** — one of the premier repositories for Gold Rush-era manuscript collections, including regional histories that name miners and settlers.

---

### Research Strategy Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — it is your best substitute for the lost 1850 federal return.
2. **Ship passenger manifests** are often the first U.S. document for immigrants who came by sea (Cape Horn or Panama route); search by departure port as well as arrival.
3. **Mining Claim Registers and Port Arrival Registers** are digitized but completely unindexed — you must browse image-by-image. Use these only when you have a time and place narrow enough to make browsing feasible.
4. **Great Registers (voter lists) begin in 1866** — useful for anyone who settled and stayed, but they miss those who left California or died before that date.
5. For foreign-born miners, check **naturalization records** in federal district courts held at the National Archives, San Bruno.

---

Let me know which ancestor you're tracking or which record type you'd like to pursue next!
