# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was chartered as a British colony in 1607 and declared independence in 1776, becoming the Commonwealth of Virginia. It was ratified as a U.S. state in 1788 (FamilySearch dateRange: +1788/).
- **Administrative centers:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1780); Richmond (state capital from 1780).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain pre-1776; independent Commonwealth 1776–1788; U.S. state 1788 onward.
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period. The 1790 federal census — the closest enumeration — was destroyed, and county tax lists from 1782 are the primary surviving population evidence for the war era.
- **Economy:** Tobacco and wheat agriculture; Chesapeake Bay and tidal river trade; wartime manufacturing and supply.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English settlers; Scottish and Irish immigrants; German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley; substantial enslaved African population. Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records).
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established church until 1786 disestablishment), Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Lutheran, Methodist.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia declaration of independence June 1776; British coastal raids; French alliance and Yorktown campaign; British surrender at Yorktown October 19, 1781.

## Boundary changes
Virginia's territory during 1775–1783 was substantially larger than the modern state. Kentucky County was created from Virginia in 1776 and remained Virginia territory until Kentucky's separate statehood in 1792. Western Virginia (now West Virginia) was part of Virginia until 1863. New counties were formed from existing ones throughout the 1770s–1780s; records follow the county that existed at the time of an event, not modern county lines. Researchers must identify the correct county for each event date and may need to search predecessor counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births or deaths existed in Virginia during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Virginia-specific vital records page; the constructed URL https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records resolved to a generic page. Virginia's statewide registration start date is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and marriage registers were kept at the **county** level throughout this period and are the primary civil marriage record. Births and deaths were not systematically registered by the government.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1734285 "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary substitute for birth and death evidence in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Lutheran.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Anglican parish registers often extend decades before the Revolution.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (1,234,567 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230); Library of Virginia; denominational archives. The wiki_place_page calls returned only a generic guide page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide), not Virginia-specific denominational detail.
- **Language:** English throughout this period for major denominations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) is the nearest to the target period but falls outside it. Critically, the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records). No 1790 Virginia federal census survives.
- **Substitute — tax lists:** County personal property tax lists from 1782 onward are the standard substitute. FamilySearch volume 005301449 (87 images, state enumerations/tax lists 1782–1799) is digitized and **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — it must be searched by text rather than by surname browse. FamilySearch collection 1456723 "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) covers the end of the target period and immediately after.
- **State census:** No Virginia-specific state census for 1775–1783 was identified in tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, county court order books.
- **Date range:** Virginia county court records date from the 1630s; records for 1775–1783 exist at the county level.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 2134567 "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (1,789,012 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). FamilySearch volume 005301448 (158 images, Augusta County court order books 1775–1795, **61% name-indexed**) is one county-level court volume confirmed by volume_search for this period.
- **Testate/intestate:** Probate files exist for both testate (wills) and intestate (administrations) estates; will books and administration bonds are the respective series to search.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state — land was granted by the colonial and state government, not the federal GLO).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Virginia Land and Property wiki URL returned only a generic page. Per wiki_search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records), Virginia granted post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to those claims.
- **Types:** Deeds, patents, land bounty warrants, mortgages, tax lists.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285); county deed books at county courthouses and Library of Virginia. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images, Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779–1800) is digitized but **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.

### Military records
This is the highest-priority record class for the 1775–1783 target period.

- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types and repositories (all from FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records):**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls — NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records — Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files — NARA Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records — Library of Virginia
  - Post-war bounty land warrants and surveys (Virginia Military District of Ohio) — Virginia State Library
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** Collection 1945678 "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (345,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) — covers the exact target period.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** 005301447 — Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (341 images, 1779–1800) — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Fold3:** https://www.fold3.com/ — returned as a curated external resource for military records (subscription required).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — returned as a curated external resource.
- **Physical records:** Church burial registers in FamilySearch collection 1598230 "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" cover this period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia had newspapers during the Revolutionary period (e.g., Virginia Gazette, Williamsburg). Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a tool-returned external resource.
- **Content value:** Wartime newspapers contained military appointment notices, muster calls, estate notices, and early death notices.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Library of Congress; university collections.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** No port-specific immigration collections for 1775–1783 were returned by tool results. Loyalists who left Virginia may appear in British claims records held at UK repositories. Modern naturalization procedures did not apply to this period.
- **Inland records:** Declarations of intention were not a Revolutionary-era record type; citizenship derived from state residency. County court records may name foreign-born residents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and land tax, assessed at the **county** level.
- **Date range:** Statewide tax records begin from 1782 per tool-returned collections and volumes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed, 1782–1799); Library of Virginia holds originals.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782–1783 personal property tax lists are the closest surviving enumeration to the wartime period itself and the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census.

### Other record types
- **Pension application narratives:** NARA RG 15 pension files frequently contain the veteran's own sworn narrative of service, family ages, and county of residence — genealogically richer than muster rolls.
- **Loyalist/Tory records:** County court order books may contain proceedings against Loyalists; Virginia confiscated Loyalist property, generating deed and court records.
- **County and town histories:** 19th-century published Virginia county histories frequently reprint early records and list founding families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (col. 1945678, 345,678 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (col. 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (col. 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (col. 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (col. 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — https://www.fold3.com/ | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free/in-person; many digitized on Fold3 |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records — https://www.findagrave.com/ | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — https://www.newspapers.com/ | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. census and other collections — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search was filtered to Military record types and returned 3 digitized volumes as a complete result set (totalResults: 3, no nextPageToken). A broader volume_search without record-type filtering would be needed to assess all digitized volumes for this place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; state tax lists; land records; state legislative and executive records; state navy records | In-person; some records digitized on FamilySearch |
| NARA (National Archives) | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; many digitized on Fold3/FamilySearch |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land warrants and surveys | In-person |
| County courthouses | Deed books; will books; marriage bonds; court order books | In-person or mail; many filmed by FamilySearch |
| Virginia Historical Society, Richmond | Family papers; published county and military histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records held at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized; only partial militia records appear in online collections.
- Pension application narrative files (NARA RG 15) — the full case files are not comprehensively digitized; Fold3 holds portions.
- Virginia State Navy records are not confirmed as fully online in any tool result for this survey.
- Virginia bounty land warrant and survey records (Virginia Military District of Ohio) at the Virginia State Library — FamilySearch volume 005301447 holds 341 browse-only images; additional records may exist only in physical form.
- Most Virginia county deed books, will books, and court order books are FamilySearch microfilm or browse-only images; name-indexing is incomplete.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records). County tax lists from 1782 are the standard substitute. No other specific record losses for 1775–1783 were stated in tool results; an empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files, not service records.** Pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA RG 15) contain personal narratives — family ages, county of residence, service descriptions — making them genealogically richer than muster rolls alone. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony.** The FamilySearch collection 1945678 "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" is the logical first search. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Use the 1782–1783 tax lists as the wartime census substitute.** The 1790 Virginia federal census does not survive. Collection 1456723 and FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) are the closest enumeration to the war years.
- **Follow bounty land warrants into Ohio.** Virginia granted lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans after the war. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their claims and may record family details even if the family never moved to Ohio. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Kentucky records for 1775–1783 are Virginia records.** Kentucky did not become a separate state until 1792; families in present-day Kentucky generated records under Virginia county jurisdictions during the war.
- **Search church registers when civil vital records are absent.** No statewide registration existed during the target period; baptisms, burials, and marriages in church registers (collection 1598230) are the primary vital evidence.
- **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page calls returned only a generic guide.** Researchers should visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for current Virginia-specific wiki guidance beyond what this automated survey captured.

- **Content value:** Wartime newspapers contained military appointment notices, muster calls, estate notices, and early death notices.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Library of Congress; university collections.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** No port-specific immigration collections for 1775–1783 were returned by tool results. Loyalists who left Virginia may appear in British claims records held at UK repositories. Modern naturalization procedures did not apply to this period.
- **Inland records:** Declarations of intention were not a Revolutionary-era record type; citizenship derived from state residency. County court records may name foreign-born residents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County personal property and land tax, assessed at the **county** level.
- **Date range:** Statewide tax records begin from 1782 per tool-returned collections and volumes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed, 1782–1799); Library of Virginia holds originals.
- **Substitute value:** The 1782–1783 personal property tax lists are the closest surviving enumeration to the wartime period itself and the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census.

### Other record types
- **Pension application narratives:** NARA RG 15 pension files frequently contain the veteran's own sworn narrative of service, family ages, and county of residence — genealogically richer than muster rolls.
- **Loyalist/Tory records:** County court order books may contain proceedings against Loyalists; Virginia confiscated Loyalist property, generating deed and court records.
- **County and town histories:** 19th-century published Virginia county histories frequently reprint early records and list founding families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (col. 1945678, 345,678 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (col. 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (col. 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (col. 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (col. 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — https://www.fold3.com/ | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ — Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free/in-person; many digitized on Fold3 |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records — https://www.findagrave.com/ | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers — https://www.newspapers.com/ | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. census and other collections — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search was filtered to Military record types and returned 3 digitized volumes as a complete result set (totalResults: 3, no nextPageToken). A broader volume_search without record-type filtering would be needed to assess all digitized volumes for this place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; state tax lists; land records; state legislative and executive records; state navy records | In-person; some records digitized on FamilySearch |
| NARA (National Archives) | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15) | In-person; many digitized on Fold3/FamilySearch |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land warrants and surveys | In-person |
| County courthouses | Deed books; will books; marriage bonds; court order books | In-person or mail; many filmed by FamilySearch |
| Virginia Historical Society, Richmond | Family papers; published county and military histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records held at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized; only partial militia records appear in online collections.
- Pension application narrative files (NARA RG 15) — the full case files are not comprehensively digitized; Fold3 holds portions.
- Virginia State Navy records are not confirmed as fully online in any tool result for this survey.
- Virginia bounty land warrant and survey records (Virginia Military District of Ohio) at the Virginia State Library — FamilySearch volume 005301447 holds 341 browse-only images; additional records may exist only in physical form.
- Most Virginia county deed books, will books, and court order books are FamilySearch microfilm or browse-only images; name-indexing is incomplete.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records). County tax lists from 1782 are the standard substitute. No other specific record losses for 1775–1783 were stated in tool results; an empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files, not service records.** Pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA RG 15) contain personal narratives — family ages, county of residence, service descriptions — making them genealogically richer than muster rolls alone. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony.** The FamilySearch collection 1945678 "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" is the logical first search. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Use the 1782–1783 tax lists as the wartime census substitute.** The 1790 Virginia federal census does not survive. Collection 1456723 and FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) are the closest enumeration to the war years.
- **Follow bounty land warrants into Ohio.** Virginia granted lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans after the war. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their claims and may record family details even if the family never moved to Ohio. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)
- **Kentucky records for 1775–1783 are Virginia records.** Kentucky did not become a separate state until 1792; families in present-day Kentucky generated records under Virginia county jurisdictions during the war.
- **Search church registers when civil vital records are absent.** No statewide registration existed during the target period; baptisms, burials, and marriages in church registers (collection 1598230) are the primary vital evidence.
- **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page calls returned only a generic guide.** Researchers should visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for current Virginia-specific wiki guidance beyond what this automated survey captured.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s is a genuinely complex research jurisdiction because the city cycled through French, Spanish, briefly French again, and then American governance all within a few decades, and two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 wiped out much of what the French and early Spanish administrations recorded. Here is what the survey found about what survived, what was lost, and where to look.

**The Civil Law Difference**
The single most important structural fact is that Louisiana runs on civil law derived from the Napoleonic Code, not English common law. This means property sales, estate proceedings (called *successions*, not probate), guardianships (called *tutorships*), and contracts were all executed before a notary and recorded in the Notarial Archives — not at a courthouse deed room as in every other U.S. state. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts going back to 1734. FamilySearch has digitized exactly one volume from that archive — 167 images of notarial acts from 1803–1820 (imageGroupNumber 004990115) — and it is 0% name-indexed, meaning it must be browsed image by image. Everything else in the Notarial Archives requires an in-person visit or written request.

**The Fires: 1788 and 1794**
The two great fires destroyed most records from the French colonial period and a substantial portion of the early Spanish period. What survived the fires is the basis of all early research:

- The **Spanish Cabildo** (colonial governing body) kept administrative and judicial records from 1769–1803 that survived intact. These are held at the **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge and the **Louisiana State Museum**.
- The **Catholic sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral** survive from 1731 but have gaps. After the 1794 fire, Bishop Peñalver y Cárdenas ordered reconstruction of damaged registers, and some pre-fire notarial acts were recopied. These reconstructed records and the Cabildo archive are the primary substitutes for destroyed material.

**Vital Records in the 1800–1850 Period**
There was no comprehensive civil registration for most of this era. Catholic church registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are the main source. FamilySearch holds these in the collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905), free to search).

Critically, St. Louis Cathedral maintained **separate sacramental register series for free people of color** (*gens de couleur libres*), a uniquely large and legally documented community in New Orleans. Researchers must search those specific register series.

**Key FamilySearch Collections**
| Collection | ID |
|---|---|
| Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | 1612905 |
| Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | 2078341 |
| Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 | 1798054 |
| Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 | 1543892 (index only, no images) |

**Flooding, Epidemics, and Hurricanes**
These repeatedly damaged archival holdings throughout the period, but no confirmed destruction of any specific 1800–1850 record set (beyond the pre-1800 fire losses) emerged from this survey. An empty search result means a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction — the repository guide above lists where each record type physically lives.

---

If you want a research plan built around specific ancestors in New Orleans during this period, the research-plan skill can build one from this locality guide.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718 by the French. It passed to Spanish control in 1763, briefly returned to France in 1800, and was transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Orleans Parish is coterminous with the city of New Orleans.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans; Orleans Parish and the city are coterminous.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French colony → Spanish colony (1763) → French territory (1800) → Orleans Territory, United States (1803) → State of Louisiana (1812)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction.
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port — maritime trade, cotton, sugar, and enslaved-person markets dominated. Significant commerce with the Caribbean, Atlantic seaboard, and Mississippi River hinterland.
- **Ethnic composition:** A highly diverse population including Creoles of French and Spanish descent, Anglo-American migrants after 1803, enslaved African Americans, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), German and Irish immigrants (especially 1830s–1840s), and Saint-Domingue (Haitian) refugees (especially after 1809).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic dominant (St. Louis Cathedral, founded 1727 on its current site); Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations established from the American period (post-1803).
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Louisiana statehood (1812), Battle of New Orleans (January 1815), repeated yellow fever epidemics throughout the period, Saint-Domingue refugee influx (ca. 1809), large-scale Irish and German immigration (1830s–1840s).

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1803:** Records created under French rule (before 1763), Spanish rule (1763–1803), and briefly French again (1800–1803) were kept by different governmental bodies under different legal systems.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transfers the territory to the United States; the Orleans Territory is organized.
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted as a state. Orleans Parish formally established as coterminous with New Orleans.
- **Civil law continuity:** Louisiana adopted the civil law (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law, a tradition maintained through statehood. Property, succession, and contract records are therefore held in notarial archives rather than common-law courthouse deed rooms — this is the single most important structural difference from every other U.S. state.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana vital records returned only generic content in this survey and did not state a specific civil registration start date for Louisiana or New Orleans. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) implies some death registration exists from 1819, but the level at which that registration was required (city, parish, or statewide) cannot be confirmed from tool results. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for current guidance.
- **What exists:** For the early 1800s, comprehensive civil vital registration did not exist. Church sacramental registers are the primary record of baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) covers this period. "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054) partially overlaps the later portion.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed, online); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge (original state-level records); Orleans Parish Civil District Court (parish-level civil records).
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era record base. St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1731 but have gaps. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial acts; records of the Spanish colonial Cabildo.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic dominant — St. Louis Cathedral served the city from its founding. Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian) appear from the American period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Catholic registers may also include confirmations and records of free people of color and enslaved persons. Separate registers were maintained for free people of color.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) — indexed with images. Original registers are at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for Catholic registers from the colonial periods; English appears from the American period (post-1803).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1612905).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** New Orleans appears in the federal censuses of 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850. All are within or at the close of the target period.
- **Territorial/state enumerations:** Louisiana conducted some territorial-era enumerations; check the Louisiana State Archives for intercensal sources.
- **Spanish-period padrones:** Under Spanish rule, periodic parish censuses (padrones) were taken. These survive with gaps at the Louisiana State Archives and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for this period are indexed and available online through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/, subscription) and FamilySearch (free).

### Probate records
- **Louisiana equivalent — Successions:** Louisiana does not use the term "probate." The civil law equivalents are successions (estate proceedings), tutorships (guardianship of minors), and interdictions (legal incapacity proceedings). New Orleans in the early 1800s is a genuinely complex research jurisdiction because the city cycled through French, Spanish, briefly French again, and then American governance all within a few decades, and two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 wiped out much of what the French and early Spanish administrations recorded. Here is what the survey found about what survived, what was lost, and where to look.

The single most important structural fact is that Louisiana runs on civil law derived from the Napoleonic Code, not English common law. This means property sales, estate proceedings (called "successions" not probate), guardianships (called "tutorships"), and contracts were all executed before a notary and recorded in the Notarial Archives — not at a courthouse deed room as in every other U.S. state. This is the primary land, property, and succession repository for the city. FamilySearch has digitized exactly one volume from that archive — 167 images of notarial acts from 1803 to 1820, imageGroupNumber 004990115 — and it is 0% name-indexed, meaning it must be browsed image by image. Everything else in the Notarial Archives requires an in-person visit or written request to the Notarial Archives Research Center.

For the fires: the 1788 and 1794 blazes destroyed most records from the French colonial period and a substantial portion of the early Spanish period. What survived the fires is the basis of all early research. The Spanish Cabildo (the colonial governing body) kept administrative and judicial records from 1769 to 1803 that survived intact — these are held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge and the Louisiana State Museum. These reconstructed records and the Cabildo archive are the primary substitutes for the destroyed material.

The Catholic church registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are the main source. - **Administrative center:** New Orleans; Orleans Parish and the city are coterminous.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French colony → Spanish colony (1763) → French territory (1800) → Orleans Territory, United States (1803) → State of Louisiana (1812)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction.
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port — maritime trade, cotton, sugar, and enslaved-person markets dominated. Significant commerce with the Caribbean, Atlantic seaboard, and Mississippi River hinterland.
- **Ethnic composition:** A highly diverse population including Creoles of French and Spanish descent, Anglo-American migrants after 1803, enslaved African Americans, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), German and Irish immigrants (especially 1830s–1840s), and Saint-Domingue (Haitian) refugees (especially after 1809).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic dominant (St. Louis Cathedral, founded 1727 on its current site); Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations established from the American period (post-1803).

- Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods throughout the period further damaged archival holdings (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans).
- No tool result confirmed specific destruction of particular record sets during the 1800–1850 target period itself (as opposed to pre-1800 losses); an empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.
- The notarial volume's coverage description as "surviving microfilm copies" implies selective survival of the originals.
- **Substitutes for lost records:** Notarial acts (some pre-fire acts were recopied); Spanish Cabildo records (survived intact); Catholic sacramental registers (partially reconstructed after 1794 by order of Bishop Peñalver y Cárdenas); published indexes and transcriptions by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society and the New Orleans Public Library.

## Research tips
- **The civil law distinction is essential.** Louisiana's Napoleonic Code-derived system means virtually all significant legal transactions were executed before a notary and recorded in the Notarial Archives, not at a courthouse deed room. Searching only courthouse records misses the main documentary source. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **St. Louis Cathedral registers are the primary vital record substitute.** For 1800–1850, search FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) first. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Plan an in-person visit or written request to the New Orleans Notarial Archives.** The 30+ million pages there are irreplaceable for property, succession, manumission, and contract research and are largely not indexed online.
- **Use Louisiana's specific terminology.** A succession is what other states call an estate/probate proceeding; a tutorship is a guardianship; an interdiction is a legal incapacity proceeding. Searches under "probate" miss these.
- **Records span three languages.** French, Spanish, and English all appear in this period. Colonial-era Catholic registers are in French or Spanish; Spanish-period notarial acts are in Spanish.
- **Free people of color records are separate and specific.** New Orleans maintained separate sacramental register series for free people of color; notarial acts document manumissions and property ownership in detail. Search these series when researching anyone from that community.
- **The Spanish Cabildo records survived the fires.** The administrative and judicial records of the Cabildo (1769–1803) are a rich pre-American source. Held at the Louisiana State Archives and Louisiana State Museum.
- **The 1809 Saint-Domingue refugee wave nearly doubled the free Black population.** Ancestors arriving ca. 1809 may have Saint-Domingue (Haitian) origins; search Caribbean records in parallel.

Here is the locality guide's findings for **New Orleans in the early 1800s**:

---

## Record Survival & Substitutes — New Orleans, Early 1800s

### The Disaster Landscape
The two great fires of **1788 and 1794** — which destroyed much of the French Quarter — occurred *before* your target period. So while those fires were devastating, the most important record classes for the early 1800s actually survived them.

### What Survived and Where to Find It

**1. Sacramental Registers of St. Louis Cathedral**
- Baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731** (with some gaps)
- FamilySearch holds a large indexed collection: *Louisiana Church Records, 1718–1925* (with images)

**2. Notarial Records**
- Now held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
- Over **30 million pages** dating to 1734
- FamilySearch has a browse-only volume of notarial acts from **1803–1820** (in French and English) — must be examined image by image

**3. Colonial Government Records (Cabildo)**
- Records of the Spanish colonial governing body, now at the **Louisiana State Museum**

---

### Key FamilySearch Collections for Early Louisiana
| Collection | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Church Records | 1718–1925 | Indexed with images |
| Louisiana Successions/Probate | 1756–1984 | Indexed with images |
| Louisiana Statewide Death Index | From 1819 | Index only |
| Louisiana Parish Marriages | From 1837 | Indexed with images |

---

### The Most Important Substitute Strategy: Notarial Acts
Because Louisiana follows **civil law** (not common law), notarial acts are the *primary substitute* whenever any other record is missing. Every property transfer, will, emancipation, contract, and business agreement passed through a notary — creating a continuous documentary trail that survived fires and floods. If a vital record is gone, start with the notarial archives.

---

### Next Steps
- Check civil registration start dates directly at the [FamilySearch Louisiana Vital Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records)
- Consider building a research plan against the specific ancestor you are tracing using these record classes as your guide

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by French colonists; Orleans Parish (the civil parish containing the city) established under American territorial administration after the Louisiana Purchase (1803)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (Louisiana uses parishes, not counties; there is no county seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812); State of Louisiana (from 1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures for this specific place and period were not returned by the survey tools
- **Economy:** Port trade, sugar and cotton export, banking, river commerce; New Orleans was the dominant port city of the Mississippi Valley
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, African-descended free persons of color, enslaved persons, Anglo-American migrants post-1803, growing German and Irish immigrant populations in the 1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (predominant; St. Louis Cathedral the principal parish); Protestant congregations arrived with Anglo-American settlement after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Louisiana statehood (1812), Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods; devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 (colonial era) destroyed much of the French Quarter and many records — these losses directly determine what survives for 1800–1850 research

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1803:** New Orleans was under Spanish colonial administration (from 1763); records created under Spanish governance in Spanish and French
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States; administrative records from the transitional moment are in both Spanish and American series
- **1804–1812:** Territory of Orleans (the territorial predecessor to statehood); territorial records held at the Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge
- **1812:** Louisiana became a state; Orleans Parish established as the civil parish jurisdiction for New Orleans

Records from 1800–1803 are part of the Spanish colonial administrative series. After 1803, records began transitioning to American forms while many residents and clerks continued using French and Spanish. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds continuous notarial records across all these jurisdictional transitions.

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is stated where the tool results provide it.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records did not return specific content in this survey (all returned a generic fallback page); confirmed civil registration start dates and levels cannot be stated. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) implies some death registration from 1819, and "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054) implies some marriage registration from 1837, but neither collection title states the jurisdictional level (parish-level, statewide, or another). Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly for confirmed dates and levels.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds the Louisiana Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (index only, no images; 2,345,678 records) and Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (indexed + images; 567,890 records, 283,945 images). These cover only portions of the target period from their stated start dates.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online); original civil records at the Louisiana State Archives and individual parish courthouses
- **Gaps:** The first portion of the target period — 1800–1819 for deaths and 1800–1837 for marriages — lacks a civil registration series in the returned FamilySearch collections; church records are the primary substitute
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral record baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps from the 1788 and 1794 fires); included in FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (predominant; St. Louis Cathedral New Orleans is the primary parish for the city); Protestant denominations established congregations following Anglo-American migration after 1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) — indexed + images, 987,654 records, 493,827 images
- **Language:** Pre-1803 registers in French and Spanish; after 1803, mixed French, Spanish, and English; French remained dominant in Catholic records for decades into the American period

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses cover this period; New Orleans and Orleans Parish appear in all of them
- **State/territorial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Census did not return specific content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census directly for any territorial or state census series.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial enumerations may exist for the 1800–1803 period in territorial archives
- **Access:** Federal census records for this period are available through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana civil law calls these **successions** (not probate); also tutorships (guardianship) and interdictions. Wills, estate inventories, succession petitions, and related documents are all in the succession series, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System.
- **Testate or intestate:** Louisiana civil law succession differs from common-law probate; search the successions series regardless of whether the person left a will, as the documents produced differ under each scenario
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) covers the full target period — indexed + images, 456,789 records, 228,394 images
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; FamilySearch collection 2078341 online

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French arpent system (long lots running back from the river or waterway), not the rectangular Public Land Survey System; Louisiana is a federal land state for grants after 1803, but colonial grants use the arpent system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Land and Property did not return specific content in this survey. For colonial-period grants (before 1803), the Spanish and French colonial archives are the relevant source. For post-1803 federal patents, the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) holds the records. Every property transfer in Louisiana was executed before a notary public.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records; **notarial acts are the primary vehicle for all land transactions** under Louisiana civil law
- **Date range:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from 1734; FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Notarial Acts (imageGroupNumber 004990115) covering 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), in French and English — this volume must be examined image by image
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters); Orleans Parish courthouse; Louisiana State Archives; FamilySearch (1 browse-only volume)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815, War of 1812); territorial militia service (1804–1812); the Civil War is outside this period
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, War of 1812 records at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** New Orleans's above-ground cemetery tradition produced distinctive burial records; St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (Catholic, established 1789) and St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (established 1823) are the principal early-19th-century cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Catholic burial registers in the sacramental series (collection 1612905); sexton records for some cemeteries held at the individual cemeteries or the Archdiocese of New Orleans

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several French- and English-language papers existed in early-19th-century New Orleans; specific titles and date ranges were not returned in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; Louisiana State Library and Tulane University for physical/microfilm holdings
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, sheriff's sale announcements (important for property and debt research), ship arrivals (relevant for immigration research)

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was the primary Gulf Coast entry point; passengers arriving from Europe, the Caribbean, and coastal US ports passed through here
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (port of New Orleans lists); naturalization declarations filed in any court of record before 1906 — in Louisiana, naturalization records may be in territorial or state district courts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry (subscription) for indexed passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and poll tax records generated at the parish level in Orleans Parish
- **Date range:** Territorial and early-state tax lists survive at the Louisiana State Archives; specific date ranges were not returned in this survey
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; some records digitized on FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and can place an ancestor in Orleans Parish during the 1800–1810 period before reliable federal census coverage for this area

### Other record types
- **Notarial records (unique to Louisiana):** Every legal transaction — property sales, wills, contracts, emancipations, apprenticeships, business partnerships — was executed before a notary and preserved in bound volumes. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters. These records survived the fires and floods that damaged other record classes and are the single most important substitute source for missing vital and court records. FamilySearch has one browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 1803–1820, 167 images, French/English).
- **Cabildo records:** Records of the Spanish colonial governing body survived and document administrative, legal, and governmental activity into the early 1800s, per the same wiki_search result. The Louisiana State Museum holds Cabildo records.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** New Orleans was the largest slave market in North America during this period. Bills of sale, emancipation documents, and slave manifests passed through notaries and courts and survive in the notarial records and in NARA holdings. The Louisiana State Archives also holds records relevant to researching enslaved ancestors.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905, 987,654 records, indexed + images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341, 456,789 records, indexed + images); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, index only, no images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054, 567,890 records, indexed + images); Notarial Acts volume 004990115 (1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only, French/English) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records including passenger lists, naturalizations, military records | Free / mail request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching Orleans Parish / New Orleans for the period 1800–1850. That single volume is detailed above and represents the complete result set — no nextPageToken was returned. Additional FamilySearch microfilm holdings may exist outside digitized volume counts.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734; continuous across all jurisdictional transitions | In-person research; inquire for remote access |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial records (1804–1812), state records from 1812, tax lists, court records | In-person / online request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Successions (probate), court records, marriage records | In-person / mail |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers | In-person / mail |
| St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans | Original sacramental registers | Contact cathedral archive |
| Louisiana State Museum | Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) | In-person |
| NARA | Federal census, military records, passenger lists, naturalizations | In-person / online via Ancestry / Fold3 |
| Tulane University and LSU libraries | Local history collections, newspapers, published family histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts beyond the single FamilySearch browse-only volume (004990115, 1803–1820) are physical only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) — held at the Louisiana State Museum; not returned as an online collection in this survey
- Original sacramental registers beyond what is captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 — Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual parishes
- Tax records for Orleans Parish — Louisiana State Archives; extent of online availability not returned in this survey
- Territorial court records (1804–1812) — Louisiana State Archives; extent of online availability not returned in this survey

## Known record losses
The Wikipedia search result (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) states that New Orleans suffered devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records, and that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings. These disasters predate the 1800–1850 target period but directly determine what is and is not available to researchers studying that era.

The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters states that despite these losses, significant genealogical sources survived: the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with some gaps), the notarial records, and the Cabildo records. No tool result in this survey names a specific record set as destroyed by a post-1800 event — empty search results for some record categories reflect digitization gaps, not confirmed losses.

**Substitutes for damaged or missing records:**
- **Notarial acts** (the most important Louisiana substitute): because every legal transaction required a notary, these records survived even where vital registers and court records were damaged; they can reconstruct family relationships, property ownership, and chronology
- **St. Louis Cathedral registers** (survived the fires): baptisms, marriages, and burials in the sacramental registers provide vital data across the entire target period and before it
- **Federal census** (1810–1850): decennial census records are independent of local archive survival
- **Tax records**: for the period between censuses and for 1800–1810, parish-level tax lists can place an ancestor in Orleans Parish
- **Passenger lists**: immigrant ancestors' arrival manifests at the Port of New Orleans are federal records, surviving independently of local archives
- **Published local histories and genealogies**: Tulane University and LSU libraries hold 19th-century New Orleans family and city histories that may preserve transcriptions of records since lost

## Research tips
- **Notarial records are essential, not optional.** Louisiana's civil law system means every legal event passed through a notary. Any ancestor who bought or sold property, made a will, freed an enslaved person, or entered a significant contract did so before a notary. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734 and is the starting point for serious research, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters.
- **Do not assume records are destroyed because fires occurred.** The fires of 1788 and 1794 were severe, but St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers, the notarial records, and the Cabildo records all survived (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Verify whether the specific record class you need is among the survivors before concluding a gap exists.
- **Louisiana uses "successions," not "probate."** Search FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) for both testate and intestate succession proceedings. Louisiana's forced heirship rules (Napoleonic Code) mean family members who might not appear in a common-law probate file may be named in a Louisiana succession.
- **Records are in multiple languages.** Colonial-era records and continuing Catholic records are in French and Spanish. After 1803, American administrative records are in English, but French remained dominant for many residents and in church records well into the 1840s. The single digitized notarial acts volume (004990115) is in French and English and requires reading the originals to use.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Orleans Parish borders Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (east), and St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near parish boundaries may have records in neighboring parishes — search those as well if the ancestor's exact location within Orleans is uncertain. Neighboring parish records were not examined in this survey.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, and Naming Customs all returned generic fallback content in this survey** rather than Louisiana-specific articles. Consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana to fill gaps this guide could not cover from returned tool results.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by French colonists; Orleans Parish (the civil parish containing the city) established under American territorial administration after the Louisiana Purchase (1803)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (Louisiana uses parishes, not counties; there is no county seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812); State of Louisiana (from 1812)
- **Population during period:** Population figures for this specific place and period were not returned by the survey tools
- **Economy:** Port trade, sugar and cotton export, banking, river commerce; New Orleans was the dominant port city of the Mississippi Valley
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, African-descended free persons of color, enslaved persons, Anglo-American migrants post-1803, growing German and Irish immigrant populations in the 1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (predominant; St. Louis Cathedral the principal parish); Protestant congregations arrived with Anglo-American settlement after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Louisiana statehood (1812), Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods; devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 (colonial era) destroyed much of the French Quarter and many records — these losses directly determine what survives for 1800–1850 research

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1803:** New Orleans was under Spanish colonial administration (from 1763); records created under Spanish governance in Spanish and French
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States; administrative records from the transitional moment are in both Spanish and American series
- **1804–1812:** Territory of Orleans (the territorial predecessor to statehood); territorial records held at the Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge
- **1812:** Louisiana became a state; Orleans Parish established as the civil parish jurisdiction for New Orleans

Records from 1800–1803 are part of the Spanish colonial administrative series. After 1803, records began transitioning to American forms while many residents and clerks continued using French and Spanish. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds continuous notarial records across all these jurisdictional transitions.

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is stated where the tool results provide it.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records did not return specific content in this survey (all returned a generic fallback page); confirmed civil registration start dates and levels cannot be stated. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) implies some death registration from 1819, and "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054) implies some marriage registration from 1837, but neither collection title states the jurisdictional level (parish-level, statewide, or another). Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly for confirmed dates and levels.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds the Louisiana Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (index only, no images; 2,345,678 records) and Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (indexed + images; 567,890 records, 283,945 images). These cover only portions of the target period from their stated start dates.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online); original civil records at the Louisiana State Archives and individual parish courthouses
- **Gaps:** The first portion of the target period — 1800–1819 for deaths and 1800–1837 for marriages — lacks a civil registration series in the returned FamilySearch collections; church records are the primary substitute
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral record baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps from the 1788 and 1794 fires); included in FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (predominant; St. Louis Cathedral New Orleans is the primary parish for the city); Protestant denominations established congregations following Anglo-American migration after 1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) — indexed + images, 987,654 records, 493,827 images
- **Language:** Pre-1803 registers in French and Spanish; after 1803, mixed French, Spanish, and English; French remained dominant in Catholic records for decades into the American period

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses cover this period; New Orleans and Orleans Parish appear in all of them
- **State/territorial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Census did not return specific content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census directly for any territorial or state census series.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial enumerations may exist for the 1800–1803 period in territorial archives
- **Access:** Federal census records for this period are available through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana civil law calls these **successions** (not probate); also tutorships (guardianship) and interdictions. Wills, estate inventories, succession petitions, and related documents are all in the succession series, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System.
- **Testate or intestate:** Louisiana civil law succession differs from common-law probate; search the successions series regardless of whether the person left a will, as the documents produced differ under each scenario
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) covers the full target period — indexed + images, 456,789 records, 228,394 images
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; FamilySearch collection 2078341 online

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French arpent system (long lots running back from the river or waterway), not the rectangular Public Land Survey System; Louisiana is a federal land state for grants after 1803, but colonial grants use the arpent system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page on Louisiana Land and Property did not return specific content in this survey. For colonial-period grants (before 1803), the Spanish and French colonial archives are the relevant source. For post-1803 federal patents, the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) holds the records. Every property transfer in Louisiana was executed before a notary public.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records; **notarial acts are the primary vehicle for all land transactions** under Louisiana civil law
- **Date range:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from 1734; FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of Notarial Acts (imageGroupNumber 004990115) covering 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), in French and English — this volume must be examined image by image
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters); Orleans Parish courthouse; Louisiana State Archives; FamilySearch (1 browse-only volume)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815, War of 1812); territorial militia service (1804–1812); the Civil War is outside this period
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, War of 1812 records at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** New Orleans's above-ground cemetery tradition produced distinctive burial records; St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (Catholic, established 1789) and St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (established 1823) are the principal early-19th-century cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers New Orleans cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Catholic burial registers in the sacramental series (collection 1612905); sexton records for some cemeteries held at the individual cemeteries or the Archdiocese of New Orleans

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several French- and English-language papers existed in early-19th-century New Orleans; specific titles and date ranges were not returned in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; Louisiana State Library and Tulane University for physical/microfilm holdings
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, sheriff's sale announcements (important for property and debt research), ship arrivals (relevant for immigration research)

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was the primary Gulf Coast entry point; passengers arriving from Europe, the Caribbean, and coastal US ports passed through here
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (port of New Orleans lists); naturalization declarations filed in any court of record before 1906 — in Louisiana, naturalization records may be in territorial or state district courts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry (subscription) for indexed passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and poll tax records generated at the parish level in Orleans Parish
- **Date range:** Territorial and early-state tax lists survive at the Louisiana State Archives; specific date ranges were not returned in this survey
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; some records digitized on FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and can place an ancestor in Orleans Parish during the 1800–1810 period before reliable federal census coverage for this area

### Other record types
- **Notarial records (unique to Louisiana):** Every legal transaction — property sales, wills, contracts, emancipations, apprenticeships, business partnerships — was executed before a notary and preserved in bound volumes. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters. These records survived the fires and floods that damaged other record classes and are the single most important substitute source for missing vital and court records. FamilySearch has one browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 1803–1820, 167 images, French/English).
- **Cabildo records:** Records of the Spanish colonial governing body survived and document administrative, legal, and governmental activity into the early 1800s, per the same wiki_search result. The Louisiana State Museum holds Cabildo records.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** New Orleans was the largest slave market in North America during this period. Bills of sale, emancipation documents, and slave manifests passed through notaries and courts and survive in the notarial records and in NARA holdings. The Louisiana State Archives also holds records relevant to researching enslaved ancestors.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
