| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905, 987,654 records, indexed + images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341, 456,789 records, indexed + images); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, index only, no images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054, 567,890 records, indexed + images); Notarial Acts volume 004990115 (1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only, French/English) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records including passenger lists, naturalizations, military records | Free / mail request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching Orleans Parish / New Orleans for the period 1800–1850. That single volume is detailed above and represents the complete result set — no nextPageToken was returned. Additional FamilySearch microfilm holdings may exist outside digitized volume counts.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734; continuous across all jurisdictional transitions | In-person research; inquire for remote access |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial records (1804–1812), state records from 1812, tax lists, court records | In-person / online request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Successions (probate), court records, marriage records | In-person / mail |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers | In-person / mail |
| St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans | Original sacramental registers | Contact cathedral archive |
| Louisiana State Museum | Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) | In-person |
| NARA | Federal census, military records, passenger lists, naturalizations | In-person / online via Ancestry / Fold3 |
| Tulane University and LSU libraries | Local history collections, newspapers, published family histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts beyond the single FamilySearch browse-only volume (004990115, 1803–1820) are physical only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) — held at the Louisiana State Museum; not returned as an online collection in this survey
- Original sacramental registers beyond what is captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 — Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual parishes
- Tax records for Orleans Parish — Louisiana State Archives; extent of online availability not returned in this survey
- Territorial court records (1804–1812) — Louisiana State Archives; extent of online availability not returned in this survey

## Known record losses
The Wikipedia search result (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) states that New Orleans suffered devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records, and that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings. These disasters predate the 1800–1850 target period but directly determine what is and is not available to researchers studying that era.

The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters states that despite these losses, significant genealogical sources survived: the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with some gaps), the notarial records, and the Cabildo records. No tool result in this survey names a specific record set as destroyed by a post-1800 event — empty search results for some record categories reflect digitization gaps, not confirmed losses.

**Substitutes for damaged or missing records:**
- **Notarial acts** (the most important Louisiana substitute): because every legal transaction required a notary, these records survived even where vital registers and court records were damaged; they can reconstruct family relationships, property ownership, and chronology
- **St. Louis Cathedral registers** (survived the fires): baptisms, marriages, and burials in the sacramental registers provide vital data across the entire target period and before it
- **Federal census** (1810–1850): decennial census records are independent of local archive survival
- **Tax records**: for the period between censuses and for 1800–1810, parish-level tax lists can place an ancestor in Orleans Parish
- **Passenger lists**: immigrant ancestors' arrival manifests at the Port of New Orleans are federal records, surviving independently of local archives
- **Published local histories and genealogies**: Tulane University and LSU libraries hold 19th-century New Orleans family and city histories that may preserve transcriptions of records since lost

## Research tips
- **Notarial records are essential, not optional.** Louisiana's civil law system means every legal event passed through a notary. Any ancestor who bought or sold property, made a will, freed an enslaved person, or entered a significant contract did so before a notary. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734 and is the starting point for serious research, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters.
- **Do not assume records are destroyed because fires occurred.** The fires of 1788 and 1794 were severe, but St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers, the notarial records, and the Cabildo records all survived (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). Verify whether the specific record class you need is among the survivors before concluding a gap exists.
- **Louisiana uses "successions," not "probate."** Search FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) for both testate and intestate succession proceedings. Louisiana's forced heirship rules (Napoleonic Code) mean family members who might not appear in a common-law probate file may be named in a Louisiana succession.
- **Records are in multiple languages.** Colonial-era records and continuing Catholic records are in French and Spanish. After 1803, American administrative records are in English, but French remained dominant for many residents and in church records well into the 1840s. The single digitized notarial acts volume (004990115) is in French and English and requires reading the originals to use.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Orleans Parish borders Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (east), and St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near parish boundaries may have records in neighboring parishes — search those as well if the ancestor's exact location within Orleans is uncertain. Neighboring parish records were not examined in this survey.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Census, and Naming Customs all returned generic fallback content in this survey** rather than Louisiana-specific articles. Consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana to fill gaps this guide could not cover from returned tool results.

## New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana — Early 1800s Locality Guide

### Disaster History and Record Loss

Two catastrophic fires (1788 and 1794) destroyed most of the French Quarter and significant colonial records **before** the early 1800s research period even begins. Additional losses came from yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and flooding throughout the 19th century. Despite these disasters, several key record series survived.

---

### What Survived — and Where to Find It

**1. St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers**
- Baptisms, marriages, and burials running from **1731**, with some gaps
- These Catholic church records are the single most important substitute for civil vital records
- Available through FamilySearch: *Louisiana Church Records, 1718–1925* (indexed with images)

**2. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
- Holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts from 1734 onward
- Covers land transfers, successions (probates), manumissions, marriage contracts, and business records — often replacing courthouse records destroyed elsewhere
- FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume of notarial acts (167 images, 1803–1820, in French and English, **not** name-indexed)
- Physical visits or correspondence with the Archives are essential — most notarial records are **not** online

**3. Spanish Cabildo Records**
- The records of New Orleans' colonial governing body survive and document the Spanish colonial period extending into the early American era

**4. Probate / Succession Records**
- FamilySearch: *Louisiana Probate Records, 1756–1984* (indexed with images)
- ⚠️ Civil law terminology: Louisiana calls probate a **"succession"** and guardianship a **"tutorship"**

**5. Death and Marriage Records**
- FamilySearch: *Louisiana Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964* (index only)
- FamilySearch: *Louisiana Parish Marriages, 1837–1957*

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts, land, successions, manumissions |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and state records |
| St. Louis Cathedral Archives | Sacramental registers |
| FamilySearch.org | Digitized and indexed collections (see above) |

---

### Critical Research Tips

- **There are no county courthouses** in Louisiana — research is conducted at the **Orleans Parish Civil District Court**
- The **civil law tradition** (inherited from French and Spanish rule) means records are structured very differently from common-law U.S. states
- For enslaved ancestors and free people of color, **notarial manumission acts** and **sacramental registers** (which often recorded race and status) are the primary sources
- Because the 1788 and 1794 fires predate your research window, the records most researchers expect to be missing often **do** survive through church registers and notarial copies

---

When you're ready, a targeted research plan can be built from this guide to search specific ancestors across these record sets.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718 by French colonial authorities. Louisiana passed from French to Spanish control in 1763, briefly reverted to France around 1800, and was purchased by the United States in 1803. Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (Orleans Parish is coterminous with the city; Louisiana uses parishes instead of counties)

| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905; ~987,654 records); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892; index only); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (DGS 004990115, 1803–1820, 167 images) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Louisiana newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, military records | Free (in-person) / some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume total for this place and period — the complete result set. This single volume covers only notarial acts 1803–1820 and is browse-only. The collections_search covers all of Louisiana (4 collections), not specifically Orleans Parish alone.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (land, succession, slave, marriage contract, commercial records) | In-person; contact the archive |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial-era records (1803–1812); state records post-1812; probate and court records | In-person; some online access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers of all parishes; burial records | In-person / written inquiry |
| St. Louis Cathedral | Original sacramental registers from 1731 | In-person / via Archdiocese |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession records, tutorships, interdictions, court files | In-person |
| Louisiana State Museum (Cabildo) | Colonial-era Cabildo records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal records for Louisiana; passenger lists | In-person / mail request |

## Records NOT online
- The overwhelming majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's 30+ million pages — the single FamilySearch volume covers only 167 images (1803–1820, browse-only). Thorough notarial research requires visiting or engaging the archive in New Orleans.
- Cabildo records (colonial governing body) — online availability was not confirmed by this survey's tools.
- Most Orleans Parish tax records for the early 1800s.
- Orleans Parish civil district court succession and tutorship records not captured in the FamilySearch probate collection.
- Church records for Protestant denominations established post-1803 — online extent not confirmed.
- Acts of Manumission and slave transaction notarial acts beyond the small digitized volume.

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki search result for [New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states that New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Wikipedia confirms these fires and additionally notes that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings over the period. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)

**What this means for 1800–1860 research:**
- The fires predate the target window but their effect is felt: records that would otherwise document family continuity from the 1700s into the early 1800s have gaps.
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731 with gaps — some entries within the 1800–1860 window may be missing due to these earlier disruptions.
- No tool result in this survey stated that specific court records, probate records, or notarial acts from the 1800–1860 window were destroyed. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss.

**Substitute sources for disaster-period gaps:**
1. **Notarial records** — The notarial archives survived the fires better than other series because acts were maintained in bound volumes. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from 1734. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
2. **Cabildo records** — The Spanish colonial governing body records survive and cover the colonial-to-American transition. (Source: same)
3. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — Survive from 1731 with gaps; primary substitute for any destroyed civil vital records.
4. **Tax records** — Can place individuals in the city when census or vital records have gaps.
5. **Passenger manifests** — Document arrival in New Orleans and bridge gaps for immigrants.

## Research tips
- **Louisiana is not like other states.** Probate = 'succession'; guardianship = 'tutorship'; counties = 'parishes.' Searching with common-law terminology will miss records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Start with notarial records, not just vital records.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the most important repository for this period. Notarial acts document virtually every significant legal transaction and survive from 1734. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Records are in French, Spanish, and English.** Pre-1803 records are primarily in French or Spanish. Post-1803 records are a mix of all three. The digitized FamilySearch notarial volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115) is in French and English and must be browsed image by image.
- **Search the FamilySearch Church Records collection first** for the early period. "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) is the broadest indexed collection before civil registration was systematically required.
- **A negative search result is not proof of absence.** The fires of 1788 and 1794 created real gaps. When a record is not found online, consult the physical repositories above before concluding it never existed. (Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **Free people of color and enslaved persons.** New Orleans had the largest free Black population of any U.S. city in this period. Free people of color appear in population censuses, church registers, and notarial acts. Enslaved persons appear in the 1850 and 1860 slave schedules by age/sex only, and in notarial acts of sale, hire, or manumission by name.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana** (vital records, church records, naming customs) did not return Louisiana-specific content during this survey — all redirected to a generic page. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly.
- **The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge** holds territorial-era records (1803–1812) that are not fully digitized. Visiting or corresponding with the archives is necessary for thorough territorial-period research. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)

## New Orleans, Early 1800s — Records, Disasters, and Where to Look

**What disasters affected the records**
Two catastrophic fires — in **1788** and **1794** — destroyed most of the French Quarter's colonial structures *before* the early 1800s even began. This means virtually no secular colonial records survive from the Spanish and French periods in their original form. Researchers should assume the gap and work with what was kept off-site or re-created afterward.

---

## What Survived and Where to Find It

### 1. Catholic Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
- **St. Louis Cathedral** kept registers going back to 1731 with some gaps — these are the primary record of life events for the Catholic majority.
- Indexed and viewable on FamilySearch: **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"**
- These survived because church record-keeping often used duplicate registers and off-site copies.

### 2. Notarial Acts (Property, Marriage Contracts, Manumissions)
- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts from 1734 onward.
- These records **survived the fires** and are the backbone for non-church research — covering property sales, wills, marriage contracts, slave manumissions, and business transactions.
- ⚠️ Only a single 167-image, browse-only volume (1803–1820) has been digitized on FamilySearch. The researcher must contact the Archives directly for the rest.
- **Contact:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — nona.org

### 3. Probate Records ("Successions")
- Louisiana used the **Napoleonic Code**, so probate records are called "successions," not "wills."
- Indexed on FamilySearch back to 1756.
- Search under Orleans Parish in the FamilySearch catalog.

---

## Key Substitutes for Lost Records

| Lost Record Type | Where to Look Instead |
|---|---|
| Colonial civil registrations | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers |
| Property & family agreements | Notarial Archives (marriage contracts, acts) |
| Estate/inheritance records | Louisiana Successions on FamilySearch |
| Manumissions & free persons of color | Notarial Archives acts |

---

## Immediate Next Steps

1. **Consult the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** for notarial holdings covering your specific family's years (nona.org).
2. **Run a FamilySearch Catalog search** for "Orleans, Louisiana" to surface microfilmed church, court, or land records not yet captured in indexed collections.
3. Check the **FamilySearch Wiki page** directly — [Louisiana Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records) — for civil registration start dates and naming conventions specific to the period.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** City founded 1718 by the French. Orleans Parish established 1807 as one of Louisiana's original 12 civil parishes. Louisiana admitted as a state 1812. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans 1803–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by `place_population` for this query — consult the Louisiana State Archives or published census studies for period figures.
- **Economy:** Major port; cotton, sugar, and the slave trade; shipping and commerce dominated the economy throughout this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved Africans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, and growing waves of German and Irish immigrants by mid-century.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, centered on St. Louis Cathedral). Protestant congregations grew after the American takeover in 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans January 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics; hurricanes and floods. The Great Fires of 1788 and 1794 (pre-period but controlling for record survival) destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records.

## Boundary changes
- **1718–1763:** French colonial city
- **1763–1800:** Spanish colonial control (Treaty of Paris 1763; retroceded by Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800)
- **1800–1803:** Brief French re-possession
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — New Orleans became the capital of the US Territory of Orleans
- **1807:** Orleans Parish created as a civil jurisdiction
- **1812:** Louisiana statehood; Orleans Parish remained the governing unit

Records created under French and Spanish rule are held in different repositories than US territorial and state-era records. Louisiana's civil law system (Napoleonic Code, not English common law) governs all legal records throughout this period. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only a generic fallback page in this survey — no specific start date or jurisdictional level can be stated from tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists online:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892) covers deaths from 1819; it is an index only with no images (2,345,678 records). No indexed civil birth or marriage collections for the early 1800s appeared in the survey results.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (see Church records below) effectively functioned as vital records for the Catholic majority throughout this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, for state-level civil records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant). The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral date from 1731 and survived the fires of 1788 and 1794, though with some gaps. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (and confirmations as a separate dated event). Free people of color and enslaved individuals were also recorded in Catholic registers.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — **indexed + images**; 987,654 records and 493,827 images. This is the primary online access point for St. Louis Cathedral registers covering the target period.
- **Where held (originals):** St. Louis Cathedral Archive and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for colonial-era and early American-period records. Researchers must be able to read those languages in the original.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was first enumerated in 1810 (the first census after territorial organization). Available federal census years for the target period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850. The 1790 and 1800 censuses did not cover Louisiana.
- **State/territorial enumerations:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Census returned generic fallback content — no specific territorial or state censuses can be confirmed from tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census directly.
- **Access:** Federal census records are searchable on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana civil law terminology:** Probate is called "successions"; guardianship is "tutorships"; incompetency proceedings are "interdictions." These are distinct from common-law equivalents and are held at the parish level, not the county level. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — **indexed + images**; 456,789 records and 228,394 images. Covers the full target period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents) prevailed for earlier grants; US rectangular survey applied to lands opened after 1803. Existing Spanish and French grants retained their original forms.
- **Critical source — Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, covering property transfers, marriage contracts, apprenticeships, and manumissions. These records survived the fires of 1788 and 1794 and are the most important non-church record class for early New Orleans. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** Image group 004990115 — 167 images of Orleans notarial acts, 1803–1820. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; records in French and English). This is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for this place and period — 1 total volume returned by `volume_search`, which was the complete result set.
- **Access to the full notarial archive:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, physical or written request. The vast majority of the 30+ million pages is not digitized.
- **Other land records:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state land records.
- **FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Land and Property** returned generic fallback content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812, culminating in the Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815); Spanish colonial militia records predate the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); War of 1812 records also available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789) and St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (opened 1823) are the principal Catholic cemeteries for this period; New Orleans's above-ground burial vaults are distinctive to the area.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers New Orleans cemeteries; coverage varies by cemetery and date.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans had an active press from the early 1800s.
- **Access:** Historical newspapers available at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, shipping notices (tracking arrivals), legal notices, and runaway slave advertisements — a critical source for researching enslaved and free Black individuals.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States during this period.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); naturalization records filed in Louisiana courts (pre-1906 naturalizations appear in any court of record).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish tax rolls; territorial and state property tax records.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Can locate individuals in years between federal censuses.

### Other record types
- **Slave and manumission records:** Manumissions were recorded as notarial acts, making the New Orleans Notarial Archives essential for researching enslaved persons and free people of color. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance):** Records of the Spanish governing body survive and are held at the Louisiana State Museum / Historic New Orleans Collection. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); 1 browse-only volume of notarial acts 1803-1820 (image group 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including War of 1812 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, military records, federal census (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish 1800–1860 — this was the complete result set (no `nextPageToken`; `totalResults: 1`). The four indexed FamilySearch collections are at the Louisiana state scope; they are not filtered to New Orleans exclusively. The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey — run a catalog search for "Orleans, Louisiana" on FamilySearch to identify microfilmed holdings not captured here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (property, marriage contracts, manumissions) | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, land records, tax records, successions (probate) | In-person; some records online |
| St. Louis Cathedral Archives / Archdiocese of New Orleans | Original sacramental registers from 1731 | Contact Archdiocese for access |
| Louisiana State Museum / Historic New Orleans Collection | Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance) | In-person |
| National Archives (NARA) | Military records, passenger lists, federal census | In-person (Washington D.C. or regional); many collections online |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages from 1734) is not digitized. FamilySearch holds only 1 browse-only volume of 167 images covering 1803–1820.
- Cabildo (Spanish colonial governance) records are physically held at the Louisiana State Museum; online availability was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey — microfilmed holdings covering church registers, court records, and other series may exist on FamilySearch microfilm but not appear in the collections list above.
- Tax rolls and many territorial court records are physical-only at the Louisiana State Archives.

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states that the Great Fires of 1788 and 1794 "destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records." This is the most significant known record loss affecting research for this period.

The Wikipedia article on New Orleans (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) notes that "repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings," but does not name specific record sets; no tool result in this survey identifies the fate of any particular record class beyond the colonial-era fire losses.

**What survived the fires (confirmed by tool results):**
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps)
- Notarial records from 1734 (New Orleans Notarial Archives)
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance)

An empty online search result is a coverage gap, not proof of destruction. The bulk of notarial and administrative records were never digitized, not lost.

## Research tips

- **The notarial archives are the research backbone.** For early 1800s New Orleans, notarial acts recorded property transactions, marriage contracts, and manumissions when no uniform civil registration system existed. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the essential starting point for non-church records. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Use civil law terminology.** Searching for "probate" in Louisiana indexes may miss records filed as "successions." Guardianship filed as "tutorships." The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341) does appear indexed under that title. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Church records are essential.** St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers from 1731 — available through "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905) — are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials across the entire early 1800s period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned generic content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records for civil registration start dates before concluding which record type controls a given year.
- **Three sovereignties, three repository systems.** Records created before 1803 under French or Spanish authority are in different repositories than US territorial records (1803–1812) and state records (1812+). Cabildo records are at the Louisiana State Museum; early church records are at the Archdiocese; US-era records move to the Louisiana State Archives and federal repositories.
- **Naming customs.** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Naming Customs returned generic content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Naming_Customs directly — naming conventions in French Creole families differ from Anglo-American practice and affect how individuals appear in indexes.
- **Run a FamilySearch Catalog search.** A Catalog search for "Orleans, Louisiana" was not completed in this survey. # Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** City founded 1718 by the French. Orleans Parish established 1807 as one of Louisiana's original 12 civil parishes. Louisiana admitted as a state 1812. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans 1803–1812; State of Louisiana from 1812
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by `place_population` for this query — consult the Louisiana State Archives or published census studies for period figures.
- **Economy:** Major port; cotton, sugar, and the slave trade; shipping and commerce dominated the economy throughout this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved Africans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, and growing waves of German and Irish immigrants by mid-century.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, centered on St. Louis Cathedral). Protestant congregations grew after the American takeover in 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans January 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics; hurricanes and floods. The Great Fires of 1788 and 1794 (pre-period but controlling for record survival) destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records.

## Boundary changes
- **1718–1763:** French colonial city
- **1763–1800:** Spanish colonial control (Treaty of Paris 1763; retroceded by Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800)
- **1800–1803:** Brief French re-possession
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — New Orleans became the capital of the US Territory of Orleans
- **1807:** Orleans Parish created as a civil jurisdiction
- **1812:** Louisiana statehood; Orleans Parish remained the governing unit

Records created under French and Spanish rule are held in different repositories than US territorial and state-era records. Louisiana's civil law system (Napoleonic Code, not English common law) governs all legal records throughout this period. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only a generic fallback page in this survey — no specific start date or jurisdictional level can be stated from tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists online:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892) covers deaths from 1819; it is an index only with no images (2,345,678 records). No indexed civil birth or marriage collections for the early 1800s appeared in the survey results.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (see Church records below) effectively functioned as vital records for the Catholic majority throughout this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, for state-level civil records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant). The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral date from 1731 and survived the fires of 1788 and 1794, though with some gaps. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (and confirmations as a separate dated event). Free people of color and enslaved individuals were also recorded in Catholic registers.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — **indexed + images**; 987,654 records and 493,827 images. This is the primary online access point for St. Louis Cathedral registers covering the target period.
- **Where held (originals):** St. Louis Cathedral Archive and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for colonial-era and early American-period records. Researchers must be able to read those languages in the original.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was first enumerated in 1810 (the first census after territorial organization). Available federal census years for the target period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850. The 1790 and 1800 censuses did not cover Louisiana.
- **State/territorial enumerations:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Census returned generic fallback content — no specific territorial or state censuses can be confirmed from tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census directly.
- **Access:** Federal census records are searchable on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana civil law terminology:** Probate is called "successions"; guardianship is "tutorships"; incompetency proceedings are "interdictions." These are distinct from common-law equivalents and are held at the parish level, not the county level. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — **indexed + images**; 456,789 records and 228,394 images. Covers the full target period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents) prevailed for earlier grants; US rectangular survey applied to lands opened after 1803. Existing Spanish and French grants retained their original forms.
- **Critical source — Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, covering property transfers, marriage contracts, apprenticeships, and manumissions. These records survived the fires of 1788 and 1794 and are the most important non-church record class for early New Orleans. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** Image group 004990115 — 167 images of Orleans notarial acts, 1803–1820. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; records in French and English). This is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for this place and period — 1 total volume returned by `volume_search`, which was the complete result set.
- **Access to the full notarial archive:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, physical or written request. The vast majority of the 30+ million pages is not digitized.
- **Other land records:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state land records.
- **FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Land and Property** returned generic fallback content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812, culminating in the Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815); Spanish colonial militia records predate the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); War of 1812 records also available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789) and St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (opened 1823) are the principal Catholic cemeteries for this period; New Orleans's above-ground burial vaults are distinctive to the area.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers New Orleans cemeteries; coverage varies by cemetery and date.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans had an active press from the early 1800s.
- **Access:** Historical newspapers available at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, shipping notices (tracking arrivals), legal notices, and runaway slave advertisements — a critical source for researching enslaved and free Black individuals.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States during this period.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); naturalization records filed in Louisiana courts (pre-1906 naturalizations appear in any court of record).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish tax rolls; territorial and state property tax records.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Can locate individuals in years between federal censuses.

### Other record types
- **Slave and manumission records:** Manumissions were recorded as notarial acts, making the New Orleans Notarial Archives essential for researching enslaved persons and free people of color. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance):** Records of the Spanish governing body survive and are held at the Louisiana State Museum / Historic New Orleans Collection. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); 1 browse-only volume of notarial acts 1803-1820 (image group 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including War of 1812 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, military records, federal census (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish 1800–1860 — this was the complete result set (no `nextPageToken`; `totalResults: 1`). The four indexed FamilySearch collections are at the Louisiana state scope; they are not filtered to New Orleans exclusively. The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey — run a catalog search for "Orleans, Louisiana" on FamilySearch to identify microfilmed holdings not captured here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (property, marriage contracts, manumissions) | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, land records, tax records, successions (probate) | In-person; some records online |
| St. Louis Cathedral Archives / Archdiocese of New Orleans | Original sacramental registers from 1731 | Contact Archdiocese for access |
| Louisiana State Museum / Historic New Orleans Collection | Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance) | In-person |
| National Archives (NARA) | Military records, passenger lists, federal census | In-person (Washington D.C. or regional); many collections online |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages from 1734) is not digitized. FamilySearch holds only 1 browse-only volume of 167 images covering 1803–1820.
- Cabildo (Spanish colonial governance) records are physically held at the Louisiana State Museum; online availability was not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey — microfilmed holdings covering church registers, court records, and other series may exist on FamilySearch microfilm but not appear in the collections list above.
- Tax rolls and many territorial court records are physical-only at the Louisiana State Archives.

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states that the Great Fires of 1788 and 1794 "destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records." This is the most significant known record loss affecting research for this period.

The Wikipedia article on New Orleans (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) notes that "repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings," but does not name specific record sets; no tool result in this survey identifies the fate of any particular record class beyond the colonial-era fire losses.

**What survived the fires (confirmed by tool results):**
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps)
- Notarial records from 1734 (New Orleans Notarial Archives)
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governance)

An empty online search result is a coverage gap, not proof of destruction. The bulk of notarial and administrative records were never digitized, not lost.

## Research tips

- **The notarial archives are the research backbone.** For early 1800s New Orleans, notarial acts recorded property transactions, marriage contracts, and manumissions when no uniform civil registration system existed. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the essential starting point for non-church records. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Use civil law terminology.** Searching for "probate" in Louisiana indexes may miss records filed as "successions." Guardianship filed as "tutorships." The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341) does appear indexed under that title. (FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Church records are essential.** St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers from 1731 — available through "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905) — are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials across the entire early 1800s period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned generic content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records for civil registration start dates before concluding which record type controls a given year.
- **Three sovereignties, three repository systems.** Records created before 1803 under French or Spanish authority are in different repositories than US territorial records (1803–1812) and state records (1812+). Cabildo records are at the Louisiana State Museum; early church records are at the Archdiocese; US-era records move to the Louisiana State Archives and federal repositories.
- **Naming customs.** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Naming Customs returned generic content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Naming_Customs directly — naming conventions in French Creole families differ from Anglo-American practice and affect how individuals appear in indexes.
- **Run a FamilySearch Catalog search.** A Catalog search for "Orleans, Louisiana" was not completed in this survey. Run it directly at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog to identify microfilmed volumes of church registers, court records, and notarial records not reflected in the collections list above.
- **Search at the Louisiana state scope on FamilySearch.** The four indexed collections in this survey are Louisiana-state-level — they are not pre-filtered to New Orleans. Apply place filters within each collection when searching.
- **Free people of color records.** New Orleans had one of the largest free Black communities in the antebellum United States. Manumission records in the notarial archives and entries in Catholic church registers are the richest sources for this population.

---

## Port of Boston — 1840s Immigration Records Survey

This guide covers the Port of Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, focusing on the 1840s through 1860 — the period of peak Irish Famine immigration.

### Key Record Sets & Repositories

**1. Customs Passenger Lists**
- **NARA Record Group 36** holds the original passenger arrival manifests
- Indexed on **FamilySearch** (collection 1784312) and also on **Ancestry**
- ⚠️ Important caveat: 1840s passenger lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — they will **not** give your ancestor's specific hometown in Ireland or elsewhere

**2. Catholic Parish Registers**
- **Archdiocese of Boston** holds registers for the major immigrant parishes
- Key parishes: Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's
- Baptism, marriage, and burial records may supply townland or parish of origin in Ireland

**3. Naturalization Records (Pre-1906)**
- Scattered across Suffolk County courts and the Federal District Court
- **FamilySearch** collection **1459213**
- Declarations of intent and petitions often name the country — sometimes the specific place — of origin

**4. Federal Censuses**
- **1850 and 1860 censuses** name every household member with birthplace
- Useful for locating your ancestor in Boston shortly after arrival

---

### Research Strategy

Because 1840s passenger manifests are sparse on geographic detail, the recommended approach is to **triangulate origin** from multiple sources:
1. Confirm arrival via the passenger list index
2. Check Catholic registers for sacramental events naming origin parish
3. Examine naturalization papers for declared birthplace
4. Use census records to establish household and neighbors (often from the same home village)

For updated FamilySearch guidance, check the **Massachusetts Genealogy wiki** directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy](https://familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy).

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston, Massachusetts (1840–1860 Immigration)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City / port:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Founded:** 1630; Suffolk County formed 1643
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Suffolk County seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. Wikipedia states that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the enormous scale of 1840s Famine immigration.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, light manufacturing, domestic service. Newly arrived immigrants concentrated in unskilled labor, construction, and domestic service.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dominant wave in the 1840s was Irish Catholic immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). Earlier arrivals included English, German, and other northern Europeans.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopal, Catholic (rapidly expanding with Irish immigration), Methodist, Baptist, Jewish congregations in Boston.
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine 1845–1852 drove the largest single immigration wave through this port in the 1840s. Wikipedia notes immigrants settled primarily in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods.

## Boundary changes
- Suffolk County was formed in 1643 and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s–1860s.
- No jurisdictional splits affected Boston or Suffolk County during the target period.
- Records created in this period are held in Suffolk County and state repositories without predecessor-jurisdiction complications.

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (primary immigration record)
- **Date range covered:** 1820–1891 (FamilySearch collection 1784312)
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston, filed under NARA Record Group 36. The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston states these lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin for the 1840s — unlike later Ellis Island-era manifests, they do not routinely give the immigrant's town or village of origin.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume for 1840–1850 (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images). This volume is 3% name-indexed and full-text searchable — it must be searched via full-text search or browsed image by image; it is not fully accessible by name search alone. The broader collection 1784312 on FamilySearch covers 1820–1891 with additional indexing.
- **Where held:** Originals at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), NARA Record Group 36. Also indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1784312) and Ancestry.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all household members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Naturalization records
- **Date range:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (FamilySearch collection 1459213): 345,678 indexed records.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention ("first papers"), petitions for naturalization, oaths of allegiance.
- **Jurisdictional note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. Search Suffolk County Probate Court, Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, and the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts (NARA) separately; the FamilySearch collection may not include all courts.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 1459213).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213); originals distributed across multiple courts.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890: 3,456,789 indexed records. Vital records in Massachusetts were registered at the town level during this period.
- **Registration level:** The Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey — the specific statewide registration start date is not confirmed by a tool result in this run. The FamilySearch wiki page https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records should be consulted directly.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 2061550).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers are the essential alternative for Irish arrivals before civil registration became comprehensive (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants), Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Jewish.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1921657, Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920: 987,654 indexed records. The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston specifically names the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's as Catholic parishes whose registers document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward.
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds Catholic parish registers. Not all pre-1870 Catholic registers are included in the FamilySearch collection — contact the Archdiocese directly for registers outside the digitized set.
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 1921657) for digitized registers; physical-only for registers held solely at the Archdiocese.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses cover Boston, Suffolk County. The 1850 census is the first to name every household member and include birthplace — critical for bracketing an immigrant's arrival date.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding the census (June 1849–May 1850) — useful for tracing Famine-era deaths among newly arrived immigrants.
- **Access:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1678901, Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991: 567,890 indexed records.
- **Court records:** Naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases in Suffolk County courts.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 1678901).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch; originals at Massachusetts State Archives and Suffolk County Courthouse.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state).
- **Relevance for immigrants:** Most 1840s arrivals were renters, not immediate landowners. Land records become useful after the 1850s as immigrants established themselves. Suffolk County Registry of Deeds holds deed books.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); some Massachusetts residents served.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files at NARA (archives.gov, also accessible via Fold3).
- **Access:** Fold3 (subscription) and NARA (archives.gov, free finding aids).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) is listed in FamilySearch's curated external links for this place and period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for Boston's Catholic cemeteries (e.g., Holy Cross Cemetery, Cambridge Catholic Cemetery) are held by the relevant parishes or diocesan offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Key resource:** The Boston Pilot (Irish Catholic newspaper) published missing-persons advertisements and arrival notices from the 1840s onward. Wikipedia identifies this as a primary supplementary source for Irish immigrants.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription) — returned in FamilySearch's curated external links for this place and period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Port:** Port of Boston is the primary port of entry for this guide.
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (NARA RG 36), declarations of intention (naturalization first papers), alien registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA at Waltham, MA (originals); FamilySearch collection 1784312 (indexed/digitized); Ancestry (indexed).
- **Content note:** See Passenger lists section above. Lists record all persons aboard, including infants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (assessed at town level), poll tax.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a person in Boston in years between federal censuses.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts State Archives; Suffolk County records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312); Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213); Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census; passenger lists; naturalization records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including The Boston Pilot | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for Record Group 36 (customs passenger lists) | Free finding aids; some records online |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records for Boston-area cemeteries | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) matching Boston passenger lists for 1840–1850; totalResults was 1 and no nextPageToken was returned, so this appears to be the complete FamilySearch digitized set for that specific record type and period. The broader FamilySearch collection 1784312 may contain additional indexed records beyond this single volume.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists, NARA Record Group 36; naturalization records | In-person; written request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1840s onward not included in FamilySearch collection | Contact archives directly |
| Suffolk County Courthouse (Boston) | Pre-1906 naturalization records filed in state courts; deed and probate records | In-person / written request |
| Massachusetts State Archives | State-level vital records, naturalization indexes, probate records | In-person / online catalog |
| Massachusetts Historical Society (Boston) | Local histories, town records, manuscript collections | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic parish registers held solely by the Archdiocese of Boston archives that are not included in FamilySearch collection 1921657 must be accessed through the Archdiocese directly.
- Suffolk County court naturalization records not included in FamilySearch collection 1459213 require in-person or written request to the Suffolk County Courthouse or Massachusetts State Archives.
- Original customs passenger list volumes beyond what FamilySearch has digitized must be viewed at NARA Waltham.
- Sexton records for Catholic cemeteries are held by the parishes or diocesan offices and are not in any online database identified by the tools in this run.

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Port of Boston passenger lists or Suffolk County court records in the 1840s–1860s were stated by any tool result in this survey. The NARA finding aids at archives.gov should be consulted to confirm which specific customs passenger list volumes survive for the target years.

## Research tips
- **1840s passenger list content is limited:** The lists record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not hometown. To find the immigrant's origin village, pair the passenger list with the 1850 or 1860 census (which asks birthplace), Catholic baptismal/marriage records, naturalization papers, and any family letters or obituaries. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Use The Boston Pilot:** This Irish Catholic newspaper published missing-persons advertisements from the 1840s onward, naming where searchers believed their relatives had emigrated from in Ireland — a direct backdoor to the origin townland. (Wikipedia)
- **Bracket the arrival with census years:** Use the 1840 census (pre-Famine) to confirm the immigrant was not yet in Massachusetts, and the 1850 census (names all household members with birthplace) to confirm presence and gather family details.
- **Search both FamilySearch and Ancestry for passenger lists:** Variant spellings may be indexed differently across the two platforms. FamilySearch collection 1784312 and Ancestry's Boston passenger list collections are independent indexing projects.
- **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (003345210) for 1840–1850 Port of Boston is 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable.** Use the full-text search feature before browsing its 389 images manually.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization was filed in any court:** Search Suffolk County Probate Court, Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, and the NARA federal district court records separately — they are not all in one place and may not all be covered by FamilySearch collection 1459213.
- **Catholic church records are essential:** For Irish immigrants, Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers (particularly Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's) are often the first records to name an origin parish in Ireland. The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds registers not fully represented on FamilySearch. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **FamilySearch Massachusetts wiki pages not fully available:** All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and specific Massachusetts topic pages returned only generic fallback content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy directly for the most current resource list and any updated collection links.

- **1840s passenger list content is limited:** The lists record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not hometown. To find the immigrant's origin village, pair the passenger list with the 1850 or 1860 census (which asks birthplace), Catholic baptismal/marriage records, naturalization papers, and any family letters or obituaries. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Use The Boston Pilot:** This Irish Catholic newspaper published missing-persons advertisements from the 1840s onward, naming where searchers believed their relatives had emigrated from in Ireland — a direct backdoor to the origin townland. (Wikipedia)
- **Bracket the arrival with census years:** Use the 1840 census (pre-Famine) to confirm the immigrant was not yet in Massachusetts, and the 1850 census (names all household members with birthplace) to confirm presence and gather family details.
- **Search both FamilySearch and Ancestry for passenger lists:** Variant spellings may be indexed differently across the two platforms. FamilySearch collection 1784312 and Ancestry's Boston passenger list collections are independent indexing projects.
- **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (003345210) for 1840–1850 Port of Boston is 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable.** Use the full-text search feature before browsing its 389 images manually.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization was filed in any court:** Search Suffolk County Probate Court, Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, and the NARA federal district court records separately — they are not all in one place and may not all be covered by FamilySearch collection 1459213.
- **Catholic church records are essential:** For Irish immigrants, Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers (particularly Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's) are often the first records to name an origin parish in Ireland. The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds registers not fully represented on FamilySearch. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **FamilySearch Massachusetts wiki pages not fully available:** All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and specific Massachusetts topic pages returned only generic fallback content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy directly for the most current resource list and any updated collection links.

---

**Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Oklahoma), mid-1800s — Tribal Rolls & Native American Records**

*(Saved as loc_001 in the project)*

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was designated **Indian Territory** — there was no civil county or state government. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) governed their own nations, each producing distinct records. This makes research fundamentally different from tracing ancestors in a U.S. state.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls**
The most important source category. Key mid-1800s rolls include:
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — for Cherokees who moved west before removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee citizens
- **Various Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole rolls** from the 1830s–1860s
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — widely known but *postdate* the mid-1800s target; use only as a gateway to earlier records
- FamilySearch: **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (567,890 indexed records)
- FamilySearch: Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870 (99% name-indexed)

**2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Records**
- **Annuity payment rolls** — list tribal members receiving treaty payments
- **Agency correspondence and reports** — held at the **National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)**, Southwest Region (Fort Worth, TX)
- School enrollment records from BIA-run and mission schools

**3. Treaties**
- Signed between the U.S. government and tribal nations; often include schedules of land assignments or payments naming heads of households
- Published at NARA and the Oklahoma Historical Society

**4. Missionary Church Registers**
- Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward
- Record baptisms, marriages, and burials for tribal members
- Some are held at denominational archives; some are at the Oklahoma Historical Society

**5. Five Civilized Tribes' Own Archives**
- Each tribe maintains its own historical records that were **never transferred to NARA or FamilySearch**
- Contact tribal historic preservation offices directly:
  - Cherokee Nation (Tahlequah, OK)
  - Choctaw Nation (Durant, OK)
  - Chickasaw Nation (Ada, OK)
  - Muscogee (Creek) Nation (Okmulgee, OK)
  - Seminole Nation (Wewoka, OK)

**6. Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)**
- A major repository for Indian Territory records, newspapers, photographs, and territorial documents
- Online catalog: okhistory.org

---

### Critical Caveats

- **The Dawes Rolls are not mid-1800s records.** They are the 1898–1914 enrollment for allotment purposes. They are useful as a starting point but must be traced back to earlier rolls.
- **Indian Territory had no civil vital records** (births, marriages, deaths registered by a county clerk) until statehood in 1907. Church registers and tribal records substitute for civil registration.
- FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma-specific content did not load correctly during this search; consult the [FamilySearch Oklahoma page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy) directly for updated collection guidance.

---

### Suggested Next Steps

Building a research plan that sequences these specific record sets against the individual or family you are tracing would be the natural next step. If you share the tribe and approximate time frame, the plan can be tailored further.
