The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) are the most widely used enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes but postdate the mid-1800s target period; use them to confirm tribal membership and work backward to earlier rolls.
Earlier rolls that fall within the mid-1800s include the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) — search these before the Dawes Rolls for mid-century families.
Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records (annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records) are held at NARA and are the federal-level parallel to tribal records for this period.

Missionary records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) name converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward and frequently predate any civil or tribal enrollment record for an individual.

FamilySearch's Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls collection (1851-1959) and the volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards (1840-1870, image group 002298871) both cover the mid-century target period and are 99% name-indexed.

The Five Civilized Tribes maintained their own courts, schools, and records. Tribal nation archives (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) hold records not duplicated at NARA or FamilySearch.

Land allotment records tied to the Dawes process (post-1887 Dawes Act, 1898 Curtis Act) are held at NARA's Southwest Region in Fort Worth and are indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry — allotment jacket files contain family-grouping data useful for earlier generations.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Oklahoma) (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was formally designated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Oklahoma Territory was organized in 1890 (western half). The two territories merged at Oklahoma statehood, 18 November 1907.
- **Administrative center:** No single county-seat structure existed for Indian Territory; governance was tribal-national, with the Five Civilized Tribes maintaining their own capitals (e.g., Tahlequah for Cherokee, Tishomingo for Chickasaw).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (U.S. Congress), with concurrent tribal sovereignty.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the tools for this jurisdiction and period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence and cash crops), ranching, trade, and later coal mining and oil discovery in the late 19th century.
- **Ethnic composition:** The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the principal peoples relocated to Indian Territory under the Indian Removal Act. Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members), intermarried non-Indians, and later white settlers also present.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward. Tribal members also maintained traditional religious practices.
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act 1830; Trail of Tears removals 1830s–1840s; Civil War (Indian Territory tribes were divided, some signing Confederate treaties); Reconstruction-era tribal treaties 1866; Dawes Act 1887; Curtis Act 1898 (dissolved tribal governments); Oklahoma statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1890: The entire present-day Oklahoma was designated Indian Territory, governed by tribal nations under federal treaty.
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory (western half) was organized as a federal territory; Indian Territory (eastern half) retained tribal governance.
- 1907: Both territories merged to form the state of Oklahoma.
- Records from the mid-1800s were created under tribal and federal authority, not under any state or county framework. Searching "Oklahoma" in databases for pre-1907 events requires using Indian Territory collections specifically.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma began statewide civil registration at statehood, 1907. No civil vital registration system existed in Indian Territory before 1907.
- **What exists for the mid-1800s:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. Tribal court records, missionary registers, and agency records are the functional substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); tribal council marriage records; BIA annuity rolls listing heads of household; census and enrollment rolls naming family members by age.
- **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records and Oklahoma Genealogy did not return Oklahoma-specific content during this survey — both resolved to a generic page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for updated guidance.

### Tribal enrollment rolls (primary record type for this period)
- **What exists:** Tribal enrollment rolls are the core genealogical source for Indian Territory families in the mid-1800s.
  - Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851): Names Cherokee who settled in Indian Territory before the main 1838–39 removal.
  - Drennen Roll (1852): An early enrollment for the Cherokee Nation.
  - Additional mid-century rolls (Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole) exist as part of the broader Indian Censuses and Rolls series.
  - Dawes Rolls (1898–1914): The most comprehensive enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes; records name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. These postdate the mid-1800s but are essential for confirming tribal membership and connecting to earlier rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). Also indexed at Ancestry. Original Dawes Roll records and allotment jacket files held at NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1987432 is searchable by name with images).
- **One digitized volume directly in the target window:** FamilySearch image group 002298871, "Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870," 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations active:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missionaries operated from the 1820s onward among the Five Civilized Tribes.
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials; school enrollment records; correspondence naming community members.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society) hold originals or additional microfilm.
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1654321).

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records
- **Types:** Annuity payment rolls (naming heads of household and family size), correspondence, school records, census reports, and tribal council minutes.
- **Date range:** From the 1820s onward.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas (https://www.archives.gov/). Also NARA Washington, D.C. (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs). Many records have been microfilmed by NARA.
- **Digitization level:** Partially microfilmed; some series are browse-only or physical-only at NARA. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized BIA and military records for this period.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The regular decennial U.S. federal census did not enumerate Indian Territory populations in the same manner as states. Special Indian census schedules were taken for some years. The 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses include some Indian Territory enumeration.
- **Tribal/Indian censuses:** Annual tribal censuses and rolls are included in FamilySearch collection 1987432 (Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959).
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1885) may capture some deaths, though coverage of Indian Territory is irregular.
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is indexed and searchable at FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) and Ancestry.

### Land records
- **Context:** Land distribution in Indian Territory was managed under treaty rather than the federal rectangular survey system. The Dawes Act (1887) and Curtis Act (1898) introduced individual land allotments, creating allotment records.
- **Types:** Treaty-era land use agreements; allotment schedules (post-1887); land patents.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872). Allotment records at NARA Fort Worth (Record Group 75).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1541872). Allotment jacket files at NARA may require a physical request.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–48); Civil War (1861–65, both Union and Confederate Indian regiments); Indian wars of the mid-to-late 19th century.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and unit rosters for Indian regiments (e.g., Cherokee and Creek regiments in the Civil War). NARA holds these under Record Group 94 (Adjutant General's Office) and Record Group 75.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 has digitized many Civil War service records and pension files (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many tribal and mission cemetery headstones in Oklahoma.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are held by individual tribal nations and mission churches. Coverage is uneven for the mid-1800s.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Nation published the *Cherokee Phoenix* (1828–1834) and later the *Cherokee Advocate* (1844–1906). These newspapers contain community notices, legal announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:** Digitized issues may be available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and through tribal nation archives and university libraries.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts handled wills, guardianships, and estates. Federal courts (U.S. District Court for Indian Territory, established 1889) handled cases involving non-Indians and later broader jurisdiction.
- **Date range:** Tribal court records exist from the mid-1800s onward; federal court records from 1889.
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth (federal records); individual tribal nation archives (tribal court records).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant movements:** Forced removals (1830s–1840s) from southeastern states to Indian Territory are documented in removal records and early enrollment rolls. Freedmen registration post-1866 is part of the Dawes Roll process.
- **Record types:** Removal records, emigration lists, treaty documents held at NARA (Record Group 75). Naturalizations of non-Indians in Indian Territory were handled through federal courts after 1889.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Tax records
- **Note:** No conventional county property tax system existed in Indian Territory before 1907. Tax substitutes are annuity rolls and per-capita payment rolls in the BIA agency records.

### School records
- **Context:** The Five Civilized Tribes operated their own school systems, including tribal seminaries (Cherokee Male and Female Seminaries, established 1851). Missionary schools also existed.
- **Record types:** Enrollment and attendance records, seminary catalogues.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society (https://www.okhistory.org/) and tribal nation archives. Some microfilm at FamilySearch.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Oklahoma) (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was formally designated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Oklahoma Territory was organized in 1890 (western half). The two territories merged at Oklahoma statehood, 18 November 1907.
- **Administrative center:** No single county-seat structure existed for Indian Territory; governance was tribal-national, with the Five Civilized Tribes maintaining their own capitals (e.g., Tahlequah for Cherokee, Tishomingo for Chickasaw).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (U.S. Congress), with concurrent tribal sovereignty.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the tools for this jurisdiction and period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence and cash crops), ranching, trade, and later coal mining and oil discovery in the late 19th century.
- **Ethnic composition:** The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the principal peoples relocated to Indian Territory under the Indian Removal Act. Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members), intermarried non-Indians, and later white settlers also present.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward. Tribal members also maintained traditional religious practices.
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act 1830; Trail of Tears removals 1830s–1840s; Civil War (Indian Territory tribes were divided, some signing Confederate treaties); Reconstruction-era tribal treaties 1866; Dawes Act 1887; Curtis Act 1898 (dissolved tribal governments); Oklahoma statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1890: The entire present-day Oklahoma was designated Indian Territory, governed by tribal nations under federal treaty.
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory (western half) was organized as a federal territory; Indian Territory (eastern half) retained tribal governance.
- 1907: Both territories merged to form the state of Oklahoma.
- Records from the mid-1800s were created under tribal and federal authority, not under any state or county framework. Searching "Oklahoma" in databases for pre-1907 events requires using Indian Territory collections specifically.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma began statewide civil registration at statehood, 1907. No civil vital registration system existed in Indian Territory before 1907.
- **What exists for the mid-1800s:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. Tribal court records, missionary registers, and agency records are the functional substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); tribal council marriage records; BIA annuity rolls listing heads of household; census and enrollment rolls naming family members by age.
- **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records and Oklahoma Genealogy did not return Oklahoma-specific content during this survey — both resolved to a generic page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for updated guidance.

### Tribal enrollment rolls (primary record type for this period)
- **What exists:** Tribal enrollment rolls are the core genealogical source for Indian Territory families in the mid-1800s.
  - Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851): Names Cherokee who settled in Indian Territory before the main 1838–39 removal.
  - Drennen Roll (1852): An early enrollment for the Cherokee Nation.
  - Additional mid-century rolls (Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole) exist as part of the broader Indian Censuses and Rolls series.
  - Dawes Rolls (1898–1914): The most comprehensive enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes; records name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. These postdate the mid-1800s but are essential for confirming tribal membership and connecting to earlier rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). Also indexed at Ancestry. Original Dawes Roll records and allotment jacket files held at NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1987432 is searchable by name with images).
- **One digitized volume directly in the target window:** FamilySearch image group 002298871, "Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870," 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations active:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missionaries operated from the 1820s onward among the Five Civilized Tribes.
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials; school enrollment records; correspondence naming community members.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society) hold originals or additional microfilm.
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1654321).

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records
- **Types:** Annuity payment rolls (naming heads of household and family size), correspondence, school records, census reports, and tribal council minutes.
- **Date range:** From the 1820s onward.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas (https://www.archives.gov/). Also NARA Washington, D.C. (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs). Many records have been microfilmed by NARA.
- **Digitization level:** Partially microfilmed; some series are browse-only or physical-only at NARA. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized BIA and military records for this period.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The regular decennial U.S. federal census did not enumerate Indian Territory populations in the same manner as states. Special Indian census schedules were taken for some years. The 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses include some Indian Territory enumeration.
- **Tribal/Indian censuses:** Annual tribal censuses and rolls are included in FamilySearch collection 1987432 (Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959).
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1885) may capture some deaths, though coverage of Indian Territory is irregular.
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is indexed and searchable at FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) and Ancestry.

### Land records
- **Context:** Land distribution in Indian Territory was managed under treaty rather than the federal rectangular survey system. The Dawes Act (1887) and Curtis Act (1898) introduced individual land allotments, creating allotment records.
- **Types:** Treaty-era land use agreements; allotment schedules (post-1887); land patents.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872). Allotment records at NARA Fort Worth (Record Group 75).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1541872). Allotment jacket files at NARA may require a physical request.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–48); Civil War (1861–65, both Union and Confederate Indian regiments); Indian wars of the mid-to-late 19th century.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and unit rosters for Indian regiments (e.g., Cherokee and Creek regiments in the Civil War). NARA holds these under Record Group 94 (Adjutant General's Office) and Record Group 75.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 has digitized many Civil War service records and pension files (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many tribal and mission cemetery headstones in Oklahoma.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are held by individual tribal nations and mission churches. Coverage is uneven for the mid-1800s.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Nation published the *Cherokee Phoenix* (1828–1834) and later the *Cherokee Advocate* (1844–1906). These newspapers contain community notices, legal announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:** Digitized issues may be available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and through tribal nation archives and university libraries.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts handled wills, guardianships, and estates. Federal courts (U.S. District Court for Indian Territory, established 1889) handled cases involving non-Indians and later broader jurisdiction.
- **Date range:** Tribal court records exist from the mid-1800s onward; federal court records from 1889.
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth (federal records); individual tribal nation archives (tribal court records).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant movements:** Forced removals (1830s–1840s) from southeastern states to Indian Territory are documented in removal records and early enrollment rolls. Freedmen registration post-1866 is part of the Dawes Roll process.
- **Record types:** Removal records, emigration lists, treaty documents held at NARA (Record Group 75). Naturalizations of non-Indians in Indian Territory were handled through federal courts after 1889.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Tax records
- **Note:** No conventional county property tax system existed in Indian Territory before 1907. Tax substitutes are annuity rolls and per-capita payment rolls in the BIA agency records.

### School records
- **Context:** The Five Civilized Tribes operated their own school systems, including tribal seminaries (Cherokee Male and Female Seminaries, established 1851). Missionary schools also existed.
- **Record types:** Enrollment and attendance records, seminary catalogues.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society (https://www.okhistory.org/) and tribal nation archives. Some microfilm at FamilySearch.

The logical next step is to identify which specific monthly meeting served the township where your ancestor family lived, then request the registers of that meeting from Swarthmore or search for its microfilmed copy in the FamilySearch Catalog.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by William Penn as a haven for Quakers (Religious Society of Friends); it became one of the original states in 1787.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early state capital; capital moved to Lancaster 1799, then Harrisburg 1812).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial), then United States (post-1776).
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population for this jurisdiction and period. By 1790 (first federal census) Pennsylvania's total population was approximately 434,000.
- **Economy:** Mixed agriculture, iron manufacturing, trade through the port of Philadelphia, and growing mercantile industry.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers predominated in the southeastern counties; German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite) in the interior; Scots-Irish Presbyterian in the west. Quaker communities were concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Baptist.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) — many Quakers refused military service; some were disowned for participating or paying war taxes. Pennsylvania Gradual Abolition Act (1780). New counties formed frequently throughout this period as the frontier moved westward.

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's external boundaries were substantially stable through this period, though internal county divisions changed frequently. New counties were carved from existing ones throughout the late 1700s.
- Records in a given county begin when that county was formed; events prior to formation are held in the parent county's records.
- The Province of Pennsylvania (colonial jurisdiction) preceded the state; land and legal records from before 1776 were created under colonial authority and are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Quaker meeting boundaries did not follow civil county lines — a monthly meeting might serve several townships across county boundaries. Identify the meeting, not just the county, before searching.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did NOT mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. There are NO civil vital records for the late 1700s at any governmental level in Pennsylvania.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registers for 1750–1800.
- **Where held:** N/A — these records do not exist for this period.
- **Primary substitutes:** Quaker meeting records (see Church Records below) and church registers of other denominations. FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records partially indexed) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records indexed) contain compiled and early records that may include Quaker marriages abstracted from meeting minutes.

### Church records (Quaker / Friends meeting records — PRIMARY SOURCE)
For Quaker families in the late 1700s, meeting records replace civil vital registration entirely and are far more detailed. Monthly meetings recorded all of the following:

**Record types within Quaker meetings:**
- **Birth registers:** Names of children born to member families, with date and parents' names, recorded at the monthly meeting level.
- **Marriage records:** Quaker marriages required meeting approval ("clearness" committees investigated whether any impediment existed). The marriage ceremony was held before the assembled meeting; every person present signed the marriage certificate as a witness. These certificates survive in large numbers and often name dozens of community members.
- **Death/burial records:** Deaths of members recorded at the monthly meeting.
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved to a new location, the originating monthly meeting issued a certificate to the receiving meeting vouching for the member's good standing. These documents name the individual, often family members, and the origin and destination meetings — making them the primary tool for tracing Quaker migration.
- **Disownment records:** When a member was removed from meeting membership (for marrying outside the faith, military service, moral offenses, etc.), the monthly meeting minutes record the person's name, the charges, and the outcome. A disownment ends the trail in Friends records; the researcher should then look for the person in non-Friends church records.
- **Monthly meeting minutes:** The governing minutes of each meeting document all business, including membership actions, appointments of committees, and responses to queries from the Quarterly Meeting. They name members in context and can reveal relationships.

**Quaker meeting hierarchy (records are kept at the monthly meeting level):**
Local preparative meeting → **Monthly meeting (records held here)** → Quarterly meeting → Philadelphia Yearly Meeting

**Core Quaker regions in Pennsylvania (late 1700s):**
Philadelphia County, Chester County, Bucks County, and Delaware County had the densest Quaker populations. Source: Wikipedia summary of Quakers in Pennsylvania.

**FamilySearch digitized volume:**
- Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (DGS/imageGroupNumber: 001188322), 145 images. This is **browse-only**: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed page by page. Yearly meeting minutes address denominational governance broadly; individual family events are recorded at the monthly meeting level.
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers; those microfilms may be accessible at the FamilySearch Library or via affiliated centers. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).

**Published abstracts:**
- William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and is indexed by name. This is the single most important finding aid for Pennsylvania Quaker genealogy. It is available at major genealogical libraries and through some online databases. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).

**Repositories:**
1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College**, Swarthmore, PA — primary repository for American Quaker records, including the original registers of many Pennsylvania monthly meetings. Many holdings are physical only and require contact with the library. Source: Wikipedia summary.
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College**, Haverford, PA — secondary repository with significant Quaker manuscript holdings. Source: Wikipedia summary.
3. **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) — holds microfilmed copies of many Pennsylvania Quaker meeting registers; the 1 digitized volume above is the only identified digitized result for 1750–1800, but additional microfilm may be findable through the FamilySearch Catalog. Source: FamilySearch Wiki.

**Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790 (Pennsylvania fully covered). It lists heads of household by name and enumerates all other household members by age and sex category only — not by name. It can confirm a family's presence and county of residence but will not name children.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state census enumerations. No substitute off-year state enumeration exists for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Some townships and counties kept tax assessment lists (see Tax Records below) that serve as census substitutes for pre-1790 years.
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed and fully available free on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianship bonds, estate inventories, and final accounts.
- **Date range:** Probate records for most Pennsylvania counties begin at county formation.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images, **browse-only** (0 name-indexed records). Images must be browsed by county and time period without a name index.
- **Where held:** County-level Orphans' Courts (the probate jurisdiction in Pennsylvania) and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Note:** Quakers were disproportionately involved in commerce and land ownership and left probate records at higher rates than some other groups. Quaker estates sometimes name the meeting or fellow members as witnesses or bondsmen.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Penn Proprietors, then by the Commonwealth after the Revolution — not by the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial era — the Penn family Proprietors (Pennsylvania Land Office). Post-1776 — Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
- **Types:** Proprietary warrants, surveys, patents, and deeds. After the Revolution, Pennsylvania continued issuing warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's Land Office.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds colonial and early Commonwealth land records. County courthouses hold deed books recorded locally.
- **Online access:** The Pennsylvania State Archives has made some colonial land records searchable online at phmc.pa.gov.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783) and various frontier conflicts.
- **Quaker considerations:** The Society of Friends was a peace church; most Quakers refused military service. Those who served were frequently disowned. Quaker men appear in militia and service records far less often than men of other denominations, but disownment records documenting their refusal to serve are themselves a record of the period.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records, Pennsylvania militia records, pension files, and bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (national service records and pension files, available on Fold3 and Ancestry); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records); FamilySearch (Fold3 access via affiliated libraries).

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Friends meetings maintained their own burial grounds, typically plainly marked. Sexton records and burial registers survive for some meetings and are held at the Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or the individual meeting.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has some Quaker cemetery listings but coverage is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers, where they survive, are generally held by the meeting or at Swarthmore.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) published marriage notices and death notices, including for prominent Quaker families.
- **Where held:** Available on Newspapers.com (subscription) and via some library digital archives. The American Antiquarian Society and Library of Congress also hold historical Pennsylvania newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices for Quaker families appear occasionally; legal notices (estate notices, land sales) can confirm family presence.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Quaker immigrants from England and Ireland in the colonial period (pre-dating this time window). By the late 1700s, most Quaker families in Pennsylvania were established; new immigration was less common than internal migration.
- **Certificates of removal:** The Quaker-internal certificate-of-removal system (see Church Records) is the primary tool for tracing movement. When a Quaker emigrated from England or Ireland, the originating British meeting issued a certificate to the receiving Pennsylvania meeting — these survive at both ends.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists, naturalization records (in Pennsylvania court records), certificates of removal.
- **Where held:** NARA, FamilySearch, Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County assessment and tax lists — assessed property, personal property, and occupations.
- **Date range:** Many Pennsylvania counties have tax lists beginning in the colonial period, including years before the first federal census.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives and county historical societies. Some have been published or microfilmed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records before 1790. An annual listing places a person in a specific township for each assessed year. They can also reveal wealth, occupation, and neighbors — clues about Quaker community membership.

### Other record types
- **Quaker meeting membership lists:** Some monthly meetings compiled membership rolls; these may be held at Swarthmore or in individual meeting archives.
- **Friends records relating to slavery and manumission:** Pennsylvania Quakers were early abolitionists; the 1780 Gradual Abolition Act followed decades of Friends pressure. Monthly meeting records may include manumission documents and records of formerly enslaved people freed by Quaker families.
- **Local and county histories:** Many 19th-century published county histories (Chester County, Bucks County, etc.) reprint Quaker genealogies and early records, and are available through Google Books, the Internet Archive, and academic libraries.
- **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania:** Published *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* contains abstracts of Quaker records. Holds research files at its Philadelphia repository.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, browse-only, 145 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 partially indexed records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census; military records via Fold3; some compiled Quaker abstracts | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War pension files, Continental Army records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Quaker cemetery listings (uneven coverage) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for federal holdings | Free finding aids; records vary |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Pennsylvania 1750–1800 for all record types; a separate Religious-only search also returned 1 volume (the same Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). This is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Additional Quaker registers microfilmed by FamilySearch may appear in the FamilySearch Catalog but were not returned as indexed volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA | Original registers of many Pennsylvania monthly meetings; largest American Quaker archive | In-person or written inquiry; some finding aids online |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford, PA | Quaker manuscripts; meeting records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Colonial and Commonwealth land records; militia records; early county records | In-person or online finding aids |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware counties) | Deed books, probate files, court records | In-person or county website |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA | Research files, published abstracts, *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* | In-person or online catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Most Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers (birth, marriage, death, and membership records) are held physically at the Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or at individual meetings and have NOT been digitized or name-indexed on any major platform.
- Certificates of removal are generally not separately indexed and must be searched within the minutes and registers of individual monthly meetings.
- Disownment records are embedded in monthly meeting minutes and have not been separately indexed online.
- County tax assessment lists before 1790 are largely physical-only at the Pennsylvania State Archives or county historical societies.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned for this survey identified a specific record-loss event affecting Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records or Pennsylvania records generally for this period. The Pennsylvania State Archives should be consulted for any known courthouse fires or collection losses in specific counties.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* is the first stop for any Pennsylvania Quaker family. It abstracts monthly meeting records by meeting name and indexes entries by surname. If the family appears in this abstract, it names the meeting — which then directs all further research. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Identify the monthly meeting before searching FamilySearch or archives.** Meeting records are organized by meeting name, not by county or township. A county-level search will miss records if you do not know which meeting the family attended. Use Hinshaw or a published meeting-house location guide to map the township to its meeting.
- **Follow certificates of removal to trace migration.** When a family moved, the certificate of removal is issued by the origin meeting and received by the destination meeting. Both meetings' records will reference the family. Search both ends. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- **Marriage witnesses are a community census.** Quaker marriage certificates carry the signatures of everyone present at the meeting on the day of the ceremony. A single certificate may name 30–80 community members, many of them relatives of the bride or groom. Transcribe the full witness list before moving on.
- **Check disownment records before assuming someone left no trace.** If a family member married out of meeting, served in the Revolution, or otherwise fell afoul of Friends discipline, a disownment record in the monthly meeting minutes is likely the last Friends record for that person. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- **Use tax lists to cover 1750–1789.** Before the 1790 federal census, county assessment and tax lists are the only recurring civil enumeration. Pennsylvania State Archives and county historical societies hold many of these.
- **Do not assume a woman took her husband's surname.** Quaker records often recorded women under both their birth surname and married name; some women continued to be identified by birth surname in meeting records throughout their lives. Search under both names.
- **The 1790 federal census can locate a family geographically but does not name children.** Use it to confirm county of residence, then map that county to its monthly meeting(s) for the Friends record search.
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (DGS 001188322) on FamilySearch are browse-only.** There is no name index and no full-text search — images must be reviewed page by page. These are governance-level minutes and will not contain individual family birth/marriage/death entries; those are in the monthly meeting records.
- **Contact Swarthmore and Haverford directly** for unpublished finding aids, manuscripts, and records not yet microfilmed or digitized. Both institutions have staff genealogists and respond to research inquiries.

- Pennsylvania's external boundaries were substantially stable through this period, though internal county divisions changed frequently. New counties were carved from existing ones throughout the late 1700s.
- Records in a given county begin when that county was formed; events prior to formation are held in the parent county's records.
- The Province of Pennsylvania (colonial jurisdiction) preceded the state; land and legal records from before 1776 were created under colonial authority and are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Quaker meeting boundaries did not follow civil county lines — a monthly meeting might serve several townships across county boundaries. Identify the meeting, not just the county, before searching.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did NOT mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. There are NO civil vital records for the late 1700s at any governmental level in Pennsylvania.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registers for 1750–1800.
- **Where held:** N/A — these records do not exist for this period.
- **Primary substitutes:** Quaker meeting records (see Church Records below) and church registers of other denominations. FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records partially indexed) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records indexed) contain compiled and early records that may include Quaker marriages abstracted from meeting minutes.

### Church records (Quaker / Friends meeting records — PRIMARY SOURCE)
For Quaker families in the late 1700s, meeting records replace civil vital registration entirely and are far more detailed. Monthly meetings recorded all of the following:

**Record types within Quaker meetings:**
- **Birth registers:** Names of children born to member families, with date and parents' names, recorded at the monthly meeting level.
- **Marriage records:** Quaker marriages required meeting approval ("clearness" committees investigated whether any impediment existed). The marriage ceremony was held before the assembled meeting; every person present signed the marriage certificate as a witness. These certificates survive in large numbers and often name dozens of community members.
- **Death/burial records:** Deaths of members recorded at the monthly meeting.
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved to a new location, the originating monthly meeting issued a certificate to the receiving meeting vouching for the member's good standing. These documents name the individual, often family members, and the origin and destination meetings — making them the primary tool for tracing Quaker migration.
- **Disownment records:** When a member was removed from meeting membership (for marrying outside the faith, military service, moral offenses, etc.), the monthly meeting minutes record the person's name, the charges, and the outcome. A disownment ends the trail in Friends records; the researcher should then look for the person in non-Friends church records.
- **Monthly meeting minutes:** The governing minutes of each meeting document all business, including membership actions, appointments of committees, and responses to queries from the Quarterly Meeting. They name members in context and can reveal relationships.

**Quaker meeting hierarchy (records are kept at the monthly meeting level):**
Local preparative meeting → **Monthly meeting (records held here)** → Quarterly meeting → Philadelphia Yearly Meeting

**Core Quaker regions in Pennsylvania (late 1700s):**
Philadelphia County, Chester County, Bucks County, and Delaware County had the densest Quaker populations. Source: Wikipedia summary of Quakers in Pennsylvania.

**FamilySearch digitized volume:**
- Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (DGS/imageGroupNumber: 001188322), 145 images. This is **browse-only**: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed page by page. Yearly meeting minutes address denominational governance broadly; individual family events are recorded at the monthly meeting level.
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers; those microfilms may be accessible at the FamilySearch Library or via affiliated centers. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).

**Published abstracts:**
- William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and is indexed by name. This is the single most important finding aid for Pennsylvania Quaker genealogy. It is available at major genealogical libraries and through some online databases. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).

**Repositories:**
1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College**, Swarthmore, PA — primary repository for American Quaker records, including the original registers of many Pennsylvania monthly meetings. Many holdings are physical only and require contact with the library. Source: Wikipedia summary.
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College**, Haverford, PA — secondary repository with significant Quaker manuscript holdings. Source: Wikipedia summary.
3. **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) — holds microfilmed copies of many Pennsylvania Quaker meeting registers; the 1 digitized volume above is the only identified digitized result for 1750–1800, but additional microfilm may be findable through the FamilySearch Catalog. Source: FamilySearch Wiki.

**Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790 (Pennsylvania fully covered). It lists heads of household by name and enumerates all other household members by age and sex category only — not by name. It can confirm a family's presence and county of residence but will not name children.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state census enumerations. No substitute off-year state enumeration exists for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Some townships and counties kept tax assessment lists (see Tax Records below) that serve as census substitutes for pre-1790 years.
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed and fully available free on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianship bonds, estate inventories, and final accounts.
- **Date range:** Probate records for most Pennsylvania counties begin at county formation.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images, **browse-only** (0 name-indexed records). Images must be browsed by county and time period without a name index.
- **Where held:** County-level Orphans' Courts (the probate jurisdiction in Pennsylvania) and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Note:** Quakers were disproportionately involved in commerce and land ownership and left probate records at higher rates than some other groups. Quaker estates sometimes name the meeting or fellow members as witnesses or bondsmen.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted by the Penn Proprietors, then by the Commonwealth after the Revolution — not by the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial era — the Penn family Proprietors (Pennsylvania Land Office). Post-1776 — Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
- **Types:** Proprietary warrants, surveys, patents, and deeds. After the Revolution, Pennsylvania continued issuing warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's Land Office.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds colonial and early Commonwealth land records. County courthouses hold deed books recorded locally.
- **Online access:** The Pennsylvania State Archives has made some colonial land records searchable online at phmc.pa.gov.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783) and various frontier conflicts.
- **Quaker considerations:** The Society of Friends was a peace church; most Quakers refused military service. Those who served were frequently disowned. Quaker men appear in militia and service records far less often than men of other denominations, but disownment records documenting their refusal to serve are themselves a record of the period.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records, Pennsylvania militia records, pension files, and bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (national service records and pension files, available on Fold3 and Ancestry); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records); FamilySearch (Fold3 access via affiliated libraries).

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Friends meetings maintained their own burial grounds, typically plainly marked. Sexton records and burial registers survive for some meetings and are held at the Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or the individual meeting.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has some Quaker cemetery listings but coverage is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers, where they survive, are generally held by the meeting or at Swarthmore.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) published marriage notices and death notices, including for prominent Quaker families.
- **Where held:** Available on Newspapers.com (subscription) and via some library digital archives. The American Antiquarian Society and Library of Congress also hold historical Pennsylvania newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices for Quaker families appear occasionally; legal notices (estate notices, land sales) can confirm family presence.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Quaker immigrants from England and Ireland in the colonial period (pre-dating this time window). By the late 1700s, most Quaker families in Pennsylvania were established; new immigration was less common than internal migration.
- **Certificates of removal:** The Quaker-internal certificate-of-removal system (see Church Records) is the primary tool for tracing movement. When a Quaker emigrated from England or Ireland, the originating British meeting issued a certificate to the receiving Pennsylvania meeting — these survive at both ends.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists, naturalization records (in Pennsylvania court records), certificates of removal.
- **Where held:** NARA, FamilySearch, Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County assessment and tax lists — assessed property, personal property, and occupations.
- **Date range:** Many Pennsylvania counties have tax lists beginning in the colonial period, including years before the first federal census.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives and county historical societies. Some have been published or microfilmed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records before 1790. An annual listing places a person in a specific township for each assessed year. They can also reveal wealth, occupation, and neighbors — clues about Quaker community membership.

### Other record types
- **Quaker meeting membership lists:** Some monthly meetings compiled membership rolls; these may be held at Swarthmore or in individual meeting archives.
- **Friends records relating to slavery and manumission:** Pennsylvania Quakers were early abolitionists; the 1780 Gradual Abolition Act followed decades of Friends pressure. Monthly meeting records may include manumission documents and records of formerly enslaved people freed by Quaker families.
- **Local and county histories:** Many 19th-century published county histories (Chester County, Bucks County, etc.) reprint Quaker genealogies and early records, and are available through Google Books, the Internet Archive, and academic libraries.
- **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania:** Published *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* contains abstracts of Quaker records. Holds research files at its Philadelphia repository.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, browse-only, 145 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 partially indexed records) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Pennsylvania 1750–1800 for all record types; a separate Religious-only search also returned 1 volume (the same Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). This is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Additional Quaker registers microfilmed by FamilySearch may appear in the FamilySearch Catalog but were not returned as indexed volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA | Original registers of many Pennsylvania monthly meetings; largest American Quaker archive | In-person or written inquiry; some finding aids online |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford, PA | Quaker manuscripts; meeting records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Colonial and Commonwealth land records; militia records; early county records | In-person or online finding aids |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware counties) | Deed books, probate files, court records | In-person or county website |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA | Research files, published abstracts, *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* | In-person or online catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Most Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers (birth, marriage, death, and membership records) are held physically at the Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or at individual meetings and have NOT been digitized or name-indexed on any major platform.
- Certificates of removal are generally not separately indexed and must be searched within the minutes and registers of individual monthly meetings.
- Disownment records are embedded in monthly meeting minutes and have not been separately indexed online.
- County tax assessment lists before 1790 are largely physical-only at the Pennsylvania State Archives or county historical societies.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned for this survey identified a specific record-loss event affecting Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records or Pennsylvania records generally for this period. The Pennsylvania State Archives should be consulted for any known courthouse fires or collection losses in specific counties.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* is the first stop for any Pennsylvania Quaker family. It abstracts monthly meeting records by meeting name and indexes entries by surname. If the family appears in this abstract, it names the meeting — which then directs all further research. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Identify the monthly meeting before searching FamilySearch or archives.** Meeting records are organized by meeting name, not by county or township. A county-level search will miss records if you do not know which meeting the family attended. Use Hinshaw or a published meeting-house location guide to map the township to its meeting.
- **Follow certificates of removal to trace migration.** When a family moved, the certificate of removal is issued by the origin meeting and received by the destination meeting. Both meetings' records will reference the family. Search both ends. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- **Marriage witnesses are a community census.** Quaker marriage certificates carry the signatures of everyone present at the meeting on the day of the ceremony. A single certificate may name 30–80 community members, many of them relatives of the bride or groom. Transcribe the full witness list before moving on.
- **Check disownment records before assuming someone left no trace.** If a family member married out of meeting, served in the Revolution, or otherwise fell afoul of Friends discipline, a disownment record in the monthly meeting minutes is likely the last Friends record for that person. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- **Use tax lists to cover 1750–1789.** Before the 1790 federal census, county assessment and tax lists are the only recurring civil enumeration. Pennsylvania State Archives and county historical societies hold many of these.
- **Do not assume a woman took her husband's surname.** Quaker records often recorded women under both their birth surname and married name; some women continued to be identified by birth surname in meeting records throughout their lives. Search under both names.
- **The 1790 federal census can locate a family geographically but does not name children.** Use it to confirm county of residence, then map that county to its monthly meeting(s) for the Friends record search.
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (DGS 001188322) on FamilySearch are browse-only.** There is no name index and no full-text search — images must be reviewed page by page. These are governance-level minutes and will not contain individual family birth/marriage/death entries; those are in the monthly meeting records.
- **Contact Swarthmore and Haverford directly** for unpublished finding aids, manuscripts, and records not yet microfilmed or digitized. Both institutions have staff genealogists and respond to research inquiries.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1905)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816; Allegheny County formed 1788. The neighboring City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River) remained a separate municipality until annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this standard place. Per Wikipedia, Pittsburgh grew substantially during this period — from a mid-sized industrial city in 1870 to over 300,000 residents by 1900 — as Carnegie Steel and other major mills attracted massive immigrant labor.
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated. Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and other firms operated mills in Pittsburgh and the surrounding mill towns of Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, and Duquesne. Tens of thousands of industrial workers were employed in iron and steel production.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant communities drawn by mill employment: Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers, per Wikipedia and the FamilySearch Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (with numerous ethnic-national parishes), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892; rapid industrial expansion 1870s–1900s; formation of Carnegie Steel (1892) and U.S. Steel (1901).

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County was formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties and its boundaries were stable through this period.
- The City of Allegheny (the "North Side"), directly across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh, was a separate incorporated city until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Residents living there before 1907 appear in records filed under "Allegheny" (city), not Pittsburgh — this affects city directories, church records, tax rolls, and court filings.
- No other boundary changes affecting record custody were identified for this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey (all resolved to https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records, not the Pennsylvania-specific page). The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) begins in 1906, consistent with statewide death registration beginning around that year. The "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" collection (collection 1921317) reflects county-level marriage registration from 1885. Birth registration dates and any earlier local-level registration could not be verified from the returned tool results — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** County marriage records from 1885 (collection 1921317, indexed, 524,189 records); civil marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, indexed, 312,045 records); compiled marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, indexed, 198,765 records, no images); death certificates from 1906 (collection 2255317, indexed, 4,218,763 records — captures workers who died after 1906).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, free); Allegheny County courthouse for originals.
- **Gaps:** Birth and death registration was incomplete or absent at the local level during most of the 1870–1905 window. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific start date for Pennsylvania vital registration levels in this survey.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; newspaper birth and death notices; cemetery headstone inscriptions.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Individual parish offices; Diocese of Pittsburgh archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed some Pennsylvania church records. Per the FamilySearch Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records), Catholic parish registers are often the best source for family data for immigrant communities.
- **Language:** English for most records; Latin for sacramental entries in older registers; Polish, Slovak, or Italian in some ethnic parish registers.
- **Critical note:** Ethnic Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by national origin. Identifying the immigrant's specific ethnic parish — not just any nearby Catholic church — is essential before searching. The wrong parish will have no record of the family.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 are available. The 1890 census was largely destroyed by a 1921 fire, creating a significant gap for 1886–1896. Per the FamilySearch Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records), the 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules list each person's occupation — making them critical for tracing industrial workers.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular intercensal statewide enumerations in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1870, 1880) record deaths in the prior year; the 1890 Veterans' Schedule (a partial survivor of the 1890 fire) covers Civil War veterans.
- **Access:** Federal censuses fully indexed on Ancestry (subscription, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/); partially on FamilySearch (free).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** From 1788 (county formation).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) with 3,200,560 browse-only images — must be browsed image by image with no name index (0% name-indexed, not fulltext-searchable). Volume 008120441 (1,180 images, 1683–1994) is one of three digitized volumes returned by volume_search for this place and period. Originals held at Allegheny County Register of Wills.
- **Note:** Working-class mill workers rarely left wills, but estate inventories and administrations can reveal family relationships and confirm identity.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state using metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Land and Property page returned generic content only in this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly for grants and patents.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1788).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (Pittsburgh). Deeds are not digitized in any online collection identified in this survey — physical access required.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many workers in Pittsburgh during the steel boom were veterans; Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (Civil War pension files are the most genealogically rich military record of this era), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/), Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (nonsectarian, founded 1844), ethnic Catholic cemeteries associated with individual parishes.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers major Pittsburgh-area cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and Pittsburgh Dispatch were active during this period.
- **Where held/access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm of local papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mill accident reports (frequent and locally reported), strike coverage, legal notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Eastern European and Southern European immigrants arrived through New York (Ellis Island/Castle Garden), Philadelphia, or Baltimore.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch), naturalization records.
- **Naturalization records:** Per the FamilySearch Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records), naturalization records are held at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia. FamilySearch volume 008120443 covers Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% name-indexed, not fulltext-searchable — partial name search possible; most must be browsed). Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all travelers including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County real estate and personal property tax.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1788).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; some transcriptions may be at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh or Heinz History Center.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records are particularly valuable for the 1890s gap created by the loss of the 1890 federal census.

### Occupational and industrial records
- **Company employment records:** Per the FamilySearch Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records), company employment records are fragmentary — some survive at the Heinz History Center (heinzhistorycenter.org) and the Rivers of Steel archives. Most mill employment records were not preserved.
- **Union membership lists:** Records of the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers may survive at union archives or the Heinz History Center.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s onward; these list occupations alongside addresses and are essential for tracking workers between census years and for the 1890s gap.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania state factory inspector reports documented mill conditions and workers. These are physical-only at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg.
- **Homestead Strike records (1892):** Court records, newspaper coverage, and congressional investigation records name workers involved; NARA and the Heinz History Center hold relevant materials.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | PA County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317, 524K indexed); PA Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957, 312K indexed); PA Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909, 199K indexed, no images); PA Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); PA Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317, 4.2M indexed); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 vol. 008120443 (351 images, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Pittsburgh-area cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization, federal court, military | Free catalog; fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania scope (the complete result set — no nextPageToken; all 3 are detailed above). Collections_search returned 6 collections at the Pennsylvania scope (complete set; the synthetic test fixture was excluded). These cover the most significant digitized holdings but do not represent all records for Allegheny County specifically — many records remain physical-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh (heinzhistorycenter.org) | Industrial employment records (fragmentary), immigration records, Pittsburgh history collection | In-person; online finding aids |
| Rivers of Steel Archives, Homestead, PA | Steel industry company records, union records, mill photographs | In-person by appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Dept. | City directories from 1810s, local newspapers on microfilm, local history materials | In-person |
| Allegheny County Courthouse, Pittsburgh | Marriage records (from 1885), court records, naturalizations, deed books | In-person / mail to Recorder of Deeds, Register of Wills |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | Naturalization records, federal court records, federal census microfilm | In-person / online request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State factory inspector reports, state-level records | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers and diocesan records | In-person by appointment |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records for Carnegie Steel and other Pittsburgh mills (fragmentary physical holdings at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives — not digitized)
- Union membership lists (physical; location varies)
- State factory inspector reports (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg)
- Allegheny County deed and mortgage records from this period
- Pittsburgh city birth records prior to statewide registration
- Ethnic Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921 — a well-documented national loss. City directories, tax records, and the 1890 Veterans' Schedule are partial substitutes.
- No tool result in this survey identified specific courthouse fires or record losses specific to Allegheny County during this period. The Pennsylvania State Archives or the Heinz History Center should be consulted to verify survival of specific record sets.

## Research tips
- **Industrial records are the distinctive strength of Pittsburgh research.** Begin with the federal census schedules for 1870, 1880, and 1900, which list each household member's occupation and can pin a worker to a specific mill town. Then use Carnegie Library city directories to track workers between census years — essential for the 1886–1896 gap. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records
- **Identify the immigrant's ethnic Catholic parish before searching church records.** Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized along national-origin lines — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities each had separate parishes. Searching the wrong parish finds nothing. Determine national origin first, then identify the ethnic parish for the neighborhood. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records
- **For naturalizations before 1906, search multiple courts.** Pre-1906 declarations could be filed in any court of record. Check Allegheny County Common Pleas, U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, and other courts; records are at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia. FamilySearch volume 008120443 is 15% name-indexed (1790–1915) — partial search possible but much must be browsed. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records
- **The City of Allegheny was separate from Pittsburgh until 1907.** Workers living north of the Allegheny River before annexation appear in records filed under Allegheny (city), not Pittsburgh. This affects city directories, church records, and court records.
- **Death certificates from 1906 onward are fully indexed and genealogically rich.** Many workers who immigrated in the 1870s–1890s survived into the 1906–1930 period. Pennsylvania death certificates (collection 2255317) state parents' names, birthplace, occupation, and informant — valuable for tracing immigrant origins.
- **For the 1890 census gap:** Use city directories (Carnegie Library, physical), county tax assessment records (Allegheny County courthouse), and the 1890 Veterans' Schedule as substitutes.
- **Consult Pennsylvania-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages directly.** The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, and Naming Customs wiki pages all returned only generic content in this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records and related pages directly for current, place-specific registration dates and record availability.

- **Types:** County real estate and personal property tax.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1788).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; some transcriptions may be at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh or Heinz History Center.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records are particularly valuable for the 1890s gap created by the loss of the 1890 federal census.

### Occupational and industrial records
