Most mill employment records were not preserved.
- **Union membership lists:** Records of the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers may survive at union archives or the Heinz History Center.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s onward; these list occupations alongside addresses and are essential for tracking workers between census years and for the 1890s gap.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania state factory inspector reports documented mill conditions and workers. These are physical-only at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg.

| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Pittsburgh-area cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania scope (the complete result set — no nextPageToken; all 3 are detailed above). | Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh (heinzhistorycenter.org) | Industrial employment records (fragmentary), immigration records, Pittsburgh history collection | In-person; online finding aids |
| Rivers of Steel Archives, Homestead, PA | Steel industry company records, union records, mill photographs | In-person by appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Dept. | City directories from 1810s, local newspapers on microfilm, local history materials | In-person |
| Allegheny County Courthouse, Pittsburgh | Marriage records (from 1885), court records, naturalizations, deed books | In-person / mail to Recorder of Deeds, Register of Wills |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | Naturalization records, federal court records, federal census microfilm | In-person / online request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State factory inspector reports, state-level records | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers and diocesan records | In-person by appointment |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records for Carnegie Steel and other Pittsburgh mills (fragmentary physical holdings at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives — not digitized)
- Union membership lists (physical; location varies)
- State factory inspector reports (physical at Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg)
- Allegheny County deed and mortgage records from this period
- Pittsburgh city birth records prior to statewide registration
- Ethnic Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921 — a well-documented national loss. City directories, tax records, and the 1890 Veterans' Schedule are partial substitutes.
- No tool result in this survey identified specific courthouse fires or record losses specific to Allegheny County during this period. The Pennsylvania State Archives or the Heinz History Center should be consulted to verify survival of specific record sets.

## Research tips
- **Industrial records are the distinctive strength of Pittsburgh research.** Begin with the federal census schedules for 1870, 1880, and 1900, which list each household member's occupation and can pin a worker to a specific mill town. Then use Carnegie Library city directories to track workers between census years — essential for the 1886–1896 gap. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records
- **Identify the immigrant's ethnic Catholic parish before searching church records.** Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized along national-origin lines — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities each had separate parishes. Searching the wrong parish finds nothing. Determine national origin first, then identify the ethnic parish for the neighborhood. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records
- **For naturalizations before 1906, search multiple courts.** Pre-1906 declarations could be filed in any court of record. Check Allegheny County Common Pleas, U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, and other courts; records are at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia. FamilySearch volume 008120443 is 15% name-indexed (1790–1915) — partial search possible but much must be browsed. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records
- **The City of Allegheny was separate from Pittsburgh until 1907.** Workers living north of the Allegheny River before annexation appear in records filed under Allegheny (city), not Pittsburgh. This affects city directories, church records, and court records.
- **Death certificates from 1906 onward are fully indexed and genealogically rich.** Many workers who immigrated in the 1870s–1890s survived into the 1906–1930 period. Pennsylvania death certificates (collection 2255317) state parents' names, birthplace, occupation, and informant — valuable for tracing immigrant origins.
- **For the 1890 census gap:** Use city directories (Carnegie Library, physical), county tax assessment records (Allegheny County courthouse), and the 1890 Veterans' Schedule as substitutes.
- **Consult Pennsylvania-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages directly.** The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, and Naming Customs wiki pages all returned only generic content in this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records and related pages directly for current, place-specific registration dates and record availability.

Here is the locality guide produced for your research:

---

**Locality Guide — Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic**
*(Survey window: c. 1780–1820)*

---

### Context

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil vital registration in 1793** (that did not begin until 1906). This makes church burial registers and contemporary published death lists the closest equivalent to death certificates for epidemic victims. The epidemic killed roughly 5,000 people between August and November 1793 — about one-tenth of Philadelphia's population.

---

### Key Sources & Repositories

#### 1. Mathew Carey's Published Death List
- **What it is:** *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793, multiple editions). Carey appended a list of persons who died during the epidemic, organized by name and sometimes street address.
- **Where to find it:** Digitized copies are available at the Internet Archive and HathiTrust. Physical copies are held at the Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP).
- **How to use it:** Start here to confirm whether an ancestor died during the epidemic.

#### 2. Church Burial Registers (Philadelphia)
- **Why critical:** The most systematic death documentation of the era. Philadelphia had dozens of congregations by 1793. The busiest burial registers during August–November 1793 will show epidemic deaths clustered densely.
- **Repositories:**
  - **Christ Church / St. Peter's (Anglican/Episcopal):** Registers digitized and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. HSP holds originals.
  - **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church:** Registers indexed on FamilySearch.
  - **St. Mary's & St. Joseph's (Catholic):** Registers at the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center.
  - **First Presbyterian, Second Presbyterian, Arch Street Friends Meeting, and others:** Many are at HSP or the Presbyterian Historical Society (PHS), 425 Lombard Street, Philadelphia.
  - **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker):** FamilySearch holds one digitized browse-only volume (Minutes, 1750–1800); fuller records are at Haverford College's Quaker & Special Collections and Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore.
- **Search tip:** Check burial registers for the months August–November 1793 specifically; entries will often note "yellow fever" or "malignant fever."

#### 3. Philadelphia Committee for Relief — Minutes & Papers
- **What it is:** The citizens' Committee (formed August 1793) organized relief, maintained Bush Hill hospital, and tracked deaths and orphans. Committee minutes record individual names, addresses, financial relief disbursements, and orphan cases.
- **Where:** Philadelphia City Archives and HSP. These are **manuscript, not digitized**, and require in-person or mail-order access.

#### 4. Bush Hill Hospital Records
- **What it is:** The improvised epidemic hospital on the outskirts of the city. Patient registers, if they survive, would document individuals treated or who died there.
- **Where:** HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; survival of records is incomplete.

#### 5. Orphans' Court Records (Philadelphia County)
- **Why:** Many children were orphaned by the epidemic. Guardianship petitions filed in late 1793 and early 1794 name the deceased parents, surviving children, and appointed guardians — a rich source for family reconstruction.
- **Where:** Philadelphia City Archives. Finding aids are available through the Philadelphia Register of Wills (wills.phila.gov) for probate filings; Orphans' Court manuscripts are at City Archives.
- **FamilySearch:** Some Philadelphia wills and administrations are indexed; search FamilySearch catalog under "Pennsylvania, Philadelphia County, Probate Records."

#### 6. Probate / Administration Records
- **Why:** Deaths in rapid succession — often both parents within days — generated estate administrations filed at the Register of Wills, Philadelphia County.
- **Where:** FamilySearch has a digitized collection: *Pennsylvania, Philadelphia County, Wills and Administrations, 1682–1900*. Also accessible via Ancestry.
- **Search strategy:** Sort or filter administrations filed October 1793 – June 1794 to find epidemic casualties.

#### 7. Newspaper Obituaries and Death Notices
- **Sources:** *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *Federal Gazette*, *General Advertiser* (later the *Aurora*) — all published in Philadelphia in 1793 and carried death notices.
- **Where:**
  - **Readex/America's Historical Newspapers** (subscription, available at many libraries)
  - **Library Company of Philadelphia** (extensive newspaper holdings, in person or duplication service)
  - **HSP** microfilm holdings

#### 8. Tax Records (Effective Supply Tax / County Tax)
- **Why:** Establish residence before and after the epidemic; note households that disappear or change between 1793 and 1794–1795 assessments.
- **Where:** Philadelphia City Archives. Some are digitized on FamilySearch under Pennsylvania tax records.

#### 9. Philadelphia City Directories
- **Why:** Pre- and post-epidemic directories show which households vanished, moved, or changed composition.
- **Key years:** 1791, 1793, 1794, 1795, 1796 editions.
- **Where:** Library Company of Philadelphia (the authoritative collection); many years digitized on Ancestry and at HathiTrust.

#### 10. Published Secondary Sources & Finding Aids
- J. Worth Estes & Billy G. Smith, eds., *A Melancholy Scene of Devastation: The Public Response to the 1793 Philadelphia Yellow Fever Epidemic* (1997) — includes bibliographic guidance and primary-source analysis.
- Billy G. Smith, *Ship of Death: A Voyage That Changed the Atlantic World* (2013) — context on the epidemic's origins.
- HSP has a subject guide specifically for the 1793 epidemic available on their website (hsp.org).

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Committee papers, church registers, newspapers, directories | In person; some digitized |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Orphans' Court, tax records, Bush Hill papers | In person or mail |
| Register of Wills, Philadelphia County | Probate, administrations | wills.phila.gov; FamilySearch |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Newspapers, directories, Carey pamphlets | In person; some digitized |
| Presbyterian Historical Society | Presbyterian registers | In person |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic registers | In person or mail |
| FamilySearch | Episcopal registers, Quaker minutes (browse-only), probate | Free online |
| Ancestry | Episcopal registers, probate, directories | Subscription |

---

### Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **Carey's death list** — confirm death during the epidemic.
2. **Church burial register** for the family's congregation — exact date of death and sometimes family notes.
3. **Probate/administration filings, Register of Wills** — estate papers name surviving heirs.
4. **Orphans' Court guardianship records** — if children survived, guardianship petitions reconstruct the immediate family.
5. **City directories and tax lists** — establish pre-epidemic residence and track survivors afterward.
6. **HSP Committee papers** — for families who received relief or whose children entered the Committee's care.

---

*Guide recorded as **loc_001** in the project research log.*

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; city of Philadelphia incorporated 1701

| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312K indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198K indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 browse-only images) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790 and 1800 Philadelphia | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Federal military records (pension files, service records) | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA | Federal records including passenger lists, naturalization, military pension files | Free finding aids; some digitized (https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Find A Grave | Major Philadelphia cemetery memorials including Christ Church Burial Ground | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| HathiTrust / Internet Archive | Mathew Carey's 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) digitized | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume_search identified 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia 1780–1820; `totalResults` was 1, so this is the complete result set for the period. Collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections; those outside the 1780–1820 window (County Marriages 1885–1950 and Death Certificates 1906–1968) are excluded from the table above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Death registers, ward tax assessments, Orphans' Court filings, Overseers of the Poor minutes, Almshouse records, deed books | In-person or mail request |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Citizens' Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, church register transcriptions, newspapers, private papers | In-person; some digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; transcriptions of colonial and early national registers | In-person; some materials on microfilm |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Carey's 'Short Account,' 18th-century printed bills of mortality, local history | In-person; digitized copies of many titles |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Commonwealth land records, militia/military records, state supply tax | In-person or mail |
| Individual congregations | Original registers where not deposited elsewhere (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, Friends' meetings, etc.) | Contact congregation directly |
| NARA Philadelphia region | Federal court naturalizations, local federal records | In-person; NARA online catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Citizens' Committee minutes and reports (1793)
- Bush Hill hospital patient records
- Philadelphia health office death registers / bills of mortality (manuscript copies)
- Philadelphia ward and township tax assessments (1780s–1800s)
- Orphans' Court guardianship dockets (1793–1794 epidemic surge filings)
- Most individual Philadelphia church registers for this period — only the Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes are in a FamilySearch digitized volume, and that volume is browse-only
- Almshouse admission and death registers
- Overseers of the Poor minute books

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported the destruction or loss of a specific Philadelphia record set for the 1793 period. The absence of records from FamilySearch's indexed collections is a digitization gap, not evidence of destruction. Researchers should confirm holdings and survival status directly with the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania before concluding a record set is lost.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's published list of the dead.** The appendices to 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) name epidemic victims by neighborhood — this is the fastest entry point for confirming whether an ancestor died in the epidemic. Digitized copies are available at HathiTrust and Internet Archive. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Church burial registers are the primary vital record.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration in 1793; statewide registration did not begin until 1906. Church registers — especially those of Christ Church and Gloria Dei — recorded the epidemic's dead and are the equivalent of death certificates for this period. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Search probate and Orphans' Court filings for late 1793 and 1794.** The epidemic produced a concentrated surge of simultaneous estate filings. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records collection (FamilySearch collection 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) has 3.2 million images but zero indexed records — you must browse by date range, not by name.
- **Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses household by household.** Members present in 1790 and absent in 1800 are candidates for epidemic victims. The 1790 and 1800 censuses are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Search newspapers for individual death and estate notices.** Philadelphia newspapers published daily during the epidemic and printed bills of mortality listing the dead by name and ward. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has digitized historical Philadelphia newspapers.
- **Look in surrounding county records for refugees.** Thousands fled to Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Bucks counties during the epidemic (August–November 1793). Tax lists, church records, and correspondence in those counties may document your family's presence during displacement.
- **Use the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's church record indexes.** GSP has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers not yet fully digitized on major platforms. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Philadelphia probate is a state-land jurisdiction using metes and bounds.** Land transfers after estate settlements will appear in the Philadelphia deed books at the City Archives — not in the federal land office records used for western states.
- **Quaker families:** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting kept detailed records of members including certificates of removal when a member moved to another meeting. The one FamilySearch digitized volume (image group 001188322, 1750–1800) is browse-only; originals are at Haverford College's Quaker Collection and Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore.
- **German-language church records:** Lutheran and Reformed congregations in Philadelphia kept registers in German during this period. A researcher must be able to read German script, or obtain a translation, to use these records directly.

## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871 Research Guide

### The Core Challenge
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and nearly all pre-fire records with it — deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Any empty search result for the pre-fire period may simply mean the record burned, not that the person wasn't there.

---

### What Survived (Pre-Fire)

| Record | Where Held |
|---|---|
| **Federal censuses** (1850, 1860, 1870) | Preserved in Washington D.C.; on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **City directories** (1840s onward) | Newberry Library |
| **Church registers** from parishes outside the burned district | Individual parish archives; some on FamilySearch |

---

### Post-Fire Reconstruction Records

| Record | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Burnt Record Act filings (1872)** | Required property owners to re-register deeds; reconstructed land-record series |
| **Chicago Title and Trust Co. collection** | Insurance and title records at the Chicago History Museum |
| **Civil vital records** | Cook County collections on FamilySearch begin in 1871 |
| **Reconstructed court records** | Digitized browse-only volumes on FamilySearch |
| **Post-fire property re-recordings** | ~41% indexed on FamilySearch |

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the primary pre-fire snapshot of any Chicago family
2. Search **surviving church registers** for baptisms, marriages, and burials
3. Check **city directories** at the Newberry Library for residence and occupation
4. Search **Burnt Record Act filings** and the Chicago Title and Trust collection for property ties
5. Move to **post-fire civil vital records** for events from late 1871 onward

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1900)
## The Great Fire and Its Genealogical Aftermath

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by tools for this query.
- **Economy:** Major rail hub, meatpacking, grain trade, and manufacturing; Chicago was one of the fastest-growing cities in the world during this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, and Scandinavian immigrant communities in the 1860s–1870s, followed by increasing Eastern European immigration after 1880.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (large Irish and German parishes), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations; the Archdiocese of Chicago is specifically named as a key repository in the FamilySearch Cook County genealogy wiki.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed roughly 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with most official pre-fire records. Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).

## Boundary changes
- Cook County was established in 1831 and its boundaries were stable through the 1860–1900 period.
- Chicago underwent territorial annexations during the 19th century but remained wholly within Cook County.
- No boundary change routes records to a different county for this period.

## The Record Loss: What the Fire Destroyed
The Cook County Courthouse, destroyed on October 8–10, 1871, housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Per the FamilySearch Cook County, Illinois Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) and the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the practical effect on genealogical records is:

- Pre-fire county deed books: destroyed
- Pre-fire probate and court files: largely destroyed
- Pre-fire birth, death, and marriage registers: destroyed
- Pre-fire tax rolls: destroyed

What survived:
- Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 (originals held in Washington, DC)
- Church registers stored outside the burned district
- City directories held at the Newberry Library
- Federal and state military records held in Washington and Springfield

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What the FamilySearch wiki states:** The specific Illinois Vital Records wiki page did not return specific content in this survey (returned generic text only). The FamilySearch Cook County, Illinois Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) states the Cook County Clerk's office holds vital records from 1871 onward.
- **What exists online:** All four FamilySearch civil vital record collections for Cook County begin in 1871, reflecting the fire's destruction of earlier records:
  - Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947 (980,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (620,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
- **Gaps:** No online-indexed civil vital records predate October 1871. The exact date Illinois required statewide registration is not confirmed by the tools in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Illinois Vital Records page directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below) and city directories.

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (285,000 records) — spans pre- and post-fire periods, as parish registers stored outside the burned district survived. **Indexed + images.**
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish, and others — reflecting the diverse immigrant population.
- **Physical repository:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Language:** Records may be in German, Polish, or other immigrant languages for ethnic-language parishes; the researcher must be able to read the original language.

### Census records
- **1860 federal census:** Survived (original in Washington, DC) — **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1870 federal census:** Survived (original in Washington, DC) — **Indexed + images**; this is the single most important pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families, taken just one year before the fire. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **1880 federal census:** Post-fire — **Indexed + images**.
- **1900 federal census:** **Indexed + images**.
- **Note on the 1890 census:** The FamilySearch tools did not return specific information about 1890 census survival for Cook County — consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki for current guidance.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire records:** Largely destroyed in the courthouse fire. FamilySearch volume 009982110 contains 38 images of reconstructed pre-fire County Court Records (1865–1871). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image.** It must be examined page by page with no search capability.
- **Post-fire records:** Held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Testate vs. intestate:** For any post-1871 decedent who left a will, search the probate will series; for intestate deaths, search the administration files — both are at IRAD for post-fire records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a public-land (federal-land) state; original land grants originate from the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO).
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Destroyed in the courthouse. The primary substitute is the Burnt Record Act of 1872, which required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire. Per the Wikipedia Great Chicago Fire article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire) and the FamilySearch Cook County Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire), these reconstructed deed books and the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum are the key substitute sources.
- **FamilySearch volume:** 009982111 contains 112 images of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (1871–1880), **41% name-indexed** — partially searchable by name, partially browse-only.
- **Types:** Reconstructed deeds, insurance and title records, post-fire tax records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) immediately preceded the fire; many Chicago families had members who served in Union forces.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era) — held at NARA and available on Fold3.com (subscription).
- **State records:** Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives, Springfield.
- **Survival:** Federal and state military records were held outside Chicago and survived the fire.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) provides cemetery transcriptions for Cook County cemeteries — free access.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; contact individual cemeteries directly.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers documented the fire period and relief efforts.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com holds digitized historical newspapers (subscription). The Newberry Library holds additional newspaper holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, fire relief lists, legal notices, and community news — particularly valuable for the period immediately after the fire when families were displaced.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island after 1892), Baltimore, New Orleans, and other Atlantic and Gulf ports served Chicago-bound immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA and on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Pre-1906 naturalization records scattered across Cook County Circuit Court (IRAD), NARA Great Lakes Region, and federal courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls were destroyed in the courthouse fire.
- **Post-fire:** Property tax records held at the Cook County Assessor's office.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library) serve a similar substitute function for intercensal years, placing a person at a specific address.

### City directories
City directories for Chicago from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library. They are the primary substitute for missing pre-fire vital records and census off-years, placing individuals at specific addresses by year. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).

## Repository guide

Locality guide written as **loc_001** in research.json.

---

Chicago, Cook County, Illinois is one of the most challenging places for 19th-century genealogy because the Great Chicago Fire of October 8-10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with nearly all pre-fire deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. What survives for the period before the fire are the federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 (which were preserved in Washington, D.C.), city directories from the 1840s onward held at the Newberry Library, and church registers from parishes whose records were stored outside the burned district. After the fire, the Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds, creating a reconstructed land-record series; insurance and title records at the Chicago History Museum's Chicago Title and Trust Company collection fill further gaps. On FamilySearch, all four Cook County civil vital collections begin in 1871, and two digitized volumes cover reconstructed court records (browse-only) and post-fire property re-recordings (41% indexed). The most important caution is that an empty search in any post-fire database does not mean the person was not there before October 1871 — it may simply mean the record burned.

The recommended next step is to search the 1870 federal census as the primary pre-fire snapshot of any Chicago family, then work outward to the surviving church registers, city directories, and post-fire Burnt Record Act filings depending on which life events need to be documented.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1900)
## The Great Fire and Its Genealogical Aftermath

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by tools for this query.
- **Economy:** Major rail hub, meatpacking, grain trade, and manufacturing; Chicago was one of the fastest-growing cities in the world during this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, and Scandinavian immigrant communities in the 1860s–1870s, followed by increasing Eastern European immigration after 1880.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (large Irish and German parishes), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations; the Archdiocese of Chicago is specifically named as a key repository in the FamilySearch Cook County genealogy wiki.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed roughly 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with most official pre-fire records. Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).

## Boundary changes
- Cook County was established in 1831 and its boundaries were stable through the 1860–1900 period.
- Chicago underwent territorial annexations during the 19th century but remained wholly within Cook County.
- No boundary change routes records to a different county for this period.

## The Record Loss: What the Fire Destroyed
The Cook County Courthouse, destroyed on October 8–10, 1871, housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Per the FamilySearch Cook County, Illinois Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) and the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the practical effect on genealogical records is:

- Pre-fire county deed books: destroyed
- Pre-fire probate and court files: largely destroyed
- Pre-fire birth, death, and marriage registers: destroyed
- Pre-fire tax rolls: destroyed

What survived:
- Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 (originals held in Washington, DC)
- Church registers stored outside the burned district
- City directories held at the Newberry Library
- Federal and state military records held in Washington and Springfield

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What the FamilySearch wiki states:** The specific Illinois Vital Records wiki page did not return specific content in this survey (returned generic text only). The FamilySearch Cook County, Illinois Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) states the Cook County Clerk's office holds vital records from 1871 onward.
- **What exists online:** All four FamilySearch civil vital record collections for Cook County begin in 1871, reflecting the fire's destruction of earlier records:
  - Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947 (980,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (620,000 records) — **Indexed + images**
- **Gaps:** No online-indexed civil vital records predate October 1871. The exact date Illinois required statewide registration is not confirmed by the tools in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Illinois Vital Records page directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below) and city directories.

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (285,000 records) — spans pre- and post-fire periods, as parish registers stored outside the burned district survived. **Indexed + images.**
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish, and others — reflecting the diverse immigrant population.
- **Physical repository:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Language:** Records may be in German, Polish, or other immigrant languages for ethnic-language parishes; the researcher must be able to read the original language.

### Census records
- **1860 federal census:** Survived (original in Washington, DC) — **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1870 federal census:** Survived (original in Washington, DC) — **Indexed + images**; this is the single most important pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families, taken just one year before the fire. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **1880 federal census:** Post-fire — **Indexed + images**.
- **1900 federal census:** **Indexed + images**.
- **Note on the 1890 census:** The FamilySearch tools did not return specific information about 1890 census survival for Cook County — consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki for current guidance.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire records:** Largely destroyed in the courthouse fire. FamilySearch volume 009982110 contains 38 images of reconstructed pre-fire County Court Records (1865–1871). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image.** It must be examined page by page with no search capability.
- **Post-fire records:** Held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Testate vs. intestate:** For any post-1871 decedent who left a will, search the probate will series; for intestate deaths, search the administration files — both are at IRAD for post-fire records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a public-land (federal-land) state; original land grants originate from the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO).
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Destroyed in the courthouse. The primary substitute is the Burnt Record Act of 1872, which required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire. Per the Wikipedia Great Chicago Fire article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire) and the FamilySearch Cook County Genealogy wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire), these reconstructed deed books and the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum are the key substitute sources.
- **FamilySearch volume:** 009982111 contains 112 images of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (1871–1880), **41% name-indexed** — partially searchable by name, partially browse-only.
- **Types:** Reconstructed deeds, insurance and title records, post-fire tax records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) immediately preceded the fire; many Chicago families had members who served in Union forces.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era) — held at NARA and available on Fold3.com (subscription).
- **State records:** Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives, Springfield.
- **Survival:** Federal and state military records were held outside Chicago and survived the fire.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) provides cemetery transcriptions for Cook County cemeteries — free access.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; contact individual cemeteries directly.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers documented the fire period and relief efforts.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com holds digitized historical newspapers (subscription). The Newberry Library holds additional newspaper holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, fire relief lists, legal notices, and community news — particularly valuable for the period immediately after the fire when families were displaced.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island after 1892), Baltimore, New Orleans, and other Atlantic and Gulf ports served Chicago-bound immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA and on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Pre-1906 naturalization records scattered across Cook County Circuit Court (IRAD), NARA Great Lakes Region, and federal courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls were destroyed in the courthouse fire.
- **Post-fire:** Property tax records held at the Cook County Assessor's office.
- **Substitute value:** City directories (Newberry Library) serve a similar substitute function for intercensal years, placing a person at a specific address.

### City directories
City directories for Chicago from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library. They are the primary substitute for missing pre-fire vital records and census off-years, placing individuals at specific addresses by year. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French and Spanish Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** La Louisiane claimed for France by La Salle, 1682; permanent settlement from 1699 (Fort Maurepas). New Orleans founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (capital of French and Spanish Louisiana throughout the colonial period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (French colonial era); Spanish Crown (after 1769)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place tools for this period. Colonial-era census rolls are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, sugar cane (after mid-century), timber; enslaved African labor was central to the plantation economy from the 1720s onward.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists; German settlers on the Côte des Allemands; Acadian (Cajun) refugees from Nova Scotia (arriving 1755–1785); Spanish colonists (after 1769); African enslaved persons (documented through Catholic registers and notarial records); free people of color; Native American peoples.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the Code Noir prohibited other religious practice in French Louisiana; this continued under Spanish rule.
- **Key historical events:** Permanent colony established 1699; New Orleans founded 1718; Seven Years' War ends 1763 — France cedes western Louisiana to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762) and eastern Louisiana to Britain (Treaty of Paris 1763); Spanish rule officially begins 1769; Britain retrocedes West Florida to Spain 1783; Louisiana retroceded to France 1800 (Treaty of San Ildefonso); Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi River basin.
- **1762–1763:** Louisiana was split. France ceded territory west of the Mississippi and the Isle of Orleans to Spain; Britain received territory east of the Mississippi (British West Florida). Records for eastern Louisiana after 1763 are under British jurisdiction until 1783.
- **1769:** Spanish governance officially begins in western Louisiana, replacing the French Superior Council with the Cabildo. Record language shifts from French toward Spanish.
- **1783:** Spain regains West Florida (eastern Louisiana) from Britain. Both banks of the lower Mississippi are now Spanish.
- **1800–1803:** Louisiana retroceded to France, then sold to the United States. Federal records begin after 1803.
- **Note:** Louisiana uses *parishes* (not counties) as its primary civil subdivision, a legacy of French and Spanish Catholic administration. Modern parish boundaries do not map directly onto colonial-era ecclesiastical or administrative divisions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the French or Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content and did not provide a specific start date for Louisiana civil registration. Civil registration began after the colonial era; researchers should confirm the date and level from the Louisiana Vital Records wiki page directly.
- **What exists for the colonial period:** Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the functional equivalent of civil vital records for 1699–1803. FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") begins in 1718, overlaps the entire colonial period, and is indexed with images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers. The Code Noir (Louisiana, 1724) required baptism of all enslaved persons, so church registers document enslaved as well as free persons.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) holds registers from 1720; original sacramental registers are with the Archdiocese of New Orleans. FamilySearch DGS 004330991 (264 images) covers 1720–1803 as browse-only images in French and Spanish.
- **Gaps:** DGS 004330991 is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image and requires ability to read French and/or Spanish. Pre-1718/1720 records are sparse or do not survive in accessible form.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only throughout the French and Spanish colonial period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons), marriages, burials, and confirmations. These are the genealogical backbone of the era.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") — **indexed + images** (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
  - FamilySearch DGS 004330991 — Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers, 1720–1803, 264 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
  - Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives — originals and volumes not yet digitized
- **Language:** French (1718–1769); French and Spanish (1769–1803). Researchers must be able to read both.
- **Note:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, the St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 are the oldest continuous Catholic registers in Louisiana.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** The French colonial administration conducted census rolls (dénombrements) from the early 1700s, listing households, enslaved persons, and livestock. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana is 1810 (post-colonial). Louisiana was not yet a state in 1790 or 1800, though a territorial census was taken in 1810.
- **Access:** Colonial census records at ANOM are largely physical-only or accessible through French archive portals; they are not represented in the FamilySearch collections returned for this period.
- **Digitization level:** Physical/archival (ANOM) for colonial-era censuses.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under French administration, the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) handled estate inventories, guardianships, contracts, court proceedings, and wills. Under Spanish rule (after 1769), the Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Both bodies generated probate and civil court records.
- **Testate records (wills):** Wills in the colonial era were notarized documents filed with the notary, not a separate court system.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) begins in 1756 and overlaps the late French and entire Spanish colonial period — indexed + images.
- **FamilySearch volume:** DGS 004330992 — French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699–1769, 149 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable, French and Spanish).
- **Where held:**
  - Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans — Superior Council records, partially digitized. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — notarial acts from the 1730s onward, including wills, marriage settlements, property transactions. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot (arpent) system — narrow strips running back from a river or bayou, not the metes-and-bounds or rectangular survey systems used in Anglo-American states.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown concessions (grants) issued by the Superior Council during the French colonial era; Spanish Crown grants issued by the Spanish colonial government after 1769. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgages, property sales.
- **Where held:**
  - American State Papers: Public Lands series — colonial grants confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase (available through Library of Congress and HathiTrust)
  - Louisiana State Land Office — colonial grants and land records
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — property transactions from the 1730s. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial administrative land records
- **Digitization level:** New Orleans Notarial Archives has partial digitization. American State Papers available online. ANOM holdings are largely physical/archival.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754–1763); American Revolution (Spanish Louisiana sided with the American colonies, 1779–1783); colonial conflicts with Native peoples.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls and service records for French colonial troops (Compagnies Franches de la Marine); Spanish colonial militia records; pension records.
- **Where held:**
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence — French colonial military records for Louisiana
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial military and administrative records (1769–1803)
  - NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — U.S. military records from 1803 onward only
  - Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) — U.S.-era military records; limited colonial coverage
- **Digitization level:** Physical/archival for the colonial era.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (established 1789 under Spanish colonial rule) is the oldest surviving cemetery. Earlier burials were in church grounds or unmarked graves.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external resource; coverage of colonial-era burials is limited.
- **Physical records:** Burial records for Catholic cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans. Some transcriptions exist for St. Louis Cemetery No. 1.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Moniteur de la Louisiane (founded 1794) is the earliest known Louisiana newspaper, published in both French and English during the late Spanish colonial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University libraries and the Louisiana Historical Society hold microfilm of early Louisiana newspapers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated resource but its coverage of 1790s Louisiana newspapers is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Content value:** Mostly limited to the final decade of the colonial period (1794–1803); obituaries and legal notices begin to appear. No newspapers exist for the bulk of the French colonial period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Colonial-era immigration was organized by the Company of the Indies (Compagnie des Indes) and the French and Spanish crowns. Colonists, transported prisoners, and "casket girls" (filles à la cassette) arrived in the 1710s–1730s. Acadian refugees arrived in waves 1755–1785.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals are irregular and largely in French administrative archives. Post-1803, standard U.S. passenger manifests apply at New Orleans.
- **Where held:**
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence — colonial-era arrival lists and emigration records from France
  - NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — passenger lists for New Orleans from 1820 onward (post-colonial)
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary colonial-era port of entry.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Colonial taxation:** Formal property tax records as a separate administrative series do not exist for the French colonial period. Property and capitation assessments appear within Superior Council proceedings and notarial records rather than as a standalone series.
- **Substitute value:** Estate inventories in probate collection 2078341 and DGS 004330992 list property values and can partially substitute for missing tax records.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, with records from the 1730s including marriage contracts, wills, emancipation papers (affranchissements), and property transactions. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **Slave records:** Under the Code Noir, baptisms of enslaved persons were mandatory and appear in Catholic registers. Emancipation papers appear in notarial records. Estate inventories list enslaved persons by name — both the Probate Records collection (2078341) and DGS 004330992 are relevant.
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM):** The primary repository for French colonial administrative records — census rolls, land grants, colonial correspondence, and military records — not available through FamilySearch. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (coll. 2078341) — indexed + images. DGS 004330991 (sacramental registers 1720–1803, 264 images, browse-only); DGS 004330992 (notarial acts/Superior Council 1699–1769, 149 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (limited colonial-era coverage) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records from 1803 onward; passenger manifests for New Orleans from 1820 | Free/in-person |
| Fold3 | U.S. military records (post-1803 for Louisiana) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for this place and period; both are detailed above — the result set was complete (no nextPageToken).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records (French colonial, 1699–1769), partially digitized | In-person; partial online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s (wills, marriage contracts, property transactions, emancipation papers) | In-person; partial online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Catholic sacramental registers from 1718; burial records | In-person / written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial census rolls, land concessions, administrative correspondence, military records | In-person; partial digitization via French archive portals |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative, military, and judicial records for Louisiana (1769–1803) | In-person; partial digitization via PARES portal |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-colonial territorial and state records; some colonial-era holdings | In-person / online |

## Records NOT online

- French colonial census rolls (dénombrements) — held at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; not in FamilySearch collections
- Spanish colonial census and administrative records — held at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; partially on PARES but not in FamilySearch
- Pre-1730 notarial acts — largely physical at New Orleans Notarial Archives
- French and Spanish colonial military muster rolls and service records — at ANOM and Archivo General de Indias respectively
- The bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives pre-1803 — partial in-person access; not comprehensively digitized
- Early Louisiana newspapers (pre-1794) — do not exist; none were published during most of the French colonial period

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified a mass destruction or loss event for colonial Louisiana records. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes and collection 1612905 are reported as present and accessible. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific record losses returned only generic content; researchers should consult the Louisiana Historical Center directly regarding the condition and completeness of the surviving Superior Council records.

## Research tips

- **Catholic parish registers are the core source.** There was no civil vital registration in colonial Louisiana. Every vital event — baptism, marriage, burial — went through the Catholic Church. Begin with FamilySearch collection 1612905 and DGS 004330991. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Dual-language reading is essential.** Records before 1769 are in French; after 1769 they shift toward Spanish, with French continuing in many parishes. Researchers need translation assistance or Latin/French/Spanish paleography skills.
- **The Superior Council and notarial records are the court and land system.** All civil legal business — contracts, wills, property sales, guardianships — went through the notary or the Superior Council. DGS 004330992 (149 images, browse-only) covers 1699–1769; the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the fuller set from the 1730s onward. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **For French colonial administrative records, go to ANOM in France.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence is the primary repository for census rolls, land concessions, and administrative correspondence not held in Louisiana. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **For Spanish colonial records (1769–1803), search Seville.** The Archivo General de Indias holds administrative, military, and judicial records for this period, accessible partially through the PARES portal.
- **The Code Noir documented enslaved persons.** The French Code Noir (Louisiana version, 1724) required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Their baptisms appear in parish registers alongside free persons. Emancipation papers (affranchissements) in notarial records are valuable for tracing free people of color.
- **Acadian families.** If tracing Acadian ancestry, the deportation from Nova Scotia beginning 1755 and resettlement in Louisiana through the 1780s is a critical migration event. Acadian families appear in church registers and notarial records in southern Louisiana from the 1760s onward.
- **Louisiana land is measured in arpents, not acres.** French long-lot (arpent) survey descriptions in land records are normal and do not indicate an error.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all returned only generic content** in this survey. Consult FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and its linked sub-articles for the most current guidance on specific record dates and availability.

Civil registration began after the colonial era; researchers should confirm the date and level from the Louisiana Vital Records wiki page directly.

FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") begins in 1718, overlaps the entire colonial period, and is indexed with images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers. The Code Noir (Louisiana, 1724) required baptism of all enslaved persons, so church registers document enslaved as well as free persons.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) holds registers from 1720; original sacramental registers are with the Archdiocese of New Orleans. FamilySearch DGS 004330991 (264 images) covers 1720–1803 as browse-only images in French and Spanish.
- **Gaps:** DGS 004330991 is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image and requires ability to read French and/or Spanish. Pre-1718/1720 records are sparse or do not survive in accessible form.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only throughout the French and Spanish colonial period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons), marriages, burials, and confirmations. These are the genealogical backbone of the era.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") — **indexed + images** (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
  - FamilySearch DGS 004330991 — Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers, 1720–1803, 264 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
  - Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives — originals and volumes not yet digitized
- **Language:** French (1718–1769); French and Spanish (1769–1803). Researchers must be able to read both.
- **Note:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, the St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 are the oldest continuous Catholic registers in Louisiana.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** The French colonial administration conducted census rolls (dénombrements) from the early 1700s, listing households, enslaved persons, and livestock. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana is 1810 (post-colonial). Louisiana was not yet a state in 1790 or 1800, though a territorial census was taken in 1810.
- **Access:** Colonial census records at ANOM are largely physical-only or accessible through French archive portals; they are not represented in the FamilySearch collections returned for this period.
- **Digitization level:** Physical/archival (ANOM) for colonial-era censuses.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under French administration, the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) handled estate inventories, guardianships, contracts, court proceedings, and wills. Under Spanish rule (after 1769), the Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Both bodies generated probate and civil court records.
- **Testate records (wills):** Wills in the colonial era were notarized documents filed with the notary, not a separate court system.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) begins in 1756 and overlaps the late French and entire Spanish colonial period — indexed + images.
- **FamilySearch volume:** DGS 004330992 — French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699–1769, 149 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable, French and Spanish).
- **Where held:**
  - Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans — Superior Council records, partially digitized. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — notarial acts from the 1730s onward, including wills, marriage settlements, property transactions. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot (arpent) system — narrow strips running back from a river or bayou, not the metes-and-bounds or rectangular survey systems used in Anglo-American states.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown concessions (grants) issued by the Superior Council during the French colonial era; Spanish Crown grants issued by the Spanish colonial government after 1769. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgages, property sales.
- **Where held:**
  - American State Papers: Public Lands series — colonial grants confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase (available through Library of Congress and HathiTrust)
  - Louisiana State Land Office — colonial grants and land records
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — property transactions from the 1730s. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial administrative land records
- **Digitization level:** New Orleans Notarial Archives has partial digitization. American State Papers available online. ANOM holdings are largely physical/archival.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754–1763); American Revolution (Spanish Louisiana sided with the American colonies, 1779–1783); colonial conflicts with Native peoples.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls and service records for French colonial troops (Compagnies Franches de la Marine); Spanish colonial militia records; pension records.
- **Where held:**
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence — French colonial military records for Louisiana
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial military and administrative records (1769–1803)
  - NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — U.S. military records from 1803 onward only
  - Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) — U.S.-era military records; limited colonial coverage
- **Digitization level:** Physical/archival for the colonial era.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (established 1789 under Spanish colonial rule) is the oldest surviving cemetery. Earlier burials were in church grounds or unmarked graves.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external resource; coverage of colonial-era burials is limited.
- **Physical records:** Burial records for Catholic cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans. Some transcriptions exist for St. Louis Cemetery No. 1.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Moniteur de la Louisiane (founded 1794) is the earliest known Louisiana newspaper, published in both French and English during the late Spanish colonial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University libraries and the Louisiana Historical Society hold microfilm of early Louisiana newspapers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated resource but its coverage of 1790s Louisiana newspapers is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Content value:** Mostly limited to the final decade of the colonial period (1794–1803); obituaries and legal notices begin to appear. No newspapers exist for the bulk of the French colonial period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Colonial-era immigration was organized by the Company of the Indies (Compagnie des Indes) and the French and Spanish crowns. Colonists, transported prisoners, and "casket girls" (filles à la cassette) arrived in the 1710s–1730s. Acadian refugees arrived in waves 1755–1785.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals are irregular and largely in French administrative archives. Post-1803, standard U.S. passenger manifests apply at New Orleans.
- **Where held:**
  - Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence — colonial-era arrival lists and emigration records from France
  - NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — passenger lists for New Orleans from 1820 onward (post-colonial)
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary colonial-era port of entry.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Colonial taxation:** Formal property tax records as a separate administrative series do not exist for the French colonial period. Property and capitation assessments appear within Superior Council proceedings and notarial records rather than as a standalone series.
- **Substitute value:** Estate inventories in probate collection 2078341 and DGS 004330992 list property values and can partially substitute for missing tax records.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, with records from the 1730s including marriage contracts, wills, emancipation papers (affranchissements), and property transactions. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **Slave records:** Under the Code Noir, baptisms of enslaved persons were mandatory and appear in Catholic registers. Emancipation papers appear in notarial records. Estate inventories list enslaved persons by name — both the Probate Records collection (2078341) and DGS 004330992 are relevant.
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM):** The primary repository for French colonial administrative records — census rolls, land grants, colonial correspondence, and military records — not available through FamilySearch. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (coll. 2078341) — indexed + images. DGS 004330991 (sacramental registers 1720–1803, 264 images, browse-only); DGS 004330992 (notarial acts/Superior Council 1699–1769, 149 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (limited colonial-era coverage) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records from 1803 onward; passenger manifests for New Orleans from 1820 | Free/in-person |
| Fold3 | U.S. military records (post-1803 for Louisiana) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for this place and period; both are detailed above — the result set was complete (no nextPageToken).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records (French colonial, 1699–1769), partially digitized | In-person; partial online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s (wills, marriage contracts, property transactions, emancipation papers) | In-person; partial online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Catholic sacramental registers from 1718; burial records | In-person / written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial census rolls, land concessions, administrative correspondence, military records | In-person; partial digitization via French archive portals |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative, military, and judicial records for Louisiana (1769–1803) | In-person; partial digitization via PARES portal |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-colonial territorial and state records; some colonial-era holdings | In-person / online |

## Records NOT online

- French colonial census rolls (dénombrements) — held at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; not in FamilySearch collections
- Spanish colonial census and administrative records — held at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; partially on PARES but not in FamilySearch
- Pre-1730 notarial acts — largely physical at New Orleans Notarial Archives
- French and Spanish colonial military muster rolls and service records — at ANOM and Archivo General de Indias respectively
- The bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives pre-1803 — partial in-person access; not comprehensively digitized
- Early Louisiana newspapers (pre-1794) — do not exist; none were published during most of the French colonial period

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified a mass destruction or loss event for colonial Louisiana records. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes and collection 1612905 are reported as present and accessible. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific record losses returned only generic content; researchers should consult the Louisiana Historical Center directly regarding the condition and completeness of the surviving Superior Council records.

## Research tips

- **Catholic parish registers are the core source.** There was no civil vital registration in colonial Louisiana. Every vital event — baptism, marriage, burial — went through the Catholic Church. Begin with FamilySearch collection 1612905 and DGS 004330991. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Dual-language reading is essential.** Records before 1769 are in French; after 1769 they shift toward Spanish, with French continuing in many parishes. Researchers need translation assistance or Latin/French/Spanish paleography skills.
- **The Superior Council and notarial records are the court and land system.** All civil legal business — contracts, wills, property sales, guardianships — went through the notary or the Superior Council. DGS 004330992 (149 images, browse-only) covers 1699–1769; the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the fuller set from the 1730s onward. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants
- **For French colonial administrative records, go to ANOM in France.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence is the primary repository for census rolls, land concessions, and administrative correspondence not held in Louisiana. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **For Spanish colonial records (1769–1803), search Seville.** The Archivo General de Indias holds administrative, military, and judicial records for this period, accessible partially through the PARES portal.
- **The Code Noir documented enslaved persons.** The French Code Noir (Louisiana version, 1724) required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Their baptisms appear in parish registers alongside free persons. Emancipation papers (affranchissements) in notarial records are valuable for tracing free people of color.
- **Acadian families.** If tracing Acadian ancestry, the deportation from Nova Scotia beginning 1755 and resettlement in Louisiana through the 1780s is a critical migration event. Acadian families appear in church registers and notarial records in southern Louisiana from the 1760s onward.
- **Louisiana land is measured in arpents, not acres.** French long-lot (arpent) survey descriptions in land records are normal and do not indicate an error.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all returned only generic content** in this survey. Consult FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and its linked sub-articles for the most current guidance on specific record dates and availability.
